q: Under the shared responsibility model, which of the following is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility, no matter the service model (IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS)?
options: Physical security of the provider's datacenters
Patching the virtualization hypervisor
The customer's data and the management of user identities and access
Maintaining the provider's backbone network
explain: Regardless of service model, the customer always owns its data, its user accounts, and who can access what. Physical security, the hypervisor, and the provider's backbone network always belong to the cloud provider.

q: A hospital runs cloud services on infrastructure dedicated solely to its own use, hosted in its own datacenter. This is an example of a:
options: Public cloud
Private cloud
Community cloud
Multicloud
explain: A private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, whether hosted on-premises or by a third party. Public clouds are shared by many customers, community clouds are shared by organizations with common concerns, and multicloud means using more than one public provider.

q: A company keeps sensitive workloads on-premises but runs its customer-facing website with a public cloud provider, with the two environments integrated and managed together. Which term describes this setup?
options: Hybrid cloud
Public cloud
Community cloud
Private cloud
explain: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises or private resources with public cloud services in one coordinated environment. Pure public or pure private describe only one side, and community cloud is shared by multiple organizations with shared concerns.

q: Several regional banks share a cloud environment built specifically for financial institutions with common regulatory requirements. This is an example of a:
options: Public cloud
Hybrid cloud
Community cloud
Multicloud
explain: A community cloud is shared by several organizations with common concerns, such as regulatory requirements in the same industry. Public clouds serve the general public, hybrid mixes deployment models, and multicloud means using multiple public providers.

q: What is the difference between a Type 1 and a Type 2 hypervisor?
options: Type 1 runs only on ARM processors; Type 2 runs only on x86 processors
Type 1 is open source; Type 2 is always commercial software
Type 1 runs virtual machines inside containers; Type 2 runs containers inside virtual machines
Type 1 runs directly on the physical hardware; Type 2 runs on top of a host operating system
explain: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware, which is why providers use it in datacenters. A Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor runs as an application on top of a host OS, which adds overhead. The distractors invent processor, licensing, and container distinctions that do not define hypervisor types.

q: A cloud administrator notices dozens of idle virtual machines that nobody owns or remembers creating, and the monthly bill keeps climbing. This situation is called:
options: Resource pooling
VM sprawl
Elasticity
Thin provisioning
explain: VM sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of virtual machines that are forgotten, idle, or unowned, wasting money and complicating management. Resource pooling is the provider-side sharing of resources, elasticity is scaling with demand, and thin provisioning allocates storage on demand — none describe uncontrolled VM growth.

q: A cloud administrator needs storage for a database server's boot volume that supports high IOPS and appears to the operating system as a local disk. Which storage type is the BEST fit?
options: Block storage
Object storage
File storage
Archive storage
explain: Block storage presents raw volumes that an OS formats and mounts like a local disk, with the low latency databases need. Object storage is accessed via APIs and cannot be a boot disk, file storage is for shared folders, and archive storage is for rarely accessed data with slow retrieval.

q: A media company must store millions of user-uploaded videos and photos, accessed over the web from anywhere. Which storage type is the BEST fit?
options: Block storage volumes attached to VMs
A relational database
Object storage
Network-attached tape drives
explain: Object storage is designed for massive amounts of unstructured data like media, accessed over HTTP-based APIs from anywhere. Block storage is for VM disks, a relational database is for structured data, and tape is for offline archival — none suit web-scale media delivery.

q: A company keeps seven years of compliance backups that are almost never read but must be retained. Which storage tier is the MOST cost-effective choice?
options: Hot tier with provisioned IOPS
Cool tier with instant access
A high-performance file share
Archive tier with delayed retrieval
explain: Archive tiers offer the lowest cost per gigabyte for data that is rarely accessed, trading slower retrieval times for savings — ideal for long-term compliance retention. Hot and cool tiers cost more for access speed the company does not need, and a high-performance file share is the most expensive option of all.

q: A cloud network has outgrown the 4,094-network limit of VLANs and needs isolated tenant networks that can span multiple datacenters. Which technology addresses this?
options: Subnetting with longer prefixes
VXLAN
Static routing
Network address translation
explain: VXLAN is a network overlay that encapsulates Layer 2 frames in UDP, supporting around 16 million isolated segments across Layer 3 boundaries — solving both the VLAN ID limit and the multi-datacenter problem. Longer prefixes do not raise the VLAN limit, static routing does not isolate tenants, and NAT only translates addresses.

q: A cloud administrator deploys a load balancer in front of three web servers. Which statement BEST describes what the load balancer does?
options: Distributes incoming traffic across the servers and stops sending traffic to unhealthy ones
Encrypts all data stored on the web servers' disks
Automatically patches the operating systems of the web servers
Compresses database backups to save storage costs
explain: A load balancer distributes client requests across healthy targets and uses health checks to route around failed servers, improving availability and performance. Encryption at rest, OS patching, and backup compression are unrelated functions handled by other services.

q: A company migrates its application to the cloud and users report they cannot reach it by its hostname, though the IP address works. Which service should the administrator check FIRST?
options: The load balancer's health checks
The backup retention policy
DNS
The hypervisor version
explain: When an IP works but a hostname does not, the problem is name resolution — DNS records likely were not updated or have not propagated after the migration. Load balancer health checks affect availability rather than name resolution, and backups and hypervisor versions are unrelated to hostname lookup.

q: Monitoring shows a virtual machine consistently uses only 8% of its CPU and 20% of its memory, yet it is sized and priced as a large instance. What should the cloud administrator do?
options: Add more memory to improve performance
Migrate the workload to a different region
Enable detailed monitoring on the instance
Right-size the instance to a smaller, cheaper size
explain: Right-sizing matches the instance to actual utilization, eliminating waste on an overprovisioned VM. Adding memory makes the waste worse, changing regions does not fix sizing, and detailed monitoring only observes the problem without solving it.

q: What is the difference between high availability and fault tolerance?
options: They are two names for exactly the same design
High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy and fast recovery; fault tolerance keeps a system running with zero interruption even if a component fails
Fault tolerance is only for databases; high availability is only for web servers
High availability requires on-premises hardware; fault tolerance requires the cloud
explain: High availability uses redundancy so a failure triggers quick failover with minimal downtime, while fault tolerance uses techniques like lockstep processing so the workload continues with no interruption at all. They are related but distinct goals, apply to any workload type, and work in any environment.

q: A company's disaster recovery plan states it can lose no more than 15 minutes of data and must be back online within 4 hours of an outage. Which terms describe these two requirements?
options: 15 minutes is the RPO; 4 hours is the RTO
15 minutes is the RTO; 4 hours is the RPO
15 minutes is the MTTR; 4 hours is the MTBF
Both values together define the SLA
explain: RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time — here, 15 minutes of transactions. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable downtime — here, 4 hours. MTTR/MTBF measure repair times and failure intervals, and an SLA is a service commitment, not these objectives.

q: A company moves its on-premises application to cloud VMs with no code changes, simply to get out of its datacenter quickly. Which migration strategy is this?
options: Rearchitect
Replatform
Rehost
Repurchase
explain: Rehost — 'lift and shift' — moves the application as-is to cloud infrastructure with no code changes, making it the fastest migration path. Replatform makes small optimizations, rearchitect rebuilds the application for the cloud, and repurchase replaces it with a SaaS product.

q: A team moves a monolithic application to the cloud and rewrites it as microservices using managed cloud services. Which migration strategy is this?
options: Rehost
Replatform
Retain
Rearchitect
explain: Rearchitect (refactor) means fundamentally redesigning the application to be cloud-native, such as breaking a monolith into microservices. Rehost moves it unchanged, replatform makes only minor tweaks, and retain means leaving it where it is.

q: During migration planning, the team discovers an old reporting application that nobody has used in two years. Which of the '6 Rs' should they apply to it?
options: Rehost
Retire
Replatform
Repurchase
explain: Retire means decommissioning applications that are no longer needed instead of wasting effort migrating them. Rehost, replatform, and repurchase all assume the application is worth keeping in some form, which does not apply to an unused system.

q: What is the difference between scalability and elasticity in cloud computing?
options: Scalability is the ability to increase capacity; elasticity is the ability to automatically scale up AND down as demand changes
Elasticity is only for storage; scalability is only for compute
They are identical terms used by different cloud providers
Scalability requires manual effort; elasticity is impossible in a private cloud
explain: Scalability means the system can handle more load by adding resources, while elasticity adds automatic scaling in both directions — growing under load and shrinking when demand drops so you stop paying for idle capacity. The terms are not provider-specific, apply to all resource types, and elasticity works in private clouds too.

q: A cloud provider hosts multiple customers' virtual machines on the same physical server. This is an example of:
options: A dedicated host
A community cloud
Multitenancy
A hybrid deployment
explain: Multitenancy is when multiple customers (tenants) share the same underlying physical infrastructure, isolated logically by the hypervisor. A dedicated host is the opposite — hardware reserved for one customer. Community cloud and hybrid deployment describe deployment models, not resource sharing.

q: A cloud administrator wants the company's application to survive the failure of an entire datacenter. Which design BEST achieves this?
options: Deploying multiple VMs in the same availability zone
Enabling detailed monitoring on all instances
Increasing the instance sizes
Deploying across multiple availability zones or regions with replication
explain: Availability zones and regions are isolated failure domains, so spreading workloads and replicating data across them survives a full datacenter loss. Multiple VMs in one zone still share that zone's fate, monitoring only observes failures, and larger instances do nothing for datacenter-level resilience.

q: A company's web application has users on five continents who complain about slow page loads. Which cloud architecture component would BEST improve their experience?
options: A larger database instance
A content delivery network (CDN)
A longer backup retention period
More verbose application logging
explain: A CDN caches static content at edge locations close to users worldwide, cutting latency for a global audience. A bigger database helps query speed but not geographic latency, longer retention affects backups rather than performance, and verbose logging would slow things down further.

q: A storage administrator provisions a 10 TB volume for a VM, but the cloud platform only consumes physical disk space as data is actually written. This is an example of:
options: Thin provisioning
Thick provisioning
RAID 10
Storage tiering
explain: Thin provisioning allocates virtual capacity up front but consumes physical storage only as data is written, improving utilization. Thick provisioning reserves all physical space immediately, RAID 10 is a disk redundancy scheme, and storage tiering moves data between performance tiers.

q: A team deploys a new application version to a second production environment, tests it with live traffic switched over at once, and keeps the old environment ready to switch back instantly. This is a:
options: Canary deployment
Rolling deployment
In-place upgrade
Blue-green deployment
explain: In a blue-green deployment, the new version (green) runs alongside the current one (blue) and traffic switches over at once, with instant rollback by switching back. Canary releases to a small subset first, rolling updates replace instances gradually, and in-place upgrades modify the existing environment with no standby to revert to.

q: A team wants to release a risky new feature to 5% of users first, monitor for errors, then gradually expand to everyone. Which deployment strategy should they use?
options: Blue-green deployment
Canary deployment
Big-bang deployment
Rehost migration
explain: A canary deployment releases to a small subset of users first so problems surface with limited blast radius before a wider rollout. Blue-green switches all traffic at once, big-bang releases to everyone simultaneously with no safety net, and rehost is a migration strategy, not a deployment technique.

q: What is the difference between automation and orchestration?
options: Automation performs a single task without human intervention; orchestration coordinates multiple automated tasks into an ordered workflow
Orchestration is manual; automation is scripted
They are the same thing with different names
Automation is only for deployments; orchestration is only for backups
explain: Automation handles one task (e.g., provisioning a VM), while orchestration strings many automated tasks together in the right order with dependencies and error handling (e.g., a full environment build). Orchestration is not manual, the terms are not synonyms, and both apply far beyond deployments or backups.

q: A cloud administrator needs to provision a virtual network, three VMs, a load balancer, and a database in the correct order with dependencies handled automatically. Which approach is BEST?
options: Log in to each console and create the resources manually in sequence
Write a single script that creates everything with no dependency handling
Use an orchestration template that defines the resources and their dependencies
Email the provider's support team to build it
explain: An orchestration template defines all resources and their dependencies so the platform provisions them in the correct order automatically and repeatably. Manual creation is slow and error-prone, a script without dependency handling fails when ordering matters, and support teams do not build customer environments.

q: What is the fundamental difference between a container and a virtual machine?
options: Containers require a hypervisor; virtual machines do not
Virtual machines are only for Windows; containers are only for Linux
Containers share the host operating system's kernel; virtual machines each run their own full guest operating system
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
explain: Containers virtualize at the OS level and share the host kernel, making them lightweight and fast to start, while each VM carries a full guest OS on a hypervisor. The distractors reverse the hypervisor relationship, invent OS restrictions, or claim the terms are synonyms.

q: A company runs dozens of containerized microservices that must scale, restart on failure, and be updated without downtime. Which platform is designed for this?
options: A hypervisor
Kubernetes
A version control system
A relational database
explain: Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that schedules containers, restarts failed ones, scales them, and performs rolling updates. A hypervisor manages VMs rather than containers, version control manages code, and a database stores data — none orchestrate containers.

q: A team defines its entire cloud environment — networks, VMs, and storage — in version-controlled text files that can be deployed identically every time. This practice is called:
options: Infrastructure as code
Technical debt
Configuration drift
Shadow IT
explain: Infrastructure as code (IaC) defines infrastructure in machine-readable files, giving repeatable, versioned, reviewable deployments. Technical debt is accumulated shortcut cost, configuration drift is environments diverging over time, and shadow IT is unsanctioned technology use.

q: A company replaces its servers with fresh builds from a template for every update instead of patching running servers. This approach is called:
options: Mutable infrastructure
Configuration drift
Immutable infrastructure
In-place upgrade
explain: Immutable infrastructure never modifies running servers — every change produces a new image or build that replaces the old one, eliminating drift and making rollbacks trivial. Mutable infrastructure is the opposite, configuration drift is the problem immutable infrastructure avoids, and in-place upgrades patch existing servers.

q: A deployment fails because the application servers were created before the database they depend on. What would have PREVENTED this ordering problem?
options: A larger instance size for the application servers
More verbose logging
A longer maintenance window
Declaring resource dependencies in the deployment template
explain: Declaring dependencies in the template tells the orchestrator to create the database before the application servers that need it. Larger instances, verbose logging, and longer windows do nothing to enforce creation order.

q: A team maintains a standardized VM image with the OS, security agents, and baseline configuration preinstalled, used for every new deployment. This is called a:
options: Snapshot backup
Golden image
Container registry
Canary build
explain: A golden image is a standardized, hardened template used as the baseline for deployments, ensuring consistency. A snapshot is a point-in-time backup of a specific disk, a container registry stores container images, and a canary build is a limited test release.

q: Over time, an administrator makes manual tweaks to a production server so it no longer matches the infrastructure-as-code template. This problem is called:
options: Configuration drift
Elasticity
Immutable infrastructure
Blue-green deployment
explain: Configuration drift is when running systems diverge from their defined templates through manual changes, breaking repeatability. Elasticity is scaling with demand, immutable infrastructure prevents drift by replacing rather than modifying, and blue-green is a deployment strategy.

q: A company replaces all its web servers at once with the new version, accepting brief downtime for simplicity. Compared to a rolling update, the main RISK of this approach is:
options: Higher licensing costs
Longer deployment scripts
A single failed deployment takes down the entire service with no working version left
Increased storage consumption
explain: Replacing everything at once (recreate/big-bang) means a bad release leaves no healthy instances serving traffic, whereas rolling updates keep old instances running until new ones prove healthy. Licensing, script length, and storage are not the distinguishing risks.

q: A CI/CD pipeline produces compiled application packages that must be stored securely with version history before deployment. Where should they be stored?
options: On the build server's local disk
An artifact repository
In the DNS zone file
In a spreadsheet
explain: An artifact repository stores versioned build outputs securely with metadata, so pipelines deploy the exact tested package. A build server's local disk is fragile and unshared, DNS stores name records, and a spreadsheet cannot store binaries.

q: An application works in development but fails in production. The environments were built manually months apart. What is the MOST likely root cause category?
options: Environment parity — the environments differ
Insufficient CPU on the developer's laptop
The wrong cloud region was chosen
Too many users
explain: When code works in one environment but not another, the environments themselves differ — versions, configuration, or dependencies (a parity problem), common with manually built environments. The developer's laptop CPU is irrelevant to production, region choice rarely causes dev/prod differences, and user load is a separate symptom.

q: A product team wants to merge a new feature into the codebase but keep it hidden from users until marketing approves the launch. Which technique allows this?
options: Deleting the feature branch
A longer maintenance window
Feature flags
Disabling monitoring
explain: Feature flags (toggles) let code ship to production in a dormant state and be enabled later without redeploying, decoupling deployment from release. Deleting the branch discards the work, maintenance windows do not hide features, and disabling monitoring only blinds the team.

q: Before a major production deployment, the team documents the exact steps to restore the previous version if something goes wrong. This is called a:
options: Post-mortem
Service-level agreement
Threat model
Rollback plan
explain: A rollback plan defines how to revert to the last known-good state if a deployment fails, and it must exist before the change — not be invented during an outage. A post-mortem happens after incidents, an SLA is a service commitment, and a threat model analyzes security risks.

q: An infrastructure template declares the desired end state — 'three web servers behind a load balancer' — and the tool figures out how to achieve it. This is an example of a:
options: Imperative script
Declarative template
Manual runbook
Backup policy
explain: Declarative templates state what the infrastructure should look like and let the tool determine the steps, making them idempotent and easier to reason about. Imperative scripts list step-by-step commands, a runbook is a manual procedure, and a backup policy governs data protection.

q: A web application needs to handle ten times its normal traffic during a sale event, then return to normal afterward. Which scaling approach is MOST cost-effective?
options: Permanently buying the largest available servers
Scaling out (adding instances) with auto-scaling, then scaling back in
Rewriting the application as a monolith
Disabling the load balancer
explain: Scaling out with auto-scaling adds instances for the traffic spike and removes them afterward, so the company only pays for extra capacity while it is needed. Permanently oversized servers waste money year-round, rewriting the architecture does not address temporary spikes, and disabling the load balancer would break distribution.

q: A deployment template is applied twice to the same environment and the second run makes no changes because everything already matches. This property is called:
options: Idempotency
Elasticity
Multitenancy
Obfuscation
explain: Idempotency means applying an operation multiple times produces the same result as applying it once — a cornerstone of reliable infrastructure as code. Elasticity is scaling with demand, multitenancy is sharing infrastructure between customers, and obfuscation is hiding code logic.

q: A cloud administrator configures an alert that fires when average CPU exceeds 85% for 10 minutes. Which statement BEST describes the relationship between monitoring and alerting here?
options: Monitoring and alerting are the same thing
Alerting replaces the need for monitoring
Monitoring is only for security events
Monitoring collects the CPU metrics; alerting notifies the team when a threshold is breached
explain: Monitoring continuously collects metrics, while alerting acts on them by notifying humans when thresholds are crossed — they are complementary, not identical. Alerting without monitoring has no data to act on, and monitoring covers performance and availability, not just security.

q: To detect abnormal behavior, a team first records normal CPU, memory, and network patterns for two weeks. What is this reference measurement called?
options: A snapshot
A baseline
A benchmark SLA
A backup
explain: A baseline captures normal operating behavior so deviations and anomalies stand out. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk, an SLA is a service commitment, and a backup is data protection — none serve as a behavioral reference.

q: Storage usage has grown 15% every quarter for a year. The administrator uses this trend to request budget for additional capacity next year. This activity is called:
options: Capacity planning
Incident response
Configuration drift
Penetration testing
explain: Capacity planning uses historical trends to forecast future resource needs so growth never causes an outage. Incident response handles active problems, configuration drift is environments diverging from templates, and penetration testing probes security weaknesses.

q: A company keeps three copies of its backups: one on local disk, one on cloud object storage, and one on tape stored offsite. This follows which backup best practice?
options: The 6 Rs of migration
Incremental forever
The 3-2-1 rule
Immutable infrastructure
explain: The 3-2-1 rule calls for 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite — exactly what this company does. The 6 Rs are migration strategies, incremental-forever is a backup method, and immutable infrastructure is about server builds.

q: A full backup runs Sunday night. Monday through Saturday, only data that changed since Sunday is backed up. Which backup type runs on weekdays?
options: Differential backup
Mirror backup
Synthetic backup
Incremental backup
explain: Incremental backups capture only data changed since the last backup of any type, making weekday runs fast and small. Differential backups capture everything changed since the last full backup, growing larger each day. Mirror and synthetic are not the standard terms for this schedule.

q: A company has an RPO of 4 hours. Which backup schedule BEST meets this objective?
options: One full backup per month
Backups at least every 4 hours
One backup per year before audit season
Backups only when an administrator remembers
explain: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss window, so backups must occur at least as often as the RPO — every 4 hours or less. Monthly, yearly, or ad-hoc backups would lose far more than 4 hours of data in a failure.

q: A cloud administrator must apply critical OS patches to production VMs. Which approach MINIMIZES risk to the business?
options: Patch during an approved maintenance window after testing in a non-production environment
Patch all production servers immediately with no testing
Never patch cloud VMs because the provider handles it
Patch only when users complain about performance
explain: Testing patches in a lower environment first, then applying them during a maintenance window, catches bad patches before they hit production while limiting user impact. Untested immediate patching risks outages, guest OS patching is the customer's job under shared responsibility, and waiting for complaints is not a strategy.

q: An administrator spends hours logging into individual servers to read logs during every incident. Which solution would MOST improve this process?
options: Disabling logging to reduce noise
Requiring longer passwords
Centralized log aggregation
Deleting logs older than one day
explain: Centralized log aggregation collects logs from all systems into one searchable location, dramatically speeding up incident investigation and correlation. Disabling or deleting logs destroys evidence, and password length is unrelated to log analysis efficiency.

q: A compliance framework requires the company to retain security logs for one year. Which control addresses this?
options: A load balancer
An auto-scaling policy
A backup schedule for databases
A log retention policy
explain: A log retention policy defines how long logs are kept and when they are securely deleted, directly satisfying the one-year requirement. Load balancers distribute traffic, auto-scaling adjusts capacity, and database backups protect data — none govern log retention.

q: A load balancer keeps sending traffic to a web server that is returning errors. Which mechanism should have removed it from the pool?
options: The backup schedule
Health checks
DNS caching
Log rotation
explain: Health checks probe each target's responsiveness, and the load balancer stops routing to targets that fail them. Backup schedules protect data, DNS caching affects name resolution, and log rotation manages disk space — none detect unhealthy servers.

q: An administrator configures auto-scaling to add web servers when average CPU exceeds 70% for 5 minutes. What is this an example of?
options: A scaling policy based on a performance metric
A backup retention rule
A firewall rule
An encryption standard
explain: This is a metric-based scaling policy: a CloudWatch-style metric (CPU) crossing a threshold triggers scaling action. Backup rules govern data copies, firewall rules govern traffic, and encryption standards govern data protection — unrelated to scaling.

q: A company needs disaster recovery that keeps a minimal copy of its environment running in another region, ready to scale up quickly after a failure. This strategy is called:
options: Backup and restore
Multi-site active-active
Pilot light
Tape rotation
explain: Pilot light keeps a minimal, always-on footprint (like a pilot flame) in the recovery region that can rapidly scale to full production. Backup-and-restore has no running footprint and recovers slowest, active-active runs full capacity in both sites at full cost, and tape rotation is an offline backup practice.

q: A company has a disaster recovery plan but has never tested it. What is the BIGGEST risk?
options: The plan costs too much to store
Auditors will ask too many questions
The documentation is too long
The plan may fail when actually needed because untested assumptions and outdated steps go unnoticed
explain: An untested DR plan is a hope, not a plan — failover testing reveals broken steps, stale credentials, and wrong assumptions before a real disaster. Storage cost and document length are trivial concerns, and auditors asking questions is a symptom, not the core risk.

q: A finance team cannot tell which department's VMs are driving the cloud bill. Which practice would BEST solve this?
options: Deleting all VMs monthly
Resource tagging
Disabling monitoring
Using a single shared admin account
explain: Resource tags (e.g., Department=Marketing) let costs be allocated and reported per team, project, or environment. Deleting VMs destroys workloads, disabling monitoring removes visibility, and a shared admin account worsens accountability rather than improving cost tracking.

q: A developer's script accidentally launches 500 large VMs, causing a massive bill. Which preventive control would have LIMITED the damage?
options: Service quotas/limits on the account
A longer password policy
More verbose logging
A bigger backup window
explain: Service quotas cap how many resources an account can provision, so a runaway script hits the limit instead of the budget. Password policies, logging verbosity, and backup windows do nothing to constrain resource creation.

q: During a 2 AM outage, the on-call engineer follows a pre-written, step-by-step procedure to restore the database. This document is called a:
options: Post-mortem
Threat model
Runbook
Risk register
explain: A runbook is a documented, repeatable procedure for routine operations and known incident scenarios, so the fix does not depend on one person's memory at 2 AM. A post-mortem is written after incidents, a threat model analyzes security risks, and a risk register tracks organizational risks.

q: Before applying a firewall rule change in production, the team submits the change for review, schedules it, and documents a backout plan. This process is called:
options: Continuous integration
Penetration testing
Social engineering
Change management
explain: Change management governs how modifications are proposed, reviewed, approved, scheduled, and rolled back, reducing the risk of change-caused outages. Continuous integration merges code frequently, penetration testing probes security, and social engineering manipulates people — none govern production changes.

q: A company worries that if a physical disk is stolen from a datacenter, its data could be read. Which control BEST addresses this risk?
options: A longer password policy
Encryption at rest
A web application firewall
Disabling unused ports
explain: Encryption at rest protects stored data so a stolen disk yields only unreadable ciphertext without the keys. Password policies govern authentication, a WAF protects web traffic, and disabling ports reduces network attack surface — none protect data on a stolen disk.

q: Data traveling between a user's browser and a cloud application must be protected from eavesdropping on the network. Which control provides this?
options: Encryption in transit (TLS)
Disk encryption
Database backups
File integrity monitoring
explain: Encryption in transit, typically TLS, protects data as it moves across networks from interception. Disk encryption protects stored data, backups protect against loss, and file integrity monitoring detects unauthorized changes — none secure data in motion.

q: A security policy requires encryption keys to be replaced every 90 days. This practice is called:
options: Key escrow
Key stretching
Key rotation
Keylogging
explain: Key rotation periodically replaces cryptographic keys, limiting how much data any single compromised key can expose. Key escrow stores keys with a third party, key stretching strengthens passwords for hashing, and keylogging is a malicious attack technique.

q: A junior administrator is granted full access to all cloud resources 'just in case.' Which security principle does this violate?
options: Defense in depth
Separation of duties
Encryption at rest
Least privilege
explain: Least privilege requires granting only the permissions needed for the job — full access 'just in case' vastly exceeds that. Defense in depth is layered security, separation of duties splits critical tasks between people, and encryption at rest protects stored data.

q: A company wants employees to log in once with their corporate credentials and gain access to multiple cloud applications without re-entering passwords. Which technology enables this?
options: A virtual private network
Federation / single sign-on (SSO)
Disk encryption
A jump server
explain: Federation with single sign-on lets one identity provider authenticate users for many applications, so one login grants access everywhere. A VPN secures remote network access, disk encryption protects stored data, and a jump server is a hardened admin access host.

q: An attacker steals an employee's password but cannot access the cloud console because a code from the employee's phone is also required. Which control stopped the attacker?
options: Multifactor authentication (MFA)
A firewall
Encryption at rest
A honeypot
explain: Multifactor authentication requires two or more independent factors (password plus phone code), so a stolen password alone is insufficient. A firewall filters network traffic, encryption at rest protects stored data, and a honeypot is a decoy system — none block a login with a stolen password the way MFA does.

q: Before deploying a new VM image, the team removes unnecessary services, disables default accounts, and applies security baselines. This process is called:
options: Load balancing
Auto-scaling
Hardening
Snapshotting
explain: Hardening reduces a system's attack surface by removing unneeded software, disabling risky defaults, and applying secure baselines. Load balancing distributes traffic, auto-scaling adjusts capacity, and snapshotting captures a point-in-time disk copy.

q: A company places its public web servers in a separate network segment from its internal databases, with a firewall between them. This design is called:
options: A flat network
A mesh topology
A VPN tunnel
Network segmentation (DMZ)
explain: Network segmentation isolates systems into zones (like a DMZ for public-facing servers) so a compromise in one segment does not reach the others. A flat network has no segmentation, a mesh topology describes interconnection patterns, and a VPN tunnel encrypts a point-to-point connection.

q: A cloud firewall rule allows inbound HTTPS from the internet to a web server and automatically allows the return traffic. This behavior describes a:
options: Stateless packet filter
Stateful firewall
Air gap
Honeypot
explain: A stateful firewall tracks connection state, so return traffic for an allowed session passes automatically. A stateless filter judges each packet in isolation and would need explicit rules for return traffic. An air gap is physical isolation, and a honeypot is a decoy.

q: What is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
options: An IDS detects and alerts on suspicious activity; an IPS can also actively block it
An IPS only works on-premises; an IDS only works in the cloud
An IDS encrypts traffic; an IPS decrypts it
There is no difference
explain: An intrusion detection system monitors and raises alerts, while an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can drop malicious traffic automatically. Both work in any environment, neither performs encryption, and the detect-vs-prevent distinction is fundamental.

q: A company labels its data as Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted, with handling rules for each level. This practice is called:
options: Data deduplication
Data compression
Data classification
Data fragmentation
explain: Data classification categorizes information by sensitivity so appropriate protections (encryption, access controls, retention) apply to each level. Deduplication removes redundant copies, compression shrinks data size, and fragmentation splits data — none involve sensitivity labeling.

q: A company wants to prevent employees from emailing customer Social Security numbers to personal accounts. Which technology is designed for this?
options: A load balancer
A content delivery network
An intrusion detection system
Data loss prevention (DLP)
explain: Data loss prevention inspects outbound content and blocks or quarantines transmissions that match sensitive-data policies, such as SSNs leaving the organization. Load balancers distribute traffic, CDNs cache content, and IDS detects intrusions — none police outbound sensitive data.

q: During a compliance audit, the auditor asks for evidence that only authorized users accessed the financial system last quarter. Which source BEST provides this evidence?
options: The marketing team's slide deck
Access and authentication logs
The company's mission statement
The backup retention schedule
explain: Access and authentication logs record who accessed what and when, providing the auditable evidence of authorized use. Marketing slides, mission statements, and backup schedules contain no access evidence.

q: A customer running VMs on a public cloud asks who is responsible for patching the hypervisor. Under the shared responsibility model, the answer is:
options: The cloud provider
The customer
Whoever configured the VM first
No one; hypervisors do not need patching
explain: The provider owns and patches the virtualization layer in every service model — the customer never touches the hypervisor. The customer patches guest operating systems and applications, not the underlying host infrastructure.

q: A developer hard-codes a database password in application source code that is committed to a shared repository. What is the BEST remediation?
options: Make the repository public so everyone can review the code
Email the password to the team for safekeeping
Store the credential in a secrets manager and reference it at runtime
Write the password on a sticky note instead
explain: A secrets manager stores credentials encrypted with access controls and audit logging, and the application retrieves them at runtime — removing secrets from code entirely. Publishing the repository, emailing passwords, or sticky notes all worsen exposure.

q: Users suddenly receive browser warnings that the company's cloud application certificate is invalid. The MOST likely cause is:
options: The load balancer is misconfigured
The database is full
The backup window was missed
An expired TLS certificate
explain: Browsers warn about invalid certificates most commonly when the TLS certificate has expired — a routine operational failure fixed by renewal. A misconfigured load balancer would more likely cause outages than certificate warnings, and database or backup issues do not trigger browser certificate errors.

q: A company designs its network so no user or device is trusted by default, requiring verification for every access request regardless of location. This approach is called:
options: Perimeter security
Zero trust
Security through obscurity
Implicit trust
explain: Zero trust eliminates implicit trust based on network location — every request is authenticated and authorized. Perimeter security trusts the inside of the network, security through obscurity relies on secrecy rather than controls, and implicit trust is the opposite of this model.

q: How often should vulnerability scans run to be MOST effective in a cloud environment with frequent deployments?
options: Continuously or on a frequent automated schedule
Once, when the system is first deployed
Only after a breach is discovered
Never; the provider handles all scanning
explain: Frequent automated scanning keeps pace with constant cloud change, catching new vulnerabilities quickly. One-time scans go stale immediately, post-breach scanning is too late, and while providers secure their infrastructure, customers must scan their own workloads under shared responsibility.

q: A security incident is suspected on a cloud VM. What is the FIRST step of the incident response process?
options: Delete the VM to destroy the malware
Notify the media
Preparation — follow the pre-established incident response plan
Ignore it and hope it resolves itself
explain: Incident response begins with preparation: the organization should already have a plan defining roles, communication, and procedures, which the team then follows. Deleting the VM destroys forensic evidence, media notification is not a first step, and ignoring incidents guarantees escalation.

q: Developers merge their code into a shared repository several times a day, and each merge triggers an automated build and test run. This practice is called:
options: Waterfall development
Big-bang integration
Manual testing
Continuous integration (CI)
explain: Continuous integration means frequently merging code with automated builds and tests, catching integration problems within hours instead of weeks. Waterfall is a sequential phase-based model, big-bang integration delays merging until the end, and manual testing lacks the automation that defines CI.

q: What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
options: They are identical practices
Continuous delivery keeps every change in a deployable state with a manual release decision; continuous deployment automatically releases every passing change to production
Continuous deployment is manual; continuous delivery is automatic
Continuous delivery only applies to mobile apps
explain: Continuous delivery ensures code is always release-ready but leaves the go-live decision to a human, while continuous deployment automates the release itself so every passing change reaches production. The distractors reverse the definitions or invent a mobile-only restriction.

q: A pipeline automatically builds code, runs unit tests, runs security scans, then deploys to staging. These automated phases are called pipeline:
options: Stages
Firewalls
Backups
Tickets
explain: Pipeline stages are the sequential phases (build, test, scan, deploy) that code passes through on its way to production. Firewalls filter traffic, backups protect data, and tickets track work items — none describe pipeline phases.

q: A team needs version control where developers can work offline and merge changes later, with full history on every machine. Which type of system fits?
options: A centralized spreadsheet
A shared network folder
A distributed version control system (e.g., Git)
Email attachments
explain: Distributed version control (Git) gives every developer a full local copy of the repository history, enabling offline work and flexible merging. Spreadsheets, shared folders, and email provide no versioning, branching, or merge capabilities.

q: A developer creates an isolated copy of the codebase to build a new feature without affecting the main branch. This is called a:
options: Fork bomb
Merge conflict
Production hotfix
Feature branch
explain: A feature branch isolates new work from the main branch until it is tested and reviewed, then merged back. A fork bomb is a denial-of-service attack, a merge conflict is what branching helps avoid, and a production hotfix is an emergency change, not an isolation technique.

q: Before merging a feature branch, a senior developer reviews the code changes for bugs and standards compliance. This practice is called:
options: A post-mortem
Code review (pull request review)
Load testing
Capacity planning
explain: Code review via pull requests catches defects and enforces standards before code reaches the main branch. A post-mortem analyzes past incidents, load testing measures performance under stress, and capacity planning forecasts resource needs.

q: A pipeline runs automated tests on every commit, catching a bug minutes after it was introduced. What is the MAIN benefit of this shift-left testing?
options: Defects are found when they are cheapest and fastest to fix
It eliminates the need for production monitoring
It guarantees the code has no bugs at all
It replaces the need for code reviews
explain: Finding defects minutes after introduction — when the code is fresh in the developer's mind — makes fixes dramatically cheaper than discovering them in production. Automated tests do not replace monitoring or reviews, and no testing guarantees zero bugs.

q: A team manages cloud infrastructure with a tool that uses declarative configuration files and tracks state, applying only the changes needed. Which tool fits this description?
options: A packet sniffer
A text editor
Terraform (infrastructure as code)
A backup agent
explain: Terraform is a declarative infrastructure-as-code tool: you describe the desired state and it plans and applies only the necessary changes, tracking everything in state. Packet sniffers analyze traffic, text editors edit files, and backup agents copy data — none manage infrastructure declaratively.

q: An infrastructure script can be run any number of times and always produces the same end state without errors or duplicates. This property is called:
options: Elasticity
Multitenancy
Obfuscation
Idempotency
explain: Idempotency means repeated application yields the same result as a single application — essential for reliable automation and configuration management. Elasticity is scaling with demand, multitenancy is shared infrastructure, and obfuscation hides code logic.

q: A bad deployment reaches production. Because every infrastructure and application change is version-controlled, the team restores the previous version in minutes. Which DevOps practice made this fast recovery possible?
options: Manual server configuration
Version-controlled deployments enabling quick rollback
Disabling all monitoring
Deleting old backups
explain: Version-controlling infrastructure and application artifacts means the last known-good state is always one revert away, enabling fast rollback. Manual configuration is slow and error-prone, disabling monitoring blinds the team, and deleting backups destroys recovery options.

q: Users report an application is down. According to standard troubleshooting methodology, what should the administrator do FIRST?
options: Identify the problem: gather information, symptoms, and scope before making changes
Reboot all servers immediately
Restore from last night's backup
Upgrade the application to the latest version
explain: Methodical troubleshooting starts with identifying the problem — symptoms, scope, and recent changes — because acting blindly (reboots, restores, upgrades) can worsen the situation or destroy evidence. The remaining steps (theory, testing, resolution, documentation) all depend on this first understanding.

q: A new VM cannot reach the internet, but other VMs on the same subnet can. The administrator has verified the VM's OS firewall is off. What should they check NEXT?
options: The backup retention policy
The DNS server's log retention
The VM's security group rules and route table
The hypervisor's licensing
explain: When sibling VMs work but one does not, the issue is specific to that VM — most likely its security group blocking outbound traffic or a missing/incorrect route. Backup policies, DNS log retention, and hypervisor licensing do not explain one VM's isolated connectivity failure.

q: An application becomes sluggish every day at 9 AM. Which troubleshooting step would BEST confirm the cause?
options: Reinstall the operating system
Delete the application logs
Add more servers immediately
Review performance metrics and logs around 9 AM to identify the bottleneck
explain: A recurring time-based slowdown calls for examining metrics and logs during the window to find the actual bottleneck (CPU, memory, I/O, scheduled job) before acting. Reinstalling, deleting logs, or adding servers treats symptoms blindly and may miss the real cause entirely.

q: A deployment pipeline fails at the deploy stage with no clear error in the console. Where should the administrator look FIRST for details?
options: The company's social media feed
The detailed deployment and application logs
The physical security camera footage
The employee handbook
explain: Deployment and application logs contain the detailed error output that consoles summarize or omit — the first place to diagnose a pipeline failure. Social media, camera footage, and handbooks contain no deployment diagnostics.

q: An application that worked yesterday now rejects all logins with 'authentication failed,' though no passwords changed. Which is the MOST likely cause?
options: An expired certificate or token used in the authentication flow
The office printer running out of toner
A full backup completing successfully
The load balancer being too efficient
explain: Sudden, universal authentication failures with unchanged passwords point to an expired certificate, token, or secret in the auth chain — a classic operational lapse. Printer toner, successful backups, and load balancer efficiency have no bearing on authentication.

q: After migrating a workload to a new cloud region, users report the application URL no longer resolves. The servers are running and reachable by IP. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The VMs need more memory
The backup schedule is wrong
DNS records still point to the old region's addresses
The hypervisor needs patching
explain: When IPs work but names do not after a migration, DNS records were not updated to the new region — the most common migration oversight. Memory, backup schedules, and hypervisor patching do not affect name resolution.

q: A VM's performance degrades gradually over several weeks until it becomes unresponsive. Logs show the system disk at 99% capacity. What is the MOST likely root cause?
options: A DDoS attack
An expired SSL certificate
A misconfigured load balancer
Disk exhaustion from unmanaged log growth
explain: Gradual degradation ending in unresponsiveness with a full disk is the classic signature of unmanaged log growth filling the volume. A DDoS attack causes sudden traffic floods, an expired certificate causes TLS errors rather than slowdowns, and a misconfigured load balancer affects traffic distribution, not disk space.

q: A system that ran fine for months breaks immediately after a scheduled patch window. What should the administrator investigate FIRST?
options: The weather at the datacenter location
The recent change — review what the patch modified and consider rolling it back
The CEO's email settings
Whether users need training
explain: When failure follows a change, the change is the prime suspect — reviewing what the patch touched and rolling back tests that theory fastest. Weather, executive email, and user training are unrelated to a post-patch failure.

q: An administrator cannot reproduce an intermittent error on demand. Which approach would BEST help capture it?
options: Enable detailed logging and monitoring to capture data the next time it occurs
Ignore it since it is intermittent
Reboot the server every hour
Delete all logs to start fresh
explain: Intermittent issues require instrumentation — detailed logging and monitoring in place so the next occurrence is captured with full context. Ignoring it guarantees recurrence, hourly reboots mask the cause, and deleting logs destroys the very evidence needed.

q: An administrator has spent three hours on an outage without progress and the SLA breach is approaching. What is the appropriate NEXT step?
options: Keep trying the same fix repeatedly
Go home and try again tomorrow
Escalate to senior engineers or vendor support per the escalation policy
Delete the affected systems and rebuild from memory
explain: Escalation policies exist precisely for this: when progress stalls and impact grows, bringing in senior engineers or vendor support is the professional response. Repeating a failed fix wastes time, abandoning the outage violates duty, and rebuilding from memory without a plan risks data loss.

q: After resolving a major outage, the team holds a meeting to discuss what happened, why, and how to prevent recurrence — without blaming individuals. This is called a:
options: Performance review
Blameless post-mortem (lessons-learned review)
Sales retrospective
Budget planning session
explain: A blameless post-mortem documents the timeline, root cause, and preventive actions while focusing on systems rather than individuals, so people report honestly. Performance reviews evaluate people, sales retrospectives cover deals, and budget sessions cover spending — none improve reliability.

q: An administrator is unsure whether a connectivity problem is in the application, the OS network stack, or the cloud network. Which technique isolates the faulty layer?
options: Reinstalling everything at once
Divide and conquer — test each layer independently, starting from the bottom (e.g., ping, then port, then application)
Increasing all timeouts to maximum
Disabling the firewall permanently
explain: Divide and conquer tests each layer independently (network reachability, then port connectivity, then application response), narrowing the fault to one layer. Reinstalling everything is destructive guesswork, raising timeouts masks problems, and permanently disabling the firewall trades security for a shortcut.

q: A visual-effects studio runs nightly video-rendering jobs that take 4 hours, can be interrupted at any time, and automatically resume from checkpoints. Which compute purchasing option is MOST cost-effective for these jobs?
options: On-demand instances for maximum flexibility
Three-year reserved instances
Spot (preemptible) instances
Dedicated hosts
explain: Spot instances sell spare capacity at deep discounts precisely for interruptible, fault-tolerant workloads like checkpointed batch rendering — an interruption just resumes later. On-demand charges full price for flexibility these jobs do not need, reserved instances demand a steady-use commitment that nightly jobs cannot fully consume, and dedicated hosts are the priciest option, meant for licensing or compliance isolation rather than savings.

q: An e-commerce application must route requests for /api/* to backend services and all other requests to web servers, terminating TLS at the load balancer. Which load balancer type is required?
options: A Layer 7 (application) load balancer
A Layer 4 (network) load balancer
DNS round-robin
A VPN gateway
explain: A Layer 7 load balancer inspects HTTP content such as URL paths and host headers, enabling path-based routing and TLS termination. A Layer 4 balancer only sees TCP/UDP and cannot route by URL — the classic exam trap. DNS round-robin has no health awareness or content routing, and a VPN gateway provides private connectivity, not traffic distribution.

q: A data science team wants to run a machine-learning training job that takes 6 hours on the company's function-as-a-service (serverless) platform. What is the fundamental problem with this plan?
options: Serverless functions cannot access the internet
FaaS platforms enforce maximum execution timeouts (typically minutes), so long-running jobs do not fit
Functions cannot be triggered by events
Serverless requires the team to manage the underlying servers
explain: Function-as-a-service platforms cap execution duration (commonly around 15 minutes), making them the wrong home for multi-hour training jobs, which belong on VMs, containers, or batch services. The distractors invert reality: functions are event-triggered, can reach the internet, and the entire point of serverless is that the provider manages the servers.

q: A German healthcare SaaS provider must guarantee patient data never leaves the European Union due to regulatory requirements. Which architectural decision BEST satisfies this?
options: Serve all content through a global CDN with edge caching
Deploy in a US region to reduce costs
Enable cross-region replication to every available region
Deploy in EU regions and restrict data storage and replication to those regions
explain: Data residency is satisfied by choosing compliant regions and constraining storage, backups, and replication to them. A global CDN caches copies worldwide and cross-region replication deliberately spreads data — both violate residency. Deploying in the US for cost ignores the regulatory constraint entirely.

q: A web application stores shopping carts in each server's memory and uses sticky sessions. When auto-scaling terminates instances, users lose their carts. What architectural change fixes this?
options: Move session state to an external distributed cache or database so application servers are stateless
Disable auto-scaling
Use larger instances
Store sessions on each server's local disk
explain: Externalizing session state makes application servers stateless, so any instance can serve any request and terminated instances lose nothing. Disabling auto-scaling sacrifices elasticity, larger instances still lose memory state on termination, and local disks share the same fate as memory when the instance goes away.

q: A production database runs at 95% CPU because of heavy daytime reporting queries, while transactional writes stay light. Which approach offloads the reporting load with the LEAST risk and cost?
options: Scale up the primary database to a larger instance
Rewrite all reports as stored procedures
Direct reporting queries to read replicas
Move the database to archive storage
explain: Read replicas absorb read-heavy analytics traffic, relieving the primary without downtime or a costly resize. Scaling up is expensive and may require downtime, stored procedures still execute on the overloaded primary, and archive storage is for rarely accessed cold data — not live reporting.

q: A retailer runs steady workloads in its own datacenter but needs ten times its normal capacity for two weeks each December. Which approach BEST handles the peak?
options: Buy ten times the hardware to keep year-round
Cloud bursting: extend into the public cloud for the peak period only
Permanently migrate everything to the cloud
Throttle customers during December
explain: Cloud bursting adds public-cloud capacity just for the seasonal spike, converting a two-week need from wasteful capital expense into pay-as-you-go operating expense. Buying year-round hardware for a two-week peak strands capital, a full migration is overkill for a temporary need, and throttling customers sacrifices revenue.

q: A company needs disaster recovery with an RTO of 2 hours and an RPO of 1 hour, but cannot afford active-active. Which strategy BEST fits?
options: Backup and restore
Pilot light
Cold site with tape
Warm standby
explain: Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but running copy of the environment that can scale to full production quickly, hitting a 2-hour RTO at moderate cost. Backup-and-restore and cold sites rebuild from scratch — too slow for 2 hours. Pilot light keeps only minimal core services (often just the database), making a 2-hour full recovery unlikely, while active-active meets the RTO but breaks the budget.

q: A company must protect critical cloud objects against accidental deletion and automatically move older versions to cheaper storage. Which combination achieves both?
options: Object versioning plus lifecycle policies
Versioning alone
CDN caching
RAID across disks
explain: Versioning preserves overwritten or deleted objects for recovery, while lifecycle policies transition aging versions to lower-cost tiers automatically. Versioning without lifecycle keeps every version in expensive hot storage, a CDN caches content for delivery rather than protecting it, and RAID is block-level disk redundancy — not object-level protection.

q: An enterprise has 20 virtual networks that need controlled interconnection with all traffic inspected by a central firewall. Which design avoids the complexity of a full peering mesh?
options: Full mesh peering between every network
Routing through the public internet
Hub-and-spoke with a transit gateway or hub network
One flat network with no segmentation
explain: Hub-and-spoke centralizes routing and inspection through a transit hub, scaling linearly instead of the n-squared connection explosion of full-mesh peering. Internet routing exposes internal traffic, and a flat network abandons segmentation entirely.

q: Two virtual networks in the same cloud provider and region need private, low-latency connectivity. Which option is BEST?
options: A site-to-site VPN over the public internet
Virtual network peering
Public IP addresses with firewall rules
A dedicated Direct Connect/ExpressRoute circuit
explain: Peering connects the networks privately over the provider backbone with low latency and no internet traversal. A VPN adds unnecessary encryption overhead and internet dependence, public IPs needlessly expose resources, and dedicated circuits are for on-premises connections — not cloud-to-cloud in the same region.

q: Database servers need to download OS patches from the internet but must never be directly reachable from the internet. Which design satisfies both requirements?
options: Assign public IP addresses and rely on security groups
Remove all internet connectivity
Use a bastion host for patch downloads
Place them in a private subnet with a NAT gateway
explain: A NAT gateway in a private subnet permits outbound-initiated traffic (like patch downloads) while blocking all unsolicited inbound connections. Public IPs make the servers directly reachable, removing connectivity breaks patching, and a bastion host provides interactive admin sessions — not a path for automated package downloads.

q: A factory's robotic arms need sub-10-millisecond responses to sensor data, but the round trip to the nearest cloud region is 80 milliseconds. Which approach solves this?
options: Edge computing: process sensor data locally at the factory
Use larger instances in the cloud region
Add a CDN
Buy more internet bandwidth
explain: Edge computing places processing physically near the data source, defeating the speed-of-light latency that no cloud tuning can fix. Larger instances do not shorten distance, a CDN caches static content rather than processing sensor streams, and bandwidth increases throughput — not latency.

q: A baseline workload runs 24/7 at steady utilization and is expected to continue for two years. Which purchasing model is MOST cost-effective?
options: On-demand instances
Spot instances
Reserved (committed-use) instances
Serverless pay-per-request
explain: Reserved or committed-use pricing trades a one- to three-year commitment for a steep discount — ideal for predictable, steady-state workloads. On-demand charges full price for flexibility the workload does not need, spot instances can be reclaimed and suit only interruptible work, and serverless fits spiky event-driven loads rather than constant baselines.

q: Enterprise software licensed per physical CPU socket requires the customer to prove which physical hosts run the workloads. Which compute option provides this?
options: Default shared tenancy
Spot instances
Serverless functions
Dedicated hosts
explain: Dedicated hosts allocate whole physical servers to one customer, giving the host visibility that socket-based (BYOL) license compliance demands. Shared tenancy hides placement, spot instances are transient shared capacity, and serverless abstracts hardware entirely — none can prove host-level placement.

q: A startup deploys two web servers, one database server with no replica, and a managed multi-AZ load balancer. Which single component failure causes a full application outage?
options: Either web server
The database server
One load balancer node
One CDN edge location
explain: The database is the single point of failure: with no replica or failover, its loss halts the application. Either web server is survived by the other, the managed load balancer spans availability zones, and a CDN has many edge locations — redundancy the database lacks.

q: During flash sales, order spikes overwhelm the payment service and orders are dropped. Which pattern lets the web tier accept orders faster than the payment service can process them?
options: A message queue between the web tier and the payment service to buffer and smooth the load
Permanently larger payment servers
Synchronous direct calls with aggressive retries
Disabling auto-scaling
explain: A message queue decouples the tiers: the web tier enqueues orders instantly while consumers process them at a sustainable rate, absorbing bursts without loss. Permanently oversized servers waste money most of the year, synchronous calls propagate spikes directly to the fragile service, and disabling auto-scaling removes elasticity rather than adding resilience.

q: A team must update 10 web servers with zero downtime but has only one production environment — no spare for a parallel swap. Which strategy fits?
options: Recreate: replace all servers at once
Rolling update: replace a few servers at a time while the rest serve traffic
Big-bang cutover during business hours
Manual in-place upgrades server by server with the site offline
explain: Rolling updates replace instances in small batches, keeping enough healthy capacity to serve users throughout — the standard zero-downtime approach with a single environment. Recreating everything at once causes downtime and risks total failure, big-bang cutovers have no safety net, and offline manual upgrades are the least reliable option.

q: A product team wants to show half of users checkout design X and half design Y, then compare conversion rates before choosing. Which technique is this?
options: Canary deployment
Blue-green deployment
Feature flag kill switch
A/B testing
explain: A/B testing splits traffic between variants to compare a business metric — here, conversion. A canary release validates the safety of one new version on a small audience rather than comparing two designs, blue-green switches all traffic at once, and a kill switch disables a feature rather than measuring it.

q: A team tags every container image ':latest'. A bad build deploys automatically and they cannot roll back because the tag already points at the bad image. Which practice prevents this?
options: Deploy :latest faster to outrun bad builds
Tag images with unique immutable identifiers such as the Git commit SHA or build number
Store images only on the build server
Deploy containers manually
explain: Immutable, unique tags let deployments pin an exact known-good image and roll back precisely; ':latest' is a moving target that destroys that ability. Deploying faster or manually does not fix unrepeatable references, and build-server storage is fragile and unshared.

q: A deployment must rename a database column with zero downtime while old and new application versions briefly run side by side. Which migration pattern works?
options: Expand and contract: add the new column, migrate data, support both columns in code, then remove the old one
Drop the old column first, then deploy
Take the application offline for the migration
Rename the column in place during deployment
explain: Expand/contract keeps the schema backward-compatible so both app versions work during the transition, removing the old column only after all instances run the new code. Dropping first breaks the old version instantly, in-place renames break running instances, and offline migrations violate the zero-downtime requirement.

q: A pipeline rebuilds the application separately for dev, test, and production, and a defect appears only in production. Which practice eliminates build-to-build variance?
options: Rebuild each environment with extra-verbose logging
Deploy from developers' laptops
Skip the test environment
Build once and promote the same immutable artifact through every environment
explain: Promoting one tested artifact through every environment guarantees production runs exactly what was tested. Rebuilding per environment invites compiler, dependency, or timing differences — the classic 'works in test' trap. Laptop deploys and skipping test reduce rigor rather than adding consistency.

q: An administrator must apply configuration to 200 Linux VMs without installing any management agents on them. Which approach fits?
options: An agent-based pull configuration tool
An agentless push tool over SSH, such as Ansible
Manual SSH sessions to each VM
Rebuild all VMs from a new image
explain: Ansible's agentless push model configures machines over SSH with nothing installed on targets — ideal when agents are prohibited. Agent-based tools require pre-installed agents, manual SSH does not scale to 200 machines, and rebuilding is drastic overkill for configuration.

q: A team deploys the same microservice to dev, test, and prod Kubernetes clusters with different replica counts and resource limits per environment. Which tool packages the manifests with per-environment values?
options: The same static YAML applied everywhere with kubectl
The Docker image
A Helm chart with per-environment values files
A separate Git branch with copied YAML per environment
explain: Helm charts templatize Kubernetes manifests so one chart deploys everywhere with environment-specific values files. Static YAML cannot vary per environment, a Docker image packages the application — not its Kubernetes manifests — and copied YAML per branch drifts out of sync.

q: A regulated company requires a manager's approval before any production deployment, enforced automatically rather than by email. Where does this control belong?
options: As an approval gate in the deployment pipeline
In an email thread
After the deployment completes
On the monitoring dashboard
explain: Pipeline approval gates technically enforce the sign-off before production code moves — auditable and unbypassable. Email approvals are unenforceable and unversioned, post-deployment review is too late, and dashboards observe rather than gate.

q: Immediately after a production deployment, the team runs a small set of critical-path checks: homepage loads, login works, checkout completes. These are called:
options: Load tests
Unit tests
Penetration tests
Smoke tests
explain: Smoke tests are a quick critical-path pass confirming the deployment is fundamentally working. Load tests measure performance under stress, unit tests validate code in isolation before deployment, and penetration tests probe security — none are the post-deploy sanity check.

q: Every configuration change — even a database connection string — forces the team to rebuild its container images. What should change?
options: Bake more configuration into the images
Externalize configuration via environment variables or config maps, separate from the image
Use larger base images
Hardcode one configuration per environment
explain: Externalized configuration lets the same immutable image run anywhere with environment-supplied values — a core twelve-factor principle. Baking config in forces rebuilds for trivial changes, larger images do not help, and hardcoding per environment multiplies images to maintain.

q: New VMs must install the monitoring agent and join the domain automatically on first boot, with per-instance settings like hostname. Which mechanism does this?
options: Manual login and configuration after creation
A golden image alone
User data / cloud-init bootstrap scripts
Emailed setup instructions
explain: User data with cloud-init executes first-boot customization, including per-instance values a static golden image cannot provide. Manual setup does not scale, a golden image alone cannot inject instance-specific settings, and emailed instructions are not automation.

q: A global SaaS deploys a new version to one region, monitors it for a day, then proceeds region by region. This strategy is called:
options: A staged (regional) rollout
A big-bang deployment
Recreating all regions simultaneously
A rollback
explain: Staged regional rollouts limit blast radius: a bad release affects one region before it is caught, rather than the global fleet. Big-bang and simultaneous recreation expose everything at once, and a rollback is the recovery action — not the release strategy.

q: A deployment template committed to Git contains a database password in plaintext. A teammate suggests Base64-encoding it. What is the BEST response?
options: Base64-encode the password in the template
Split the password across two files
Restrict Git repository access and keep the plaintext
Parameterize the secret and pull it from a secrets manager at deploy time
explain: Secrets must be referenced from a secrets manager at deploy time so they never live in templates or version control. Base64 is encoding — not encryption — and fools no one; splitting plaintext is still plaintext, and access restrictions do not fix a secret already committed to history.

q: One container consumes all of a Kubernetes node's memory, starving neighboring containers and causing evictions. Which setting prevents this?
options: Adding more nodes
Setting resource requests and limits on each container
Using larger container images
Disabling the scheduler
explain: Resource limits cap how much CPU and memory a container may consume, while requests inform scheduling decisions — together they stop noisy-neighbor evictions. More nodes without limits just relocates the hogging, image size is irrelevant, and disabling the scheduler breaks orchestration.

q: A deployment migrates the database schema forward, then corrupts data in a way reverting the code cannot fix. What is the appropriate recovery?
options: Roll back the code anyway
Delete the database and restore nothing
Roll forward with a hotfix, since rollback cannot undo the data change
Wait for the next scheduled release
explain: Rollback only restores code — once data or schema has moved forward irreversibly, the fix must also move forward via a corrective deployment. Rolling back code against migrated data typically breaks the application worse, deleting data destroys the business, and waiting prolongs the outage.

q: Before applying an infrastructure-as-code template, the team wants to preview exactly which resources will be created, modified, or destroyed. Which capability provides this?
options: A dry run / plan / what-if analysis
Deploying and watching what happens
Reading the template aloud in a meeting
Taking a backup first
explain: Plan/what-if/dry-run modes compute the exact change set before anything is modified, catching destructive surprises safely. Deploy-and-watch discovers mistakes in production, meetings do not execute templates, and backups mitigate rather than preview.

q: A team runs a PaaS web app and needs zero-downtime releases with instant rollback, without managing two full environments. Which PaaS feature fits?
options: Scaling up the single production instance
Uploading files directly over FTP
Deleting and redeploying the app
Deployment slots with swap
explain: Deployment slots provide a staging slot inside the PaaS that swaps with production instantly — blue-green-style safety without managing duplicate infrastructure. Scaling up does not version releases, FTP uploads offer no atomicity or rollback, and delete-and-redeploy guarantees downtime.

q: A contract promises customers 99.9% monthly uptime with service credits, while engineering internally targets 99.95% to keep a safety buffer. Which terms describe these two numbers?
options: Both are SLAs
99.9% is the SLA; 99.95% is the SLO
Both are SLIs
99.9% is the SLO; 99.95% is the SLA
explain: The SLA is the contractual commitment to customers, backed by credits; the SLO is the stricter internal target providing buffer before the contract is breached; the SLI is the actual measurement. The distractors swap the terms or collapse all three into one.

q: A service burns through its entire quarterly error budget by week six. According to SRE practice, what should happen next?
options: Ship features faster to make up time
Delete the SLO
Freeze feature releases and invest in reliability until the budget recovers
Reduce monitoring sensitivity to stop burning budget
explain: Error budgets exist to balance velocity against reliability: an exhausted budget means engineering effort shifts to stability until reliability is restored. Shipping faster deepens the hole, deleting the SLO abandons the commitment, and dulling monitoring hides the problem instead of fixing it.
