Passwords and backup frequency do not constrain an authenticated attacker's delete calls.

q: An API accepts bearer tokens without checking their signature or expiry, and forged tokens are now accessing other users' data. Which validation MUST the API perform?
options: Accepting any well-formed token
Checking only the username claim
Validating the token signature, expiry, and audience on every request
Using longer tokens
explain: Signature validation proves the token was issued by the trusted authority and is unmodified, while expiry and audience checks bound its lifetime and scope — skipping any of these invites forgery. Accepting well-formed tokens trusts attacker-crafted input (the trap), username-only checks ignore authenticity entirely, and token length is not a security property.

q: Attackers hammer the login endpoint with thousands of credential-stuffing attempts per minute. Which control BEST blunts this attack?
options: Requiring longer passwords
Rate limiting and account lockout on the login endpoint, ideally backed by a WAF
Hiding the login page URL
Adding more login servers
explain: Rate limiting throttles automated guessing and lockouts neutralize persistent targeting of one account — the direct counter to credential stuffing. Longer passwords do not slow an attacker's attempt rate (the trap), obscurity fails against scanning, and more servers just absorb more attack traffic.

q: The sole cloud administrator is locked out during an outage and no one else can access the console. Which account strategy PREVENTS this single point of failure?
options: One shared admin password used daily
Disabling MFA for administrators
Break-glass emergency accounts with sealed, audited credentials used only for recovery
No backup access — security first
explain: Break-glass accounts provide audited emergency access whose sealed credentials are only unsealed during genuine lockouts — availability without daily standing privilege. Shared daily passwords destroy accountability, disabling MFA weakens every login, and no backup access converts any lockout into a full outage.

q: An audit finds ex-employees still hold cloud access months after leaving, and contractors carry permissions far beyond their tasks. Which process PREVENTS this drift?
options: Never reviewing access
Adding more administrators
Trusting HR emails alone
Periodic access recertification where managers confirm each person's entitlements are still needed
explain: Recertification forces regular, accountable review of who holds what, catching stale and excessive access systematically. Never reviewing guarantees accumulation, more admins multiply the problem, and HR emails alone miss contractor scope creep and missed offboarding steps.

q: Employees keep uploading company data to unsanctioned file-sharing SaaS apps that IT has never vetted. Which solution gives visibility and control over this shadow IT?
options: A cloud access security broker (CASB) discovering SaaS usage and enforcing data policies
Blocking all internet access
Ignoring it until a breach occurs
Antivirus on laptops
explain: A CASB discovers which cloud apps are in use and applies data-loss and access policies to them — purpose-built for shadow IT. Blocking all internet is unworkable, ignoring it invites the breach, and laptop antivirus cannot see or govern cloud-to-cloud data flows.

q: A regulated product needs planned releases with isolated release branches and a formal hotfix process for production issues. Which branching strategy fits?
options: GitFlow with develop, release, and hotfix branches
No branches — everyone commits to main
Trunk-based development with no release branches
Emailing code patches
explain: GitFlow's release and hotfix branches match regulated, planned-release workflows where production fixes must be isolated and traceable. Branchless main cannot isolate a hotfix (the trap for trunk enthusiasts), and emailed patches abandon version control entirely.

q: A bad commit was already pushed and pulled by the team. Which Git operation undoes it WITHOUT rewriting shared history?
options: git reset --hard on the shared branch
git revert, which creates a new commit undoing the change
Deleting the repository and re-cloning
Force-pushing an older commit
explain: git revert adds a compensating commit, preserving the full shared history everyone already has — safe for published work. reset --hard and force-push are the traps: they rewrite history and strand every teammate's clone. Deleting the repo destroys history rather than correcting it.

q: Developers push directly to main, bypassing review, and broken code reaches production. Which repository control enforces the review process?
options: Trusting developers to remember
Deleting the main branch
Protected branches requiring pull-request reviews and passing status checks before merge
Creating more branches
explain: Branch protection technically blocks merges until reviews approve and CI checks pass — the process becomes unbypassable. Trust is not enforcement, deleting main destroys the workflow, and more branches without protection just multiply the unguarded paths.

q: A library must be built and tested against three operating systems and two language runtimes — six combinations. Which CI feature runs all combinations efficiently?
options: One manual build per combination
Dropping platform support
Sequential shell scripts
A build matrix fanning out parallel jobs per combination
explain: A build matrix declaratively fans out every OS/runtime combination in parallel, with results aggregated per combination. Manual builds do not scale, dropping platforms abandons customers, and sequential scripts turn six combinations into six times the wait.

q: A team wants tests to drive design decisions and catch regressions within minutes of introduction. Which development practice embodies this?
options: Test-driven development: writing failing tests first, then the code to pass them
Testing only after release
Manual testing by a separate team weeks later
Skipping tests to ship faster
explain: TDD's red-green-refactor loop makes tests the design specification and runs them continuously, so regressions surface minutes after introduction. Post-release or weeks-later testing finds bugs long after the context is cold, and skipping tests trades speed today for incidents tomorrow.

q: The team must find the breaking point of a new checkout service beyond expected peak load. Which performance test type does this?
options: Load testing at expected peak
Stress testing beyond peak to find the failure point
Soak testing for 72 hours
Unit testing
explain: Stress testing deliberately exceeds expected capacity to discover where and how the system breaks — the stated goal. Load testing is the trap: it validates behavior at expected levels but never finds the cliff. Soak tests endurance over time, and unit tests never exercise system capacity.

q: A memory leak only manifests after 48 hours of continuous uptime and never appears in short test runs. Which test type would have caught it?
options: Unit tests
Smoke tests
Soak (endurance) testing running the system under load for an extended period
Static code analysis alone
explain: Soak testing sustains load for hours or days specifically to expose gradual degradation like leaks and resource exhaustion. Unit and smoke tests run too briefly to accumulate the leak, and static analysis rarely catches runtime growth patterns.

q: A file parser crashes on malformed input, and the team suspects more edge cases lurk. Which automated testing technique systematically feeds unexpected inputs to find crashes?
options: Manual code review
Happy-path testing only
Ignoring edge cases
Fuzz testing with generated malformed and random inputs
explain: Fuzzing bombards the parser with millions of malformed, random, and boundary inputs to trigger the crashes humans would never think to try. Manual review cannot enumerate input space, happy-path tests avoid the dangerous inputs by definition, and ignoring edge cases is how the crashes reached production.

q: Dependencies drift for months until a critical vulnerability forces a painful mass upgrade. Which automation keeps dependencies fresh incrementally?
options: Automated dependency update tools (Dependabot/Renovate) opening small, testable pull requests
Never updating dependencies
One massive manual upgrade per year
Forking every dependency
explain: Automated updaters propose small, individually testable version bumps continuously, so upgrades stay routine instead of traumatic. Never updating accumulates the vulnerability debt (the trap), annual mega-upgrades are the painful event being avoided, and forking everything creates a maintenance burden larger than the original problem.

q: Builds behave differently on each developer's machine — 'works on my machine' — because dependency versions float. Which file guarantees identical dependency versions everywhere?
options: Floating version ranges in the manifest
A lockfile pinning every transitive dependency to an exact version
No dependency declarations
Always using the newest releases
explain: A lockfile records the exact resolved version of every dependency, so CI, staging, and every laptop install byte-identical trees. Floating ranges are the cause of the drift (the trap), missing declarations make builds unrepeatable, and newest-always guarantees tomorrow's build differs from today's.

q: Someone changed infrastructure in the cloud console, and the IaC templates no longer match reality. Which capability detects this divergence?
options: Ignoring the console changes
Deleting the IaC templates
Drift detection comparing live infrastructure against the declared desired state
Manually auditing every resource monthly
explain: Drift detection continuously reconciles actual versus declared state, surfacing console changes as actionable findings before they cause incidents. Ignoring drift lets reality and templates diverge until the next apply surprises everyone, deleting templates surrenders to ClickOps, and monthly manual audits are too slow and too toilsome.

q: A GitOps workflow keeps all manifests in Git, but secrets cannot sit in plaintext in the repository. Which approach stores secrets safely in Git?
options: Plaintext secrets in the Git repo
Emailing secrets to the cluster admin
Skipping GitOps for secret management
Sealed Secrets or External Secrets: encrypted in Git, decrypted only inside the cluster
explain: Sealed Secrets encrypt values with the cluster's key so the repository holds only ciphertext, while External Secrets pulls from a vault at deploy time — both keep Git as the source of truth without exposing secrets. Plaintext in Git is the breach waiting to happen (the trap), email is unversioned and insecure, and carving secrets out of GitOps breaks the single-source-of-truth model.

q: The team re-debates the same architecture decisions every few months, and new hires lack context for why systems look the way they do. Which lightweight documentation practice fixes this?
options: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) capturing the context, options, and rationale per decision
Oral history passed between engineers
No documentation to stay agile
Longer design meetings
explain: ADRs record what was decided, why, and what was rejected — in version control alongside the code — ending repeat debates and onboarding amnesia. Oral history leaves when people leave, no documentation guarantees the re-debates continue, and longer meetings discuss without recording.

q: The on-call engineer needs to trigger a safe deployment from a phone without VPN or a laptop. Which practice enables operations from chat?
options: Giving everyone production SSH access
ChatOps: audited deployment commands executed from the team chat tool
Banning all on-call deployments
Emailing approvals and waiting
explain: ChatOps exposes controlled, permissioned, fully audited operations inside the chat tool the on-call engineer already has — fast and traceable. Universal SSH destroys least privilege, banning deploys delays incident recovery, and email approvals add hours to urgent actions.

q: Lead time from commit to production is six weeks, but nobody can say where the time goes. Which technique maps the whole flow to find the bottlenecks?
options: Working longer hours
More status meetings
Value stream mapping of every step from commit to production with wait times
Blaming the slowest team
explain: Value stream mapping makes every handoff and queue visible with measured wait times, so the real bottlenecks — usually waiting, not working — become undeniable. Longer hours treat a flow problem as an effort problem, meetings add overhead without data, and blame suppresses the honesty improvement requires.

q: Every product team builds its own CI/CD pipeline from scratch, producing inconsistent security scanning and deployment practices. Which platform approach standardizes this without removing team autonomy?
options: Banning internal platforms
Mandating one rigid tool with no choices
Letting the inconsistency continue
An internal developer platform offering paved-road 'golden paths' teams can adopt
explain: Golden paths make the secure, compliant pipeline the easiest option — teams adopt it voluntarily because it saves them work, standardizing practice without mandates. Banning platforms abandons leverage, rigid mandates breed workarounds, and unchecked inconsistency is the current failure.

q: New instances fail to launch in a subnet with 'insufficient IP addresses,' though the VPC has plenty of total space. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: The subnet's CIDR block is exhausted — expand it or add subnets and redistribute workloads
The instances are too large
A DNS misconfiguration
The instances need rebooting
explain: Each subnet draws from its own fixed CIDR allocation, so one full subnet blocks launches even when the VPC overall has room — expanding the range or adding subnets is the fix. Instance size does not consume extra subnet IPs, DNS plays no role in launch failures, and rebooting cannot create addresses that do not exist.

q: Private-subnet workloads lose internet access whenever one availability zone has issues. Investigation shows a single NAT gateway lives in that zone. What is the BEST fix?
options: Assigning public IPs to all private workloads
Deploying a NAT gateway in each availability zone and routing each subnet locally
A larger NAT gateway instance
Ignoring the outage
explain: A single-AZ NAT gateway is a zonal single point of failure; per-AZ gateways with local routes keep each zone's outbound traffic independent. Public IPs on private workloads abandon the private-subnet design, a bigger gateway still dies with its zone, and ignoring outages is not a strategy.

q: Connection attempts to a service hang indefinitely (timeout) rather than failing fast with 'connection refused.' What does the timeout indicate about WHERE the problem lies?
options: A DNS resolution failure
An application bug in the service code
A timeout means packets are being silently dropped — suspect firewall rules or routing, not the application
The client needs more memory
explain: Timeouts versus refusals are diagnostic gold: 'connection refused' means packets reached a host with nothing listening (application layer), while a hang means something in the path — firewall or route — drops packets silently. DNS failures produce resolution errors rather than hangs, application bugs typically refuse or reset, and client memory is unrelated to network behavior.

q: Large file transfers across a site-to-site VPN stall and time out, while small requests work fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Insufficient bandwidth
An application bug
A DNS issue
An MTU/fragmentation problem: large packets are dropped, so lower the MTU or clamp MSS
explain: VPN encapsulation adds overhead that pushes large packets past the path MTU; when fragmentation is blocked, big transfers stall while small packets sail through — the classic MTU black hole. Bandwidth affects speed rather than causing stalls, application bugs do not discriminate by packet size, and DNS is uninvolved once transfers start.

q: A DNS record was corrected an hour ago, yet some clients still resolve the old address. The authoritative server serves the right answer. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Cached records: resolvers and clients honor the old TTL, including negative caching of the earlier failure
The server is down
A firewall blocking DNS
The application needs reinstalling
explain: DNS is a caching system: resolvers, OS caches, and browsers all honor TTLs, and a cached negative response persists for its own TTL — propagation is waiting, not broken. If the authoritative server answers correctly, it is not down; firewall blocks would fail all lookups rather than serving stale ones, and reinstalling the app cannot flush network caches.

q: A server shows 90% CPU usage, but most of it is iowait and the application is sluggish. What does this indicate, and what is the WRONG fix?
options: A CPU bottleneck — add more vCPUs
High iowait means the CPU is idle waiting on disk — the bottleneck is storage, so adding vCPUs wastes money
A memory leak
A network outage
explain: iowait counts CPU time spent stalled on disk I/O, so the CPUs are starved by storage rather than overworked — the fix targets disk latency or throughput. Adding vCPUs is the expensive trap: more processors waiting on the same slow disk changes nothing. Memory leaks show as swap and OOM pressure, and network issues do not inflate iowait.

q: A server grows sluggish over days, swap usage climbs steadily, and the OOM killer eventually terminates the database. What is the underlying problem?
options: A slow disk
An undersized CPU
Memory pressure: a leak or growth exhausting RAM, forcing swap and triggering the OOM killer
A misconfigured firewall
explain: Steadily climbing swap ending in OOM kills is the signature of memory exhaustion — a leak or unbounded growth consuming RAM until the kernel sacrifices processes. Slow disks cause iowait rather than swap growth, CPU sizing does not drive swapping, and firewalls affect connectivity rather than memory.

q: Writes fail with 'no space left on device,' yet the disk shows 40% free space. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: File permission errors
A full CPU
Network storage latency
Inode exhaustion: millions of small files consumed all inodes while block space remains
explain: Filesystems track files with inodes separately from data blocks — exhausting inodes blocks new files even with free gigabytes, typically from runaway millions of tiny files. Permissions produce 'permission denied' rather than 'no space,' CPU and network latency manifest nothing like a space error, and adding disk space is the trap that does not add inodes.

q: After a storage glitch, all writes fail with 'read-only file system.' A reboot did not help. What is the appropriate recovery?
options: Running fsck to repair the filesystem, then remounting read-write
Rebooting again
Changing file permissions with chmod
Buying a larger disk
explain: The kernel remounted the filesystem read-only to protect it after detecting corruption — fsck repairs the damage so it can safely remount read-write. Rebooting preserves the protective read-only state (the trap), chmod cannot override a read-only mount, and disk size is unrelated to filesystem corruption.

q: A block volume refuses to attach to an instance, with no permission errors in the logs. What should be checked FIRST?
options: The volume's filesystem type
Whether the volume and the instance are in the same availability zone — volumes cannot attach cross-zone
The instance's CPU count
The DNS configuration
explain: Block volumes are zonal resources: attachment across availability zones is physically impossible, making zone mismatch the first check. Filesystem type matters only after attachment succeeds, CPU count is irrelevant to storage attachment, and DNS plays no role in volume operations.

q: A Kubernetes pod sits in Pending state indefinitely. Describing it shows 'Insufficient cpu.' What is the MOST likely cause?
options: A bug in the application code
A DNS misconfiguration
The pod's CPU requests exceed available capacity on every schedulable node, or taints repel it
The container registry is down
explain: Pending with 'Insufficient cpu' is a scheduling failure: the scheduler cannot place the pod's requested resources (or tolerations do not match taints), so it waits rather than failing. Code bugs surface after scheduling, DNS does not block scheduling, and a down registry produces ImagePullBackOff rather than Pending.

q: A Kubernetes Service exists and its pods are Running, yet the Service shows zero endpoints. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The cluster needs more nodes
A firewall blocking the pods
Recreating the Service blindly
A label selector mismatch: the Service selector does not match any pod's labels
explain: Services discover pods purely through label selectors — a typo or mismatch leaves the Service with no endpoints despite healthy pods. Node count does not affect endpoint discovery, firewalls block traffic rather than endpoint registration, and recreating the Service with the same wrong selector reproduces the problem.

q: An application restarts every two minutes because the liveness probe fails while the app is still in its slow startup routine. Which probe change fixes this?
options: Adding a startup probe (or initial delay) so liveness checks wait until initialization completes
Removing all probes
Adding more CPU
Ignoring the restarts
explain: Startup probes gate liveness checks until the application signals it has finished initializing, ending the kill-during-startup loop. Removing probes is the trap — it hides the symptom while losing all health supervision. More CPU does not reorder startup versus probing, and ignoring restarts normalizes the failure.

q: After a database failover, the application keeps connecting to the old writer and writes fail. The application was configured with the old instance's direct endpoint. What is the BEST fix?
options: Rebooting the application servers
Pointing the application at the cluster (writer) endpoint, which always resolves to the current primary
Scaling up the database
Moving the database to a new VPC
explain: Cluster endpoints float to whichever instance is primary after failover, while instance endpoints are pinned to one host — the application must use the floating endpoint. Reboots are the trap: they may briefly help via DNS refresh but leave the misconfiguration in place. Scaling and VPC moves do not address endpoint selection.

q: A database suddenly rejects all writes, and monitoring shows the transaction log volume is 100% full. What is the appropriate remediation?
options: Adding more data files
Rebooting the database server
Backing up the transaction log to allow truncation, then fixing whatever prevented log reuse
Ignoring it until the next maintenance window
explain: A full transaction log halts writes by design; backing it up permits truncation, and the root cause — failed log backups, replication lag, or an open transaction — must be fixed to stop recurrence. Data files are the trap: they address data space, not log space. Reboots do not free log, and waiting converts a recoverable incident into an extended outage.

q: A query that once ran in milliseconds now takes minutes; EXPLAIN shows a full table scan over millions of rows after a data import. What is the MOST likely fix?
options: A larger database instance
Caching the entire table in the application
Rewriting the whole application
Adding an index on the filtered columns so the planner seeks instead of scanning
explain: A new full scan after data growth points at a missing or invalidated index on the filter path — restoring the index returns the planner to seeks. Larger instances are the expensive trap that masks rather than fixes access-path problems, full-table caching wastes memory on data nobody reads, and rewrites are drastic overkill for an indexing issue.

q: A vendor markets its hosted application as 'cloud' because customers access it over the internet. An architect notes it lacks on-demand self-service, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. Which of the following is NOT one of the five essential characteristics of cloud computing defined by NIST?
options: On-demand self-service
Broad network access
Dedicated single-tenant hardware for every customer
Measured service
explain: NIST defines five essential characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. Dedicated single-tenant hardware for every customer contradicts resource pooling and multitenancy — it describes traditional hosting, not cloud. Internet access alone does not make something cloud.

q: A CFO asks why moving to the cloud changes how IT spending appears on the financial statements. Which answer is correct?
options: Cloud converts large upfront capital expenditures (CapEx) into pay-as-you-go operational expenditures (OpEx)
Cloud eliminates all IT spending
Cloud spending is always lower than on-premises spending
Cloud requires larger upfront hardware purchases than a datacenter
explain: The cloud's measured-service model shifts spending from CapEx (buying servers) to OpEx (metered usage), which changes budgeting and financial treatment. It does not eliminate spending, is not automatically cheaper in every case, and requires no upfront hardware purchases at all.

q: A database administrator needs storage for a write-heavy transactional database requiring both strong performance and survival of disk failures. Which RAID level is the BEST fit?
options: RAID 10 (mirrored stripes)
RAID 0 (striping only)
A single disk with no RAID
RAID 5
explain: RAID 10 combines striping for performance with mirroring for redundancy, and unlike parity RAID it has no write penalty — ideal for write-heavy databases. RAID 0 stripes for speed but any disk loss destroys all data, a single disk has no protection at all, and RAID 5's parity calculations penalize heavy write workloads.

q: An architect must store 100 TB of infrequently accessed compliance data. Triple replication would consume 300 TB of raw capacity. Which technique reduces this overhead while still tolerating disk and node failures?
options: RAID 0
Disabling all redundancy
Synchronous replication to a second region
Erasure coding
explain: Erasure coding splits data into data plus parity fragments spread across disks or nodes, tolerating failures with far less overhead than full replication (often around 1.3-1.5x instead of 3x). RAID 0 adds no protection, disabling redundancy risks total loss, and synchronous replication doubles cost while adding latency.

q: Immediately after uploading a replacement image to object storage, a user refreshes the page and briefly sees the old image before the new one appears. Which concept explains this?
options: Strong consistency
Eventual consistency
Synchronous replication
Cache poisoning
explain: Many object stores are eventually consistent: replicas converge over time, so a read immediately after a write can briefly return the prior version. Strong consistency would guarantee the new version on every read, synchronous replication is a mechanism rather than the consistency model, and cache poisoning is a malicious attack, not normal behavior.

q: A bank requires zero data loss (RPO of zero) between its primary and secondary datacenters 20 km apart, and accepts slightly higher write latency to get it. Which replication mode meets this requirement?
options: Asynchronous replication
Eventual consistency
Nightly snapshot shipping
Synchronous replication
explain: Synchronous replication acknowledges a write only after both sites confirm it, guaranteeing zero data loss at the cost of latency — acceptable over a short 20 km distance. Asynchronous replication risks losing in-flight writes, nightly snapshots leave a huge RPO gap, and eventual consistency is a data model, not a replication guarantee.

q: A serverless API powers a customer-facing checkout. Users complain the first request after idle periods takes seconds while later requests are fast. What is the cause, and which mitigation fits this latency-sensitive endpoint?
options: Cold starts; use provisioned concurrency or scheduled warming to keep execution environments ready
DNS propagation; wait 48 hours for records to settle
Missing database indexes; add indexes to every table
TLS handshake overhead; disable encryption
explain: Cold starts happen when the platform initializes a new execution environment after idle; provisioned concurrency or warming keeps environments ready for latency-sensitive endpoints. DNS propagation does not explain first-request-only delays, indexing does not correlate with idle periods, and disabling TLS trades security for speed — never an acceptable fix.

q: A team names each server, hand-configures it over SSH, and nurses it back to health when it fails — causing long outages. Which shift does cloud/DevOps practice recommend?
options: Buy larger servers so they fail less often
Treat servers as cattle, not pets: automate builds and replace rather than repair
Disable monitoring to reduce alert noise
Give each server a more memorable name
explain: The pets-vs-cattle principle says infrastructure should be disposable, automated, and replaceable rather than hand-tended and unique. Larger servers still fail and take longer to heal manually, disabling monitoring blinds the team, and naming does nothing to change the repair-instead-of-replace practice causing the outages.

q: An architect deploys two VMs for a critical service and must ensure a single rack power failure or a host patching event cannot take both down. Which placement construct provides this?
options: A resource group
A virtual network
An availability set with fault domains and update domains
A larger VM size
explain: Availability sets spread VMs across fault domains (separate racks/power) and update domains (separate patching batches), so one hardware or maintenance event cannot hit both. Resource groups are for management and billing, virtual networks provide connectivity not isolation, and larger VMs do nothing to separate failure domains.

q: A three-node database cluster must never place two members on the same physical host, since a single host failure would then kill quorum. Which rule enforces this placement?
options: A backup schedule
An anti-affinity rule
An affinity rule
A firewall rule
explain: Anti-affinity rules keep workloads separated across hosts, protecting quorum from a single host failure. Affinity is the exam trap — it does the opposite, co-locating workloads, which is exactly what must be avoided here. Backup schedules and firewall rules have nothing to do with workload placement.

q: A developer stores uploaded user files on a VM's ephemeral instance-store disk to save money. After a routine host maintenance event, all files are gone. What should the architect explain?
options: Ephemeral instance-store disks are temporary: data is lost on stop, termination, or host maintenance, so persistent volumes must hold anything that must survive
The cloud provider maliciously deleted the files
Instance-store disks are encrypted and the key expired
The files are recoverable from the hypervisor cache
explain: Instance/ephemeral storage lives on the physical host and does not survive stop, termination, or host events — it is for caches and temporary data only, while persistent network volumes are the durable choice. The provider did not act maliciously, key expiry is invented, and no hypervisor cache recovers the data.

q: A small internal wiki gets brief traffic bursts but idles most of the day. Which instance type gives the LOWEST cost while still handling the bursts?
options: Memory-optimized instances
GPU instances
Dedicated hosts
Burstable instances that accumulate CPU credits while idle
explain: Burstable instances bank CPU credits during idle periods and spend them during bursts — the cheapest fit for low-average, spiky workloads. Memory-optimized and GPU instances serve sustained specialized needs at far higher cost, and dedicated hosts are the priciest option, meant for compliance or licensing isolation.

q: A team runs an in-memory analytics engine needing 512 GB of RAM but modest CPU, plus a video-transcoding farm needing maximum CPU per dollar. Which selection is correct?
options: GPU instances for both workloads
The same general-purpose size for both to keep it simple
Memory-optimized instances for analytics; compute-optimized instances for transcoding
Burstable instances for both workloads
explain: Instance families should match the bottleneck: memory-optimized for RAM-heavy analytics, compute-optimized for CPU-heavy transcoding. GPUs help neither workload, one-size-fits-all wastes money on the wrong resource, and burstable instances cannot sustain either workload's demand.

q: A company must modernize a 20-year-old monolith but cannot risk a big-bang rewrite. Which migration pattern lets new services gradually take over functionality behind the same interface?
options: The strangler fig pattern: incrementally route functionality to new services until the monolith can be retired
Rehost the monolith unchanged forever
Shut down the monolith on a Friday night and hope
Rewrite everything in a single release
explain: The strangler fig pattern progressively replaces pieces of the legacy system behind a facade, de-risking modernization one slice at a time. Rehosting avoids modernization entirely, while shutdown-and-hope and single-release rewrites are the risky big-bang approaches the pattern exists to avoid.

q: A checkout service calls a flaky fraud-check API; when it slows down, checkout threads pile up waiting and the whole site cascades into failure. Which pattern stops the cascade?
options: Retry forever with no delay
A circuit breaker that trips after repeated failures and fails fast until the dependency recovers
Increase every timeout to 10 minutes
Remove all error handling
explain: A circuit breaker trips open after failures, failing fast to shed load and let the dependency recover, then half-opens to test recovery before closing. Infinite retries and huge timeouts worsen thread pile-ups, and removing error handling guarantees the cascade it should prevent.

q: A product catalog page hammers the database with identical queries. Which caching pattern helps, and what prevents serving stale prices indefinitely?
options: Write-behind caching with no invalidation
Cache-aside (lazy loading) with a TTL and invalidation strategy so entries expire or refresh
Disabling the database query cache
Storing catalog data only in application memory with no expiry
explain: Cache-aside loads data into the cache on a miss, while TTLs and invalidation bound how long stale data can be served. Write-behind with no invalidation risks permanent staleness, disabling caches increases database load, and unbounded in-memory storage leaks memory and never refreshes.

q: A bootstrap script on a VM needs the VM's own instance ID and region without hardcoding credentials or calling the public cloud API. Which mechanism provides this?
options: The instance metadata service, a link-local address such as 169.254.169.254 queried from inside the VM
A public DNS lookup
Reading the hypervisor's private key
Guessing from the VM's IP address
explain: The instance metadata service is a link-local endpoint reachable only from within the instance, providing identity, networking, and user-data details with no credentials needed. Public DNS does not hold instance identity, hypervisor keys are inaccessible to guests, and IP addresses do not reliably encode identity or region.

q: A company's servers sit behind firewalls that block all inbound connections from the management network, but outbound HTTPS is allowed. Which configuration management model can still manage them?
options: A pull model, where each agent periodically polls the configuration server over outbound HTTPS
A push model requiring inbound SSH from the controller
Manual configuration over remote desktop
Email-based configuration
explain: Pull-model agents initiate outbound connections to fetch configuration, traversing firewalls that block inbound traffic. Push models need inbound access from the controller, which the firewall denies; manual and email approaches are not configuration management at all.

q: A team deploys containers in an air-gapped environment and wants deployments to use only images already present on nodes, failing fast otherwise. Which image pull policy enforces this?
options: Always
IfNotPresent
Never
Using the :latest tag
explain: The Never pull policy uses only images already on the node and fails if absent — correct for air-gapped environments. Always tries to reach a registry on every start, IfNotPresent still pulls when the image is missing, and :latest is a tag, not a pull policy (a common exam trap).

q: A Kubernetes Job runs a nightly data export that must be retried if it crashes but must NOT restart after completing successfully. Which restart policy is correct?
options: Always
OnFailure
Never
Recreate
explain: OnFailure retries crashed containers but stays stopped after successful completion — exactly right for batch Jobs. Always would restart even after success, Never would not retry a crash, and Recreate is a deployment strategy, not a container restart policy.

q: A pod is repeatedly evicted from nodes despite using little CPU, and the scheduler refuses to place it on nodes with plenty of free capacity. Which misconfiguration is MOST likely?
options: CPU limits set too low
CPU requests set far higher than the container actually needs
The image pull policy
A missing liveness probe
explain: CPU requests reserve capacity at scheduling time, so inflated requests make the pod unschedulable and mark it as over-provisioned when nodes come under pressure. Low limits cause throttling rather than eviction, the pull policy affects image retrieval only, and probes affect health detection, not scheduling math.

q: Expensive GPU nodes must run ONLY GPU workloads; regular pods keep landing on them and wasting money. Which mechanism reserves the nodes?
options: Delete the GPU nodes
Use a DaemonSet
Increase every pod's CPU requests
Apply a taint to the GPU nodes so only pods with a matching toleration schedule there
explain: Taints repel pods that lack a matching toleration, which is the standard way to reserve specialized nodes for specific workloads. Deleting the nodes removes the capacity entirely, a DaemonSet runs a pod on every node (the opposite of reservation), and CPU requests do not steer placement decisions.

q: Every node in a cluster must run exactly one copy of the log-shipping agent, including nodes added next month. Which workload type guarantees this?
options: A Deployment with 50 replicas
A CronJob
A DaemonSet
A StatefulSet
explain: A DaemonSet ensures one pod per matching node and automatically covers nodes added later. A Deployment with fixed replicas does not track node count, CronJobs run on a schedule rather than per node, and StatefulSets provide stable identity and storage, not per-node coverage.

q: A database cleanup task must run at 2 AM daily inside the cluster, with retries on failure. Which Kubernetes object is designed for this?
options: A CronJob
A DaemonSet
A one-off pod created manually each night
A Service
explain: CronJobs schedule recurring work with retry, deadline, and history controls built in. DaemonSets run continuously per node rather than on a schedule, manual pods are not automated, and Services expose network endpoints rather than running scheduled work.

q: An application needs its non-sensitive settings (feature toggles, endpoint URLs, log level) injected without rebuilding the image. Which object fits, and why not the alternative?
options: A Secret; ConfigMaps cannot be mounted into pods
Hardcode the values in the container image
Store the values in the container's writable layer
A ConfigMap; Secrets are for sensitive data and are only base64-encoded rather than encrypted by default
explain: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration decoupled from images, while Secrets are reserved for credentials — and Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted, by default, so they are the wrong home for plain settings. Hardcoding or using the writable layer re-couples config to the image and defeats the purpose.

q: Developers wait days for operations to manually create volumes for each new database. Which Kubernetes feature provisions storage automatically when claimed?
options: Static volume provisioning by administrators
A StorageClass with dynamic provisioning
HostPath volumes on every node
Storing data inside container images
explain: A StorageClass defines a provisioner so that creating a PersistentVolumeClaim triggers automatic volume creation — no manual ticket needed. Static provisioning is the manual bottleneck being replaced, hostPath ties data to a single node, and container images are immutable and unsuitable for data.

q: A Helm upgrade introduced a regression. The team needs to return to the previous release quickly, including its prior values. Which approach fits?
options: helm rollback to the previous revision
Delete the namespace and reinstall everything
Edit the live pods by hand
helm install with a brand-new release name
explain: Helm tracks revisions, so rollback atomically restores the prior release state including its values. Deleting the namespace causes downtime and data risk, hand-editing pods creates drift from desired state, and a new release name creates a duplicate rather than reverting.

q: Audit findings show database passwords shared across services, never rotated, and visible in pipeline logs. Which approach BEST fixes all three issues?
options: Longer static passwords stored in a shared document
Embedding the passwords in application source code
Short-lived, dynamically generated credentials issued per service by a secrets broker with automatic rotation
Disabling database authentication
explain: Dynamic secrets are unique per client, expire automatically, and rotate without human handling — eliminating sharing, staleness, and log exposure at once. Longer static passwords are still shared and never rotated, embedding in code worsens exposure, and disabling authentication removes security entirely.

q: After a widely reported vulnerability in a common open-source component, leadership asks which of the company's applications include it. Which artifact answers this fastest?
options: The marketing website
Developers' memories
The firewall logs
A software bill of materials (SBOM) listing every component in each build
explain: An SBOM inventories all dependencies per build, enabling instant blast-radius analysis when a component vulnerability is announced. Marketing pages, human memory, and firewall logs cannot enumerate which builds contain which libraries.

q: A critical zero-day vulnerability is being actively exploited on Friday night. The normal change process requires a two-week review, and a change freeze starts Monday. What is the appropriate path?
options: Wait for the next review meeting in two weeks
Use the emergency change process: expedited approval, implement immediately, then document and review afterward
Do nothing until the freeze lifts
Patch silently with no record
explain: Emergency changes exist for urgent risks: expedited approval allows immediate action, with documentation and post-implementation review preserving accountability. Waiting or doing nothing leaves active exploitation unaddressed, while silent patching breaks auditability and change control.

q: A team ships on a fixed schedule and wants version numbers that instantly communicate release timing to customers. Which scheme fits?
options: Calendar versioning (e.g., 2026.10)
Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH)
Random build numbers
Git commit hashes as version numbers
explain: Calendar versioning encodes the release date, matching time-based release trains so customers instantly see recency. Semantic versioning signals compatibility rather than timing, while random numbers and commit hashes communicate nothing meaningful to customers.

q: The artifact repository has grown to 40 TB because every nightly build is kept forever, and storage costs are spiking. Which policy BEST controls this?
options: Keep everything forever for safety
Store artifacts on engineers' laptops instead
An artifact retention policy that keeps recent and released builds while purging old snapshots
Disable the CI pipeline
explain: Retention policies balance reproducibility and audit needs against cost by keeping what matters and purging the rest. Keeping everything is the current problem, laptops are not a repository, and disabling CI destroys delivery to save storage.

q: A pod serves traffic fine, but a deadlock freezes request handling while the process stays alive. Which probe should trigger a restart, and which should only control traffic routing?
options: Readiness for restart; liveness for traffic
Liveness for restart; readiness for traffic routing
Startup probe for both purposes
No probes; restart the nodes instead
explain: Liveness failures cause the kubelet to restart the container, which clears deadlocks; readiness only adds or removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting. Swapping them restarts pods on every slow start or keeps deadlocked pods receiving traffic, and node restarts are a blunt misfire.

q: A team needs to expose three HTTP microservices on one public IP with path-based routing (/orders, /users, /billing) and TLS termination. Which Kubernetes resource provides this?
options: A ClusterIP Service
A DaemonSet
NodePort on every node
An Ingress with routing rules and TLS configuration
explain: Ingress is the Layer 7 entry point that provides host and path-based routing plus TLS termination on a single address. ClusterIP is internal-only, DaemonSet is a workload type rather than an entry point, and NodePort exposes raw ports per node with no Layer 7 routing.

q: A ransomware attack encrypts a database; synchronous replication faithfully copies the encrypted data to the secondary site within seconds. Why did replication fail to protect the company, and what would have helped?
options: Replication was too slow to keep up
The secondary site needed more CPU
Backups are unnecessary when replication exists
Replication is not a backup — it mirrors corruption and deletions instantly; isolated, immutable backup copies would have provided recovery
explain: Replication propagates every change including encryption, corruption, and accidental deletion, so it cannot serve as a recovery point — only independent, isolated backup copies survive logical damage. Speed and CPU are irrelevant here, and the idea that replication replaces backups is the dangerous misconception this scenario exposes.

q: A trading platform needs an effective RPO of zero but cannot afford synchronous replication's latency penalty. Which data protection technology journals every write to enable recovery to any point in time?
options: Nightly full backups
Continuous data protection (CDP) with a write journal
Weekly snapshots
RAID 1
explain: CDP captures every write in a journal, allowing rollback to any second without synchronous replication's latency cost. Nightly and weekly backups leave large data-loss windows, while RAID 1 protects only against disk failure, not logical corruption or ransomware.

q: Which statement correctly describes how traditional incremental and differential backups use the archive bit?
options: Incremental backups clear the archive bit; differential backups leave it set, so differentials grow larger until the next full backup
Both backup types clear the archive bit
Differential backups clear the bit; incremental backups leave it set
The archive bit is only used by full backups
explain: Incremental backups clear the archive bit, so the next incremental captures only newer changes; differentials leave it set, so each differential accumulates everything changed since the last full. The distractors swap the behavior or deny the mechanism entirely.

q: A VM has 40 snapshots chained over six months and its disk performance has severely degraded, since reads now traverse the entire chain. What is the appropriate remediation?
options: Take another snapshot
Add more RAM to the VM
Consolidate the snapshot chain, keeping only the recovery points actually needed
Defragment the guest filesystem
explain: Long snapshot chains force every read through many delta files; consolidation merges them back down and restores performance. Another snapshot lengthens the chain further, RAM does not fix I/O path length, and guest defragmentation cannot collapse the snapshot chain.

q: A database VM is backed up via a storage snapshot taken mid-transaction. The restore boots, but the database needs crash recovery and loses the in-flight transaction. Which backup type would have captured a clean, transactionally consistent state?
options: A crash-consistent snapshot taken more frequently
A file copy of the database files while the database is running
Backing up only the transaction logs
An application-consistent backup using a VSS writer (or pre/post scripts) to quiesce the database
explain: Application-consistent backups coordinate with the database through VSS writers or quiesce scripts to flush in-flight work, yielding a transactionally clean image. Crash-consistent snapshots are like pulling the plug — usually recoverable but not guaranteed; hot file copies risk corruption, and logs alone are not a complete backup.

q: A physical backup server's motherboard fails. The team has full image backups but no identical spare hardware. Which recovery approach gets them running fastest on different hardware?
options: File-level restore of selected documents
Bare-metal restore of the system image to dissimilar hardware, then inject the correct drivers
Reinstall the OS and manually recreate all configuration from memory
Wait for identical hardware to be manufactured
explain: Bare-metal restore recovers the full system image onto different hardware, handling driver differences, which is far faster than rebuilding. File-level restore misses the OS and configuration, manual rebuild is slow and error-prone, and waiting for identical hardware is not a recovery plan.

q: A user accidentally deletes one spreadsheet from last Tuesday. The team has nightly image-level VM backups. What is the MOST efficient recovery?
options: Restore the entire VM image to production, overwriting everything
Tell the user the file is unrecoverable
Perform a file-level (granular) restore of just the spreadsheet from the backup
Restore the image to an isolated location and copy the file out
explain: File-level granular recovery restores just the deleted object without disrupting the running VM or losing newer data. A full-image restore causes downtime and rolls back everything, isolated restore works but is slower than direct granular recovery, and the file is absolutely recoverable.

q: Branch offices with slow WAN links must back up to the central datacenter. Which deduplication approach MINIMIZES data sent over the WAN?
options: Target deduplication at the central backup server
Source deduplication on the branch clients, sending only unique blocks
No deduplication; send full backups
Compress everything after sending it
explain: Source-side deduplication fingerprints blocks before transfer and sends only new unique data — critical for constrained links. Target deduplication still ships everything across the WAN first, full backups ignore the constraint, and compressing after sending does nothing to reduce transferred bytes.

q: Which statement BEST compares agent-based and agentless monitoring?
options: Agent-based monitoring collects richer, deeper metrics but requires software on each host; agentless monitoring uses protocols like SNMP or WMI with no installed software but gathers less detail
Agentless monitoring always provides deeper metrics than agents
Agents are never needed in cloud environments
Both approaches are identical in capability and overhead
explain: Agents enable deep, custom metrics at the cost of deployment and maintenance overhead, while agentless monitoring avoids installs but is limited to what remote protocols expose. The distractors invert the trade-off, dismiss agents entirely, or pretend no trade-off exists.

q: A monitoring system scrapes metrics from each service's /metrics endpoint on a schedule, automatically discovering new instances. Which model is this, and what is its main advantage?
options: Push model; services control the timing of delivery
Neither model; monitoring requires installed agents only
Push model; no central server is needed
Pull model; the server discovers targets and scrapes them, simplifying firewall rules and target management
explain: In the pull model the monitoring server discovers targets and scrapes them on its schedule, centralizing configuration and needing only outbound-allowed endpoints. Push has clients send data (better for ephemeral jobs behind NAT), so the distractors mislabel the model or invent limitations.

q: A network team must monitor switches and printers that support no agents, with encrypted credentials and immediate alerting on link failures. Which combination fits?
options: SNMPv3 for encrypted polling plus SNMP traps for event-driven alerts
SNMPv1 with default community strings
Manual Telnet scraping
SNMPv2c, which provides strong authentication
explain: SNMPv3 adds real authentication and encryption, while traps push events like link-down immediately instead of waiting for the next poll. SNMPv1 and v2c send community strings in cleartext with no real security, and Telnet scraping is insecure and manual.

q: The security team asks which internal host is sending large volumes of data to an unknown external IP, but full packet capture is too heavy to run everywhere. Which technology provides conversation-level flow summaries from routers?
options: Full packet capture on all links
SNMP interface counters only
NetFlow/IPFIX flow records showing source, destination, ports, and byte counts per conversation
DNS logs only
explain: NetFlow/IPFIX records summarize who-talked-to-whom with volumes — lightweight and ideal for hunting exfiltration. Full capture is too heavy at scale, SNMP counters lack per-conversation detail, and DNS logs miss traffic to direct IPs.

q: Synthetic login checks run green every 5 minutes, yet real users in one region report slow logins. Which monitoring addition would capture the actual user experience?
options: More synthetic checks from the same location
Real user monitoring (RUM) capturing actual browser timing from genuine sessions
Longer log retention
Disabling monitoring in that region
explain: RUM measures real users under real conditions (region, device, network), revealing problems synthetic probes in other locations cannot see. More same-location synthetics repeat the blind spot, log retention does not measure experience, and disabling monitoring hides the problem.

q: A major outage is resolved by restarting a service, but it recurs every few weeks. The team opens a record to find and eliminate the underlying cause. Which ITIL distinction applies?
options: Incident management restores service quickly; problem management investigates root cause to prevent recurrence, often using a known-error database
Incident management and problem management are the same process
Problem management pages engineers faster than incident management
Incident management is only for security events
explain: Incidents focus on restoring service fast; problems focus on root cause and permanent fixes, tracked with workarounds in a known-error database. They are distinct processes, paging speed is not the difference, and incident management covers all outages, not just security.

q: The infrastructure team commits to the application team that database failover completes within 15 minutes, supporting the customer-facing uptime promise. What is this internal commitment called?
options: An SLA
A EULA
An operational-level agreement (OLA)
A purchase order
explain: OLAs are internal agreements between teams that underpin the external customer-facing SLA. Calling it an SLA confuses internal targets with customer commitments, while EULAs and purchase orders are unrelated commercial documents.

q: Engineers spend most of their week on manual, repetitive operational tasks like ticket-driven VM provisioning. According to SRE practice, what is this work called and what should happen to it?
options: Engineering excellence; it should be expanded
Technical debt; it should be ignored
Innovation time; it should be protected
Toil; it should be measured, capped, and eliminated through automation
explain: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work — SRE practice measures it, caps it, and automates it away so engineers can do real engineering. Celebrating, ignoring, or protecting toil keeps the team on a treadmill of busywork.

q: A junior administrator accidentally deletes a production resource group, taking down the environment. Which preventive control would have blocked the deletion?
options: A longer password policy
A resource lock (delete lock) on critical resources
More frequent backups
A larger cloud budget
explain: Delete locks block deletion of critical resources until explicitly removed — the direct preventive control for authorized-but-mistaken actions. Passwords do not stop legitimate mistakes, backups aid recovery rather than prevention, and budget is irrelevant to the incident.

q: An architect deploys a WAF, network segmentation, host hardening, and encrypted backups. An attacker bypassing the WAF still faces the other layers. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Single point of failure
Defense in depth
Security through obscurity
Implicit trust
explain: Defense in depth layers independent controls so that one failure does not equal a breach. A single point of failure is what the layering avoids, security through obscurity relies on secrecy rather than controls, and implicit trust is the opposite mindset.

q: A team needs subnet-wide stateless filtering as a coarse guardrail plus per-instance stateful rules for application ports. Which pairing is correct?
options: Security groups for the subnet; NACLs for the instances
Two firewalls in series at each instance
NACLs only, since they are stateful
NACLs (stateless, subnet-level) plus security groups (stateful, instance-level)
explain: NACLs are stateless subnet-level guardrails while security groups are stateful instance-level rules — they complement each other. Swapping them is the classic trap, stacked instance firewalls are not the model, and NACLs are stateless, not stateful.

q: A compliance scan flags a load balancer still negotiating TLS 1.0 and 1.1. What is the correct remediation?
options: Disable TLS entirely for better performance
Switch the site to plain HTTP
Enforce TLS 1.2 or higher and disable the deprecated protocols
Ignore the finding; old protocols are fine
explain: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 have known weaknesses, so modern compliance requires TLS 1.2 or higher with the old versions disabled. Disabling TLS or downgrading to HTTP destroys transport security, and ignoring the finding fails the audit.

q: A developer must encrypt large database backups for storage and also exchange the decryption key with a partner over an insecure channel. Which combination is standard practice?
options: Asymmetric encryption for the bulk data; symmetric encryption for the key exchange
Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) for the bulk data; asymmetric encryption to protect the symmetric key in transit
Hash the backups instead of encrypting them
Base64-encode the backups
explain: Symmetric encryption is fast for bulk data, while asymmetric encryption solves key distribution by protecting the session key — the standard hybrid approach. Swapping the roles makes bulk encryption impractically slow, hashing is one-way and unrecoverable, and Base64 is encoding, not encryption.

q: A breach exposes a user table. Passwords stored with bcrypt and unique salts resist cracking, while those stored with plain MD5 fall quickly. Which practice does this demonstrate?
options: Encrypt passwords with AES so they can be decrypted later
Store passwords in plaintext for easy recovery
Email users their passwords monthly
Store passwords as salted, slow hashes (e.g., bcrypt); never use fast unsalted hashes or reversible encryption
explain: Salted, computationally expensive hashes resist rainbow tables and brute force, which is why the bcrypt passwords survived. Reversible encryption is the wrong tool since passwords should never be recoverable, and plaintext storage or emailed passwords are breaches waiting to happen.

q: A vendor sends a signed software update. The customer verifies the signature with the vendor's public key. Which security properties does this provide?
options: Confidentiality of the update contents
Faster download speeds
Authentication of the sender and integrity of the update, providing non-repudiation
Automatic installation of the update
explain: Digital signatures prove who signed the data and that it is unaltered, giving authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation. Signatures do not encrypt, so there is no confidentiality; download speed and installation behavior are unrelated.

q: A retailer wants to keep credit card numbers out of its analytics environment to shrink PCI DSS scope, while still joining records across systems. Which technique replaces card numbers with non-sensitive substitutes mapped in a secure vault?
options: Tokenization
Compression
Base64 encoding
Truncation to the last four digits only
explain: Tokenization substitutes random tokens for card numbers, keeping real values in a hardened vault — analytics can join on tokens without PCI scope. Compression and encoding do not de-identify data, and truncation destroys the ability to join records.

q: A tenant leaves a cloud provider and needs assurance its data on shared storage is unrecoverable. Which technique makes this practical at scale?
options: Overwrite every disk sector three times
Crypto-shredding: destroy the per-tenant encryption keys, rendering all ciphertext permanently unreadable
Delete only the file pointers
Trust the provider's verbal assurance
explain: With per-tenant encryption keys, destroying the keys makes all ciphertext permanently unreadable — instant, scalable, and verifiable. Sector overwrite is infeasible on shared virtualized storage, pointer deletion leaves data intact, and verbal assurance is not a control.

q: Attackers bombard an employee with repeated MFA push notifications at 3 AM until, half-asleep, the employee approves one. Which attack is this, and which MFA upgrade resists it?
options: Credential stuffing; use longer passwords
SQL injection; add input validation
DDoS; deploy a WAF
MFA fatigue (push bombing); phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys
explain: MFA fatigue (push bombing) exploits approve-style pushes through sheer notification volume; FIDO2/WebAuthn requires physical presence and resists phishing entirely. Credential stuffing, SQL injection, and DDoS are unrelated attacks with unrelated defenses.

q: A company needs web single sign-on for employees (authentication) and also wants a mobile app to access a partner API on users' behalf without sharing passwords (delegated authorization). Which standards fit each need?
options: SAML for employee SSO authentication; OAuth 2.0 (often with OIDC) for delegated API authorization
OAuth for SSO; SAML for API authorization
FTP for both needs
Shared service accounts for both needs
explain: SAML (and OIDC) federate identity for single sign-on, while OAuth 2.0 delegates scoped API access via tokens without sharing passwords. Swapping them misapplies each standard, and FTP or shared accounts are the anti-patterns these standards replace.

q: HR hires and terminations take days to reflect in cloud applications, leaving ex-employees with access. Which standard automates user provisioning and deprovisioning from the identity provider?
options: SNMP
FTP
SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management)
Manual CSV uploads
explain: SCIM automates identity lifecycle synchronization between the identity provider and applications, so joiners, movers, and leavers are handled promptly. SNMP manages network devices, while FTP and manual CSV uploads are the slow manual processes causing the problem.

q: Attackers poison a resolver's cache to redirect a bank's customers to a lookalike site. Which DNS security extension lets resolvers cryptographically validate that responses are authentic?
options: Plaintext DNS on port 53
Longer TTL values
Disabling DNS
DNSSEC
explain: DNSSEC digitally signs zone data so resolvers can detect forged responses and reject cache-poisoning attempts. Plaintext DNS is the vulnerable status quo, TTLs do not authenticate anything, and disabling DNS breaks name resolution entirely.

q: A site faces two attacks: a high-volume UDP flood saturating its links, and a low-volume HTTP flood exhausting application threads. Which pairing of attack types and mitigations is correct?
options: Both are volumetric attacks; buy more servers
Volumetric network-layer flood mitigated by upstream scrubbing and anycast absorption; application-layer (L7) flood mitigated by WAF rate limiting and caching
Both are fixed by a single firewall rule
Pay the ransom demand
explain: Volumetric floods must be absorbed upstream before they saturate links, while application-layer floods require Layer 7 defenses like WAF rules, rate limiting, and caching. More servers cannot absorb link saturation, one firewall rule does not fit both attack types, and paying ransom is not mitigation.

q: A suspected breach is reported. Which order follows the standard incident response lifecycle?
options: Preparation, then detection and analysis, then containment, then eradication, then recovery, then lessons learned
Eradicate first, then prepare, then detect
Recover first, then detect the incident
Lessons learned first, then containment
explain: The standard lifecycle runs from preparation through lessons learned in order, with containment before eradication to stop spread while preserving evidence. The distractors scramble the sequence in ways that would destroy evidence or skip critical phases.

q: Responders find a compromised VM actively running malware. A junior admin suggests pulling the power immediately. Why is network isolation without powering off the better FIRST containment, and what must be preserved?
options: Powering off is always best; memory contents do not matter
Delete the VM immediately to save time
Network isolation stops the spread while preserving volatile memory for forensics, with a documented chain of custody for all evidence collected
Rebooting the VM will fix the malware
explain: Memory holds encryption keys, running processes, and network connections that vanish on power-off, so isolation contains the threat without destroying evidence, and chain of custody keeps that evidence admissible. Powering off, deleting, or rebooting all destroy forensic value.

q: A scanner finds an unpatched service (a weakness), threat intel shows ransomware groups actively exploiting it (a danger), and the team assesses the business impact of a successful attack. Which terms apply, in order?
options: Vulnerability, threat, risk
All three are called vulnerabilities
Threat, vulnerability, risk
Risk, risk, risk
explain: A vulnerability is the weakness, a threat is the actor or event that could exploit it, and risk is the likelihood times business impact — the classic exam distinction. The distractors conflate the three terms, which is exactly the trap the question tests.

q: A company wants to test both its external defenses realistically and its internal monitoring deeply. It commissions one test with no insider knowledge and another with full architecture documentation and credentials. Which pair is this?
options: Both are gray-box tests
A vulnerability scan and an audit
Two rounds of social engineering
Black-box (no prior knowledge) and white-box (full knowledge) penetration tests
explain: Black-box testing simulates an external attacker with no insider knowledge, while white-box testing maximizes coverage using full knowledge and credentials. Gray-box is partial knowledge (neither extreme here), and scans or audits are not penetration tests.

q: One project requires fixed requirements up front, delivers once after 18 months, and resists mid-course changes. A second project delivers working software every two weeks and adapts to feedback. Which labels apply, in order?
options: Waterfall; Agile
Agile; Waterfall
Both are DevOps
Both are Scrum
explain: Waterfall is sequential with big-bang delivery and frozen requirements, while Agile is iterative, incremental, and adaptive to feedback. The distractors swap the labels or misapply DevOps and Scrum, which describe culture/practice and a specific framework rather than these project shapes.

q: A team works in fixed two-week iterations, holds a daily 15-minute synchronization meeting, and a product owner prioritizes the backlog. Which framework is this?
options: Waterfall
ITIL
Scrum
Six Sigma
explain: Sprints, daily standups, a product owner, and a prioritized backlog are defining Scrum elements. Waterfall is sequential with no iterations, ITIL is IT service management, and Six Sigma is a process-quality methodology.

q: A support team handles unpredictable incoming work and wants to visualize flow and limit concurrent tasks without fixed-length iterations. Which method fits better than Scrum here?
options: Kanban, with its continuous flow and WIP limits instead of sprints
Scrum with longer sprints
Waterfall
No process at all
explain: Kanban suits continuous, unpredictable work through WIP limits and flow visualization, while Scrum's fixed sprints fit planned product increments. Longer sprints do not fix the mismatch, Waterfall is entirely wrong for operational work, and no process means no improvement.

q: A value-stream map reveals features waiting weeks for approval, partially done work going stale, and handoffs losing context. Which Lean concept names these, and what is the goal?
options: Value; add more of it
Velocity; measure it harder
Blame; assign it quickly
Waste (muda); eliminate it to improve flow
explain: Lean identifies waiting, partially done work, and handoff losses as waste (muda) to be eliminated so value flows faster. The distractors miss the point: adding undefined value, measuring harder, or assigning blame does not remove the waste.

q: A DevOps transformation assessment covers Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, and Sharing. Which model is this?
options: Waterfall
CALMS
The OSI model
Maslow's hierarchy of needs
explain: CALMS (Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing) is the widely used model for DevOps values and transformation assessment. Waterfall is a project methodology, the OSI model describes networking layers, and Maslow's hierarchy describes human motivation.

q: A team accelerates delivery (flow), builds fast feedback from production back to development, and treats every incident as a learning opportunity. Which DevOps theory describes these three principles?
options: The Three Ways: flow, feedback, and continual learning and experimentation
Three-tier architecture
The CIA triad
The 3-2-1 backup rule
explain: Gene Kim's Three Ways underpin DevOps: systems thinking and flow, amplifying feedback loops, and a culture of continual learning. The distractors borrow the number three from architecture, security, and backup concepts that are unrelated.

q: In one company, messengers of bad news are punished and failures are hidden; in another, information flows freely and inquiry is valued. Which model classifies these as pathological and generative cultures?
options: The OSI model
Westrum's organizational culture model
Moore's law
The CAP theorem
explain: Westrum classifies cultures as pathological (power-oriented), bureaucratic (rule-oriented), or generative (performance-oriented), and DevOps research links generative culture to better delivery outcomes. The OSI model, Moore's law, and the CAP theorem describe networking, hardware, and distributed systems — not culture.

q: A team already tests early in the pipeline but wants to validate behavior with real production traffic and users. Which practice complements their shift-left testing?
options: Stop testing entirely and rely on users
Test only on developers' laptops
Shift-right testing: validating in production via canary analysis, feature flags, and chaos experiments
Delete the staging environment
explain: Shift-right extends testing into production safely using canaries, flags, and controlled experiments to validate real-world behavior. The distractors abandon testing discipline rather than extending it.

q: A SaaS team deploys multiple times daily from short-lived branches merged to main after review. Which branching model fits better than GitFlow's release branches here?
options: GitFlow with monthly release branches
Committing directly to production with no review
Emailing patches between developers
GitHub Flow: branch, review, merge to main, deploy
explain: GitHub Flow uses short-lived branches merged to main for continuous delivery, matching multiple-deploys-per-day cadence. GitFlow's develop and release branches suit scheduled releases, direct-to-production skips review, and email is not version control.

q: An open-source project receives contributions from thousands of strangers who cannot be granted write access. Which Git workflow enables this safely?
options: Give everyone push access to main
The forking workflow: contributors fork the repo, make changes, and submit pull requests from their own copies
Accept code contributions via screenshots
Disable external contributions
explain: The forking workflow lets untrusted contributors propose changes through pull-request review without write access to the canonical repo. Open push access is reckless, screenshots are not code, and disabling contributions defeats open source.

q: A company debates one repository for all services versus one repository per service. Which trade-off is accurate?
options: Monorepos are always superior in every case
Polyrepos eliminate all merge conflicts
Monorepos ease cross-service refactoring and unified versioning but bring tooling scale challenges; polyrepos isolate teams but complicate shared changes
Repository strategy does not matter
explain: The real trade-off: monorepos simplify atomic cross-cutting changes at the cost of scale and tooling complexity, while polyrepos give team autonomy at the cost of coordination overhead. The absolute claims in the distractors are false, and strategy genuinely shapes workflow.

q: Two developers share one workstation: one writes code while the other reviews in real time, swapping roles regularly. Which practice is this, and what is its main benefit?
options: Rubber-duck debugging
A performance review
Mandatory overtime
Pair programming; continuous review that catches defects immediately and spreads knowledge
explain: Pair programming provides instant review and knowledge sharing through the driver-navigator dynamic. Rubber-duck debugging is a solo explanation technique, while performance reviews and overtime are unrelated to the practice described.

q: A team writes acceptance criteria as Given/When/Then scenarios in plain language before implementing a user story. Which practice is this?
options: Test-driven development at the unit level only
Behavior-driven development (BDD)
Waterfall requirements gathering
Ad-hoc testing
explain: BDD expresses expected behavior in ubiquitous Given/When/Then language, aligning developers, QA, and business stakeholders before code is written. Unit-level TDD focuses on design through tests rather than shared behavior specs, while waterfall and ad-hoc approaches lack the collaborative specification.

q: Unit tests fail intermittently because they call a real payment gateway sandbox. Which technique isolates the unit under test?
options: Run the tests only in production
Delete the flaky tests
Test doubles (mocks and stubs) that simulate the gateway's responses
Call the real gateway more often
explain: Mocks and stubs replace external dependencies with predictable simulated responses, making unit tests fast, deterministic, and independent of the sandbox. Testing in production is reckless, deleting tests loses coverage, and calling the real gateway more often increases flakiness.

q: A team celebrates 95% code coverage, yet critical bugs still escape to production. Which understanding of coverage is correct?
options: Coverage guarantees bug-free code
Coverage measures developer productivity
Low coverage is always better than high coverage
Coverage measures which lines executed during tests; high coverage does not guarantee correct assertions or behavior
explain: Coverage is a completeness signal, not a correctness proof — tests can execute code without asserting the right behavior, which is how bugs escape despite high numbers. The distractors overclaim what coverage proves, misread it as productivity, or invert its value.

q: A company's software architecture mirrors its org chart's communication paths, creating friction. Leadership reorganizes into stream-aligned teams owning services end to end. Which concepts are at play?
options: Conway's law observed the mirroring; Team Topologies prescribes stream-aligned teams to enable fast flow
Moore's law; buy faster servers
The Peter principle; promote everyone
Parkinson's law; work expands to fill the time anyway
explain: Conway's law observes that systems mirror organizational communication structures, and Team Topologies deliberately designs team types (stream-aligned, platform, enabling) to optimize for flow. The distractors are unrelated laws about hardware, promotion, and work expansion.

q: An administrator follows the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology. Which sequence is correct?
options: Identify the problem, then establish a theory, then test the theory, then establish a plan, then implement, then verify and document
Implement a fix first, then identify the problem, then document, then test
Document first, then guess, then reboot, then hope
Test, then identify, then implement, then theorize
explain: The six-step methodology runs in order: identify, theorize, test, plan, implement, then verify functionality and document findings. Jumping straight to implementation skips theory and testing, risking wrong fixes; the distractors scramble or skip steps entirely.

q: Users cannot reach a cloud application. Ping to the server fails. Traceroute shows responses through hop 8, then timeouts from hop 9 onward. What does this indicate?
options: The local workstation is at fault
DNS resolution is broken
The failure lies at or beyond hop 9 — the last responding hop bounds the problem location
The application code has a bug
explain: Traceroute maps the packet path hop by hop, so the last responding hop shows how far traffic travels and bounds where the fault lies. A local fault would fail at hop 1, DNS issues present as resolution errors rather than ping failure, and code bugs do not stop ICMP.
