q: An old embedded device cannot establish TLS with a hardened server, though modern browsers connect fine. Packet captures show the handshake failing during cipher negotiation. What is the cause?
options: Cipher-suite and protocol mismatch: the server disabled the legacy protocols and ciphers the old device requires — update the device or, if the risk is accepted, enable a compatible suite
An expired certificate
A DNS resolution issue
The device needs more RAM
explain: Failure specifically at cipher negotiation with modern clients succeeding isolates the cause to protocol/cipher overlap — the hardened server dropped what the legacy device speaks. An expired certificate would fail all clients, DNS never reaches the handshake, and RAM does not affect negotiation.

q: A load balancer returns HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout, not 502. The backend servers are up and healthy. What does 504 specifically indicate, and where should investigation focus?
options: The backend is down, the same as a 502
504 means the backend accepted the connection but responded too slowly (upstream timeout): investigate backend latency, slow queries, or thread exhaustion — not backend availability
A DNS failure between the client and the load balancer
The load balancer needs a reboot
explain: 504 means the upstream was reachable but too slow, directing investigation at backend performance (queries, thread pools) rather than reachability. 502 indicates the backend is down or refusing, DNS failures occur before the balancer responds, and rebooting the balancer treats the messenger.

q: Pods are Running but cannot resolve each other's service names, though direct pod-IP connections work. External DNS from the nodes is fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The application code is broken
A full disk on the worker nodes
In-cluster DNS failure (e.g., CoreDNS pods down or misconfigured): pod-IP connectivity proves the network works, so name resolution inside the cluster is the broken layer
A cloud provider DNS outage
explain: Working pod-IP traffic isolates the fault to name resolution, and healthy node DNS isolates it further to the cluster DNS service itself. Application code does not break DNS for all pods, disk pressure presents differently, and a provider outage would also break node DNS.

q: A high-frequency trading firm needs block storage for its matching engine with sub-millisecond latency. iSCSI over the shared Ethernet network adds too much latency and CPU overhead. Which storage networking approach BEST meets this requirement?
options: NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF), which carries the NVMe protocol over RDMA or Fibre Channel for near-local-SSD latency
iSCSI over a 1 Gbps link, which is cheaper
Object storage accessed over HTTPS
Tape backup
explain: NVMe-oF extends the NVMe protocol across a fabric using RDMA or Fibre Channel, delivering latency close to locally attached NVMe drives with minimal CPU overhead — exactly what a latency-sensitive matching engine needs. iSCSI over slow Ethernet keeps the latency problem, object storage is high-latency API-based storage unsuitable for block workloads, and tape is for archival, not live trading.

q: A distributed database cluster must survive the simultaneous loss of multiple racks. Cluster placement groups put instances close together for low latency, which is the opposite of what is needed here. Which placement strategy spreads instances across distinct underlying hardware fault domains?
options: Cluster placement group
Spread placement group, which places each instance on distinct underlying hardware
A single availability zone with larger instances
Spot instances spread across regions
explain: Spread placement groups explicitly place a small number of instances on distinct physical hardware, so a rack-level failure cannot take multiple members — the right tool for fault isolation. Cluster placement optimizes for low latency by grouping hardware together, a single AZ with bigger instances concentrates risk rather than spreading it, and spot placement across regions does not control hardware fault domains.

q: A healthcare company needs single-tenant hardware for compliance, but it does NOT need visibility into physical socket placement or control over which host its VMs land on. Which is the MOST cost-effective option that still guarantees no other customer shares the hardware?
options: Default shared tenancy
Spot instances
Dedicated instances, which run on hardware dedicated to one customer without the added cost of full host control
Serverless functions
explain: Dedicated instances guarantee single-tenant hardware for compliance at a lower price than dedicated hosts, which add socket visibility and placement control the company does not need. Default tenancy shares hardware with other customers, spot pricing does not change tenancy, and serverless abstracts hardware entirely rather than dedicating it.

q: A fleet of web servers runs well on x86 instances, but the provider's ARM-based instances promise better price-performance for this workload. What must the architect verify FIRST before migrating?
options: That ARM instances exist in every region, which is the only concern
That ARM is always faster, so no testing is needed
That the provider allows ARM, which is never an issue
That the application, language runtime, and all dependencies have working ARM builds or images
explain: ARM instances use a different instruction set, so the application and every dependency must be compiled for ARM — an x86-only binary or container image simply will not run. Regional availability matters but is secondary to binary compatibility, assuming ARM is always faster skips validation, and provider permission is not the gating issue.

q: A fintech company faces strict audits and must reconstruct any account's exact state at any point in the past. Its CRUD design overwrites history with each update. Which pattern provides a complete, replayable record of every state change?
options: Event sourcing with an append-only event log, rebuilding state by replaying events
CRUD with nightly full backups
A shared database with row-level locking
Caching account state in memory
explain: Event sourcing stores every change as an immutable event in an append-only log, so any past state can be rebuilt by replaying events up to that point — purpose-built for auditability. Nightly backups give day-old granularity while CRUD still destroys intraday history, locking controls concurrency rather than preserving history, and caches are volatile by design.

q: An online store's read traffic outnumbers writes 100 to 1, and complex reporting queries against the order model slow down checkout writes. Which pattern lets the team optimize separate models for reads and writes?
options: A single larger database server
CQRS — separate read and write models, each tuned for its workload
Disabling the reporting queries
Database sharding by customer
explain: CQRS separates the write model (optimized for transactional integrity) from read models (optimized for queries and reporting), so heavy reads no longer contend with writes. A bigger server postpones the contention without resolving it, disabling reports sacrifices the business need, and sharding distributes load but keeps reads and writes fighting on the same model.

q: A queue consumer crashes on malformed poison messages. The broker redelivers them endlessly, and each redelivery blocks real messages behind them. Which feature quarantines messages that repeatedly fail processing?
options: Increasing the visibility timeout
Sending larger batches
A dead-letter queue that receives messages after a configured number of failed receives
Switching to FIFO ordering
explain: A dead-letter queue automatically routes messages that fail processing a set number of times to a separate queue for inspection, freeing the main queue to keep flowing. Longer visibility timeouts only delay the inevitable redelivery, larger batches do not fix poison content, and FIFO ordering preserves sequence but still chokes on the bad message.

q: An order-processing stream must handle each customer's events strictly in order while still scaling across many parallel consumers. Which design preserves per-customer ordering without forcing everything through one consumer?
options: A single global queue with one consumer
Randomly distributing events across consumers
Polling the database from each consumer
Partitioning the stream by customer key, so all of one customer's events land in the same ordered partition
explain: Partitioning by customer key guarantees ordering within each partition while different partitions are consumed in parallel — ordering where it matters, scale where it does not. A single queue and consumer serializes everything and cannot scale, random distribution destroys ordering, and database polling reintroduces the bottleneck the stream was meant to remove.

q: Internal microservices exchange thousands of small structured messages per second under strict contracts, and the team measures real overhead from REST/JSON serialization. Which alternative is the better fit for service-to-service calls?
options: gRPC with Protocol Buffers — binary serialization and contract-first service definitions
REST with verbose JSON payloads
File transfers over FTP
Email-based messaging
explain: gRPC with Protocol Buffers uses compact binary serialization and generates client/server stubs from a shared contract, cutting both payload size and integration drift for high-volume internal calls. Verbose JSON keeps the measured overhead, FTP is a file protocol unsuited to RPC-style calls, and email is neither real-time nor structured.

q: A live operations dashboard has 10,000 browsers polling an API every 2 seconds, and most polls return no new data while hammering the backend. Which technology pushes updates to browsers only when data actually changes?
options: Polling every 500 milliseconds instead
WebSockets (or server-sent events), keeping an open channel for server-pushed updates
Larger backend servers
A CDN in front of the API
explain: WebSockets keep a persistent bidirectional channel so the server pushes updates the moment data changes, eliminating 10,000 mostly-empty polls. Faster polling multiplies the waste, bigger servers absorb the load without removing it, and a CDN caches responses rather than delivering live pushes.

q: A team maintains two pipelines computing the same metrics — one batch, one streaming — and every logic change must be implemented twice. Which architecture replaces both with a single streaming path that can reprocess history by replaying the log?
options: Lambda architecture, which keeps both paths
Nightly ETL jobs
Kappa architecture — one immutable event log serves both real-time and reprocessing needs
A data warehouse with no streaming
explain: Kappa architecture treats the event log as the single source of truth: streaming jobs serve real-time needs and reprocessing history is just replaying the log, so logic exists once. Lambda architecture is the dual-path design causing the duplication, nightly ETL abandons real-time entirely, and a warehouse alone does not stream.

q: A search index must reflect database writes within seconds, but polling the database every second overloads it and still misses changes between polls. Which technique captures row-level changes directly from the database's transaction log?
options: Polling the database more frequently
Application code sending emails on each write
A nightly full-table dump
Change data capture (CDC), reading committed changes from the transaction log
explain: CDC tails the database transaction log, delivering every committed row change with minimal overhead on the database — no polling load and no missed writes. Faster polling worsens the load it was meant to fix, email notifications are unreliable plumbing, and nightly dumps cannot meet a seconds-level freshness requirement.

q: Analytics jobs in private subnets must read from object storage without crossing the public internet or paying NAT gateway data-processing charges. Which provides private connectivity from the VPC to the storage service?
options: A VPC endpoint for the storage service, keeping traffic on the provider's private network
An internet gateway with public IPs on the instances
A VPN tunnel to the storage service
Opening the instances' security groups to the internet
explain: A VPC endpoint routes traffic to the storage service over the provider's private backbone — no internet traversal and no NAT charges. An internet gateway with public IPs exposes the instances, a VPN connects remote networks rather than reaching provider services, and opening security groups to the internet is the opposite of the requirement.

q: A global application runs in three regions, but users are sometimes routed to a distant region with high latency. Which DNS routing policy directs each user to the healthy endpoint with the lowest latency from their location?
options: Simple routing, which returns one fixed answer
Latency-based routing, measuring latency from the requester to each endpoint
Weighted routing with equal weights
Failover routing, which only switches on failure
explain: Latency-based routing directs each DNS requester to the region with the lowest measured latency, fixing the distant-region problem automatically. Simple routing ignores geography, equal weights split traffic without regard to latency, and failover routing only reacts to outages rather than optimizing every request.

q: A hospital must process patient data in the cloud under a requirement that even the cloud provider's own administrators cannot read data while it is being processed. Which technology encrypts data in use, inside memory?
options: TLS for data in transit
Disk encryption for data at rest
Confidential computing — hardware-based memory encryption and attested enclaves
A VPN tunnel to the cloud
explain: Confidential computing encrypts memory contents with hardware-managed keys and runs workloads in attested enclaves, so data in use stays unreadable even to the provider's administrators. TLS protects data on the wire, disk encryption protects stored data but not live memory, and a VPN only secures the network path.

q: A company uses 90-day certificates and has suffered two outages from engineers forgetting manual renewals. Which approach eliminates manual renewal work entirely?
options: A shared spreadsheet tracking expiry dates
Ten-year self-signed certificates
Disabling TLS on internal services
ACME-based automation, where agents request, install, and renew certificates from a CA automatically
explain: The ACME protocol lets agents automatically obtain and renew certificates before expiry, removing the human step that caused both outages. A spreadsheet still depends on humans acting, decade-long self-signed certificates are untrusted by clients and violate policy, and disabling TLS abandons encryption rather than managing it.

q: A network security appliance needs direct access to CPU virtualization extensions and must load custom kernel modules that nested virtualization on standard instances cannot provide. Which instance type gives full control of the physical server?
options: Burstable instances
Spot instances
Bare metal instances — no hypervisor between the workload and the hardware
Serverless functions
explain: Bare metal instances expose the entire physical server with no virtualization layer, allowing custom hypervisors, kernel modules, and direct hardware feature access. Burstable and spot are standard virtualized instances with the same hypervisor restrictions, and serverless abstracts hardware away entirely.

q: A bad serverless deployment is serving errors in production. The team must return all traffic to the previous function version immediately, without waiting for a rebuild. Which mechanism makes this a one-step operation?
options: Function versions with aliases — repoint the alias to the previous published version
Redeploying from a developer's laptop
Deleting the function and recreating it
Waiting for the next scheduled deployment
explain: Immutable function versions combined with aliases let the team shift 100% of traffic back to the last-known-good version instantly, with no build or deploy wait. Laptop redeploys are slow and unreviewed, deleting the function causes an outage, and waiting leaves errors serving users.

q: A rolling update runs in a cluster at its resource quota limit — it must never exceed the current pod count while updating. The team sets maxUnavailable to 1. Which maxSurge setting guarantees no extra pods are created above the desired count?
options: maxSurge: 50%
maxSurge: 0, so new pods only start as old ones terminate
maxSurge: 100%
Deleting the deployment first
explain: maxSurge: 0 caps the number of pods above the desired count at zero, so replacements only start after old pods terminate — respecting the quota. Any positive maxSurge allows extra pods that would breach the quota, and deleting the deployment first causes a full outage rather than a rolling update.

q: A DaemonSet runs a log agent on 500 nodes. The team must roll out a new agent version without taking too many nodes' logging offline at once. Which setting controls how many DaemonSet pods update simultaneously?
options: The DaemonSet must be deleted and recreated for any update
The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
maxUnavailable in the DaemonSet's rolling update strategy
Doubling the node count first
explain: DaemonSets support a rolling update strategy where maxUnavailable limits how many nodes' pods are down during the update, pacing the rollout across the fleet. DaemonSets do support rolling updates natively, HPA scales replica counts rather than pacing updates, and doubling nodes is wasteful overkill.

q: A Helm chart ships with default values, the team maintains a per-environment values file, and an operator occasionally needs a one-off override at install time. Which takes the HIGHEST precedence?
options: The chart's built-in default values
Values from a parent chart
Editing the chart templates directly
Values passed with --set or -f at install/upgrade time
explain: Helm applies the highest precedence to values supplied on the command line (--set or -f files), overriding values files and chart defaults — which is why one-off overrides work there. Chart defaults are the lowest precedence, parent chart values sit in the middle, and editing templates is not a values mechanism at all.

q: A team deploys a third-party vendor’s Kubernetes YAML bundle that must not be edited — vendor upgrades would overwrite any changes. The company still needs its standard labels, image pull secrets, and resource limits applied to every object at deploy time. Which tool patches these manifests without forking them?
options: Kustomize, applying patches and overlays to the vendor base at deploy time
Editing the vendor YAML files directly
Maintaining a forked copy of the vendor bundle
kubectl create commands typed by hand each deploy
explain: Kustomize treats the vendor bundle as an immutable base and layers patches — labels, pull secrets, limits — on top at deploy time, so upgrades never clobber company customization. Editing vendor files breaks on upgrade, forking doubles maintenance, and hand-typed commands are unrepeatable.

q: A team consumes a community Terraform module without a version constraint. A new major release of the module renames resources and the next apply destroys production infrastructure. Which practice prevents this?
options: Always using the newest module version
Pinning the module version with a constraint, upgrading deliberately after testing
Copying the module source into every configuration
Deleting the module cache before each apply
explain: A version constraint pins the module to a tested release, so breaking upstream changes cannot silently flow into production applies — upgrades become deliberate, tested events. Always taking newest invites exactly this breakage, copying source forks the module and loses upstream fixes, and the cache has nothing to do with version selection.

q: One VM in a Terraform-managed fleet has OS-level corruption, but its configuration is correct and identical to its healthy siblings. The team wants to recreate ONLY that VM. Which approach targets just the damaged resource?
options: Destroying and recreating the entire fleet
Rebuilding the VM by hand in the console
Tainting (or -replace targeting) the single resource so the next apply recreates only it
Editing the state file with a text editor
explain: Tainting marks one resource for recreation, so the next apply replaces exactly the corrupted VM while leaving the fleet untouched. Fleet-wide destroy causes unnecessary outage, hand rebuilding reintroduces drift, and hand-editing state risks corruption.

q: An Ansible playbook manages nginx across 200 servers. Restarting nginx on every playbook run would cause needless brief outages; it should restart only when the configuration actually changes. Which construct implements this?
options: A restart task that runs unconditionally every time
A cron job restarting nginx hourly
Setting ignore_errors on the restart
A handler that runs only when notified by a task reporting a change
explain: Handlers run at the end of a play only when notified by a task that changed something, so nginx restarts exactly when its config changes and never otherwise. Unconditional restarts cause the outages being avoided, cron restarts are time-based rather than change-based, and ignore_errors only suppresses failures.

q: Ansible playbooks are stored in Git and need database passwords at deploy time. A teammate suggests Base64-encoding the passwords, but Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Which Ansible feature encrypts secrets at rest in the repository?
options: Ansible Vault, which encrypts secret files and variables with a password
Base64 encoding
Storing passwords in plaintext comments
Pasting passwords into the chat for deploys
explain: Ansible Vault provides real AES encryption for secret variables and files, decrypting only at playbook runtime with the vault password. Base64 is trivially reversible encoding, plaintext comments expose secrets to every repo reader, and chat-based sharing is unversioned and insecure.

q: A CloudFormation template has grown to 1,800 resources, hitting template size limits and becoming impossible to review or reuse across teams. Which decomposes it into manageable, independently maintainable pieces?
options: Keeping one giant template and scrolling faster
Nested stacks — a parent template composing reusable child stacks
Deleting resources until the template fits
Splitting into unrelated stacks deployed by hand in the right order
explain: Nested stacks let a parent template reference child stacks as resources, breaking a monolith into reviewable, reusable modules deployed as one unit. A giant template keeps the unmaintainable status quo, deleting resources removes functionality, and hand-ordered stacks reintroduce the sequencing failures automation was meant to prevent.

q: A company deploys from clusters in three regions, but all container images live in one regional registry. Cross-region pulls are slow and incur egress charges on every deployment. Which keeps tested images available close to each cluster?
options: Pulling across regions on every deploy and accepting the cost
Building a separate image per region
Registry geo-replication, automatically copying images to a registry in each region
Storing images on a shared file server
explain: Geo-replication keeps a copy of each image in every region's registry, so pulls stay local, fast, and free of cross-region egress. Accepting cross-region pulls bakes in the cost and latency, per-region builds triple the build matrix and risk divergence, and a file server is not a container registry.

q: A risky new pricing feature must be shippable to production but instantly disableable within seconds if it misbehaves — without a redeploy or rollback. Which pattern provides this?
options: Redeploying the previous release, which takes 20 minutes
A database restore
More pre-production testing
A kill switch — a remotely toggled feature flag defaulting to off
explain: A kill switch lets operations disable the feature in seconds by flipping a flag, with no build, deploy, or data surgery. Redeploys take 20 minutes of exposure, database restores do not remove code behavior, and testing reduces but never eliminates the need for an instant off-ramp.

q: A critical security fix lands on the main branch, but the release branch is mid-cycle and cannot take all of main's new features. How can the team apply ONLY the fix commit to the release branch?
options: cherry-pick the fix commit onto the release branch
Merge all of main into the release branch
Rebase the release branch onto main
Manually retype the fix into the release branch
explain: cherry-pick applies exactly the chosen commit onto another branch, delivering the fix without dragging in unrelated features. Merging or rebasing pulls in everything on main, and retyping by hand invites transcription errors and loses history.

q: A regulated company must cryptographically prove that each commit was authored by the claimed developer, not merely that the name was typed into the commit. Which Git feature provides this?
options: Descriptive commit messages
GPG- or SSH-signed commits, verifiable against the author's public key
Branch naming conventions
Commit timestamps
explain: Signed commits attach a cryptographic signature verifiable against the author's public key, proving authorship in a way names and timestamps cannot. Messages, branch names, and timestamps are all trivially forgeable metadata.

q: During rolling deployments, instances are deregistered from the load balancer and in-flight requests die immediately, causing user-facing errors on every deploy. Which load balancer feature lets existing connections complete before the instance is removed?
options: Deploying faster so fewer requests are in flight
Increasing backend timeouts
Connection draining (deregistration delay), holding the instance briefly to finish open requests
Enabling sticky sessions
explain: Connection draining keeps a deregistered instance briefly to complete in-flight requests while sending no new ones, eliminating deploy-time errors. Faster deploys do not save requests already in flight, longer timeouts do not keep the instance registered, and sticky sessions pin users rather than draining gracefully.

q: During rolling updates, pods receive SIGTERM and die mid-request because the application needs 20 seconds to finish work and close connections. Which ensures Kubernetes waits for graceful shutdown?
options: Killing pods faster to finish the rollout sooner
Adding more nodes
A liveness probe
A preStop hook combined with a sufficient terminationGracePeriodSeconds
explain: The preStop hook runs before SIGTERM and terminationGracePeriodSeconds gives the pod time to drain, so in-flight work completes instead of being cut off. Faster kills worsen the truncation, more nodes do not change shutdown behavior, and liveness probes detect stuck pods rather than pacing shutdown.

q: An engineer renames a Terraform resource to match a new naming standard. Without special handling, Terraform would destroy the production database and create a new empty one. Which preserves the existing resource under its new name?
options: Letting Terraform destroy and recreate, then restoring from backup
A moved block (or state mv), telling Terraform the resource only changed addresses
Deleting the state file and re-importing everything
Renaming in the console to match
explain: A moved block records that the resource's address changed without its identity changing, so Terraform updates state instead of destroying the database. Destroy-and-recreate causes data loss and downtime, wiping state loses all tracking, and console renames create drift rather than resolving it.

q: A Prometheus dashboard computing 99th-percentile latency over 30 days times out because the query scans enormous raw data on every load. Which precomputes the expensive aggregation on a schedule so dashboards read the result?
options: Recording rules, evaluating the query periodically and storing the result as a new metric
Alerting rules
Adding more RAM to Prometheus
Deleting old metrics
explain: Recording rules run heavy queries on an interval and store the output as fresh time series, turning a 30-day scan into a cheap lookup. Alerting rules fire notifications rather than precomputing, RAM does not fix query complexity, and deleting history destroys the data being analyzed.

q: When one region has network trouble, 200 related alerts fire and page the on-call engineer 200 times. Which reduces this to a single actionable notification?
options: Adding more on-call engineers
Alertmanager grouping and inhibition, collapsing related alerts into one
Disabling alerts during incidents
Sending alerts to email instead
explain: Alertmanager groups alerts by labels like region and can inhibit downstream alerts when the root cause is known, delivering one notification instead of 200 pages. More engineers spreads the noise without reducing it, disabling alerts blinds the team, and email just moves the flood.

q: After a developer adds a user-ID label to a request counter, Prometheus memory usage explodes and queries slow to a crawl. What caused this?
options: Normal metric growth
Too-short retention
High-cardinality labels — one time series per user ID multiplies series count exponentially
Slow disks
explain: Every unique label combination creates a new time series, so a user-ID label turns one counter into millions of series, exhausting memory — the classic cardinality explosion. This is not normal growth, retention length is unrelated to series count, and disks do not explain memory exhaustion.

q: The team tracks average API latency, but averages hide the slow outliers customers actually feel. Which metric type lets them compute accurate p95 and p99 latencies?
options: A counter of total requests
A gauge of current latency
Log lines with timestamps
A histogram, bucketing observations so quantiles are computable
explain: Histograms record observations in buckets, enabling accurate quantile calculations like p95/p99 over any window. Counters only sum events, gauges show a single current value with no distribution, and logs require expensive ad-hoc parsing for the same answer.

q: Crash-consistent snapshots of a database VM boot on restore but always require crash recovery, and once replay failed and lost transactions. Which backup type coordinates with the application to capture a clean, transactionally consistent image?
options: Application-consistent backups, quiescing the database so the snapshot needs no recovery
Crash-consistent snapshots
Copying database files while the database runs
RAID mirroring
explain: Application-consistent backups signal the database to flush and quiesce before the snapshot, producing an image that restores cleanly with no crash recovery or lost transactions. Crash-consistent snapshots are exactly what caused the replay failure, live file copies risk torn writes, and RAID protects disks rather than providing point-in-time backups.

q: Weekly full backups no longer fit in the backup window, but restoring from a full plus 30 incrementals is painfully slow. Which builds a new full backup from the last full plus subsequent incrementals — without reading from the client again?
options: Running full backups every night
Synthetic full backups, assembled server-side from existing backup data
Stopping backups entirely
Snapshots only, with no backup software
explain: Synthetic fulls construct a full image from the previous full and the incrementals already stored, giving fast single-image restores without the client-side cost of a real full. Nightly fulls worsen the window problem, stopping backups abandons recovery, and snapshots alone lack the backup catalog and off-site properties needed.

q: Patching the entire server fleet in one window risks a bad patch taking down everything at once. Which strategy applies patches to a small pilot group first, bakes them, then proceeds fleet-wide only if the pilot stays healthy?
options: Patching all servers simultaneously on Friday night
Never patching production
Canary (ring-based) patch rollout with bake time and health gates between rings
Patching one server per week by hand forever
explain: Ring-based rollouts limit a bad patch's blast radius to the pilot group and the bake period catches regressions before the fleet is exposed. Big-bang patching maximizes blast radius, never patching accumulates vulnerability debt, and one-server-a-week never converges.

q: An expired TLS certificate caused a four-hour outage last quarter. Which control ensures the team learns about expiring certificates weeks in advance?
options: Buying longer-lived certificates and hoping
A calendar reminder owned by one engineer
Self-signed certificates that never expire
Automated certificate-expiry monitoring with alerts well before the deadline
explain: Automated expiry monitoring watches every certificate and alerts with lead time, removing the human memory the outage depended on. Longer lifetimes only delay the same failure mode, a single calendar reminder is a single point of failure, and self-signed certificates are untrusted by clients.

q: Leadership wants every department to see its cloud consumption starting this quarter, but finance says internal cross-charging cannot begin until next year's budget cycle. Departments currently ignore costs because central IT pays one combined bill. Which FinOps practice fits this staged approach?
options: Showback — reporting each department's consumption without billing them
Chargeback with internal invoices
Hiding the bill from departments
Across-the-board budget cuts
explain: Showback creates cost visibility and accountability per department without the accounting overhead of chargeback, which is exactly the see-but-don't-bill-yet stage. Chargeback adds internal invoicing leadership is not ready for, hiding bills preserves the free-resource illusion, and blind cuts punish efficient teams equally.

q: Finance suspects widespread over-provisioning across 500 VMs but has no per-VM utilization data in one place. Which uses historical utilization to recommend smaller, cheaper instance types?
options: Guessing based on application names
Rightsizing recommendations from cost-management tooling
Upsizing everything to be safe
Moving everything to spot instances
explain: Rightsizing engines analyze actual CPU, memory, and I/O history per resource and recommend the cheapest size that fits observed demand. Guessing is ungrounded, upsizing worsens the waste, and spot changes pricing rather than fixing oversized shapes.

q: A tagging policy exists on paper, but half of all new resources launch untagged and cost allocation keeps breaking. Which enforces mandatory tags at provisioning time?
options: Quarterly reminder emails
Trusting teams to remember
Policy-as-code that denies or remediates provisioning missing required tags
A spreadsheet tracking owners
explain: Policy-as-code evaluates every provisioning request and blocks or auto-remediates untagged resources, making the policy self-enforcing. Emails and trust are the failed status quo, and spreadsheets track the mess without preventing it.

q: Development and test environments sit idle every night and weekend, burning compute spend for zero benefit. Which automatically stops them during off-hours and starts them before engineers arrive?
options: Deleting dev environments permanently
Running dev on the largest instances for speed
Asking engineers to remember to shut down manually
Scheduled start/stop automation based on business hours
explain: Scheduled automation stops idle environments nights and weekends and restarts them before the workday, capturing the savings with no daily human effort. Deleting dev destroys productivity, bigger instances cost more, and manual shutdowns are forgotten — which is why the waste exists.

q: Target-tracking scaling reacts too gradually to a step-function traffic spike: the service needs one extra instance at 60% CPU, two more at 75%, and three more at 90%. Which scaling policy expresses these aggressive step adjustments?
options: Step scaling, mapping metric thresholds to specific capacity adjustments
Target tracking, which only maintains a single target value
Scheduled scaling on a fixed timetable
Manual scaling by the on-call engineer
explain: Step scaling defines exactly how much capacity to add at each threshold breach, matching the aggressive response the spike demands. Target tracking smoothly maintains one target and reacts too gently here, scheduled scaling cannot follow unpredictable spikes, and manual scaling is slow and error-prone.

q: A batch fleet uses spot instances for cost savings. The provider reclaims instances with a two-minute warning, and unprepared workers lose in-progress work. Which design handles reclamation gracefully?
options: Ignoring the warnings and letting workers die
Handling interruption notices: checkpointing work, draining, and letting the fleet replace the instance
Requesting larger spot instances that are never reclaimed
Abandoning spot and paying on-demand for everything
explain: Interruption notices give two minutes to checkpoint and drain, so the fleet replaces capacity without losing work — the standard resilient spot pattern. Ignoring warnings loses work, no spot size is exempt from reclamation, and retreating to on-demand surrenders the savings that motivated spot.

q: An auto-scaling group launched six months ago still runs instances from the original AMI, even though new launches use the patched image. New instances are fine; old ones drift further behind. Which rolls every instance to the current launch template gradually?
options: Terminating all instances at once
Creating a second auto-scaling group and deleting the old one
Instance refresh, replacing instances in controlled batches with health checkpoints
Rebooting the old instances
explain: Instance refresh systematically replaces running instances with the current launch template in batches, verifying health between batches. Mass termination causes an outage, a second group is heavyweight for a routine update, and reboots do not change the AMI.

q: A policy requires database credentials to rotate every 90 days, but manual rotations are missed and cause outages when someone finally rotates without telling the application team. Which removes humans from the rotation entirely?
options: Writing the rotation date on a whiteboard
Using one password that never changes
Rotating only when an auditor asks
A secrets manager with automatic rotation integrated with the database and applications
explain: Automatic rotation generates new credentials on schedule and updates both the database and consuming applications atomically, eliminating missed rotations and surprise outages. Whiteboards, static passwords, and audit-driven rotation are the manual failure modes being replaced.

q: The team needs to prove its disaster-recovery failover actually works, but testing against production risks a real outage. Which validates failover without touching the production environment?
options: An isolated failover test — restoring into a fenced bubble network with no route to production
Never testing, to avoid any risk
Failing over production during business hours to see what happens
A conference-room walkthrough only
explain: A bubble-network test executes the real failover procedure against restored copies with production networking fenced off, proving the mechanics with zero production risk. Never testing preserves the biggest risk of all, live failover gambling is reckless, and walkthroughs cannot catch the technical failures that only real restores reveal.

q: An attacker is recording encrypted traffic today, hoping to decrypt it years later if the server's private key is ever stolen. Which TLS property ensures captured sessions stay unreadable even if the long-term private key is compromised?
options: Perfect forward secrecy — ephemeral session keys from Diffie-Hellman key exchange
A 4096-bit RSA key
A larger certificate chain
Serving the site over HTTP as well
explain: With perfect forward secrecy, each session uses ephemeral keys that are never stored, so stealing the server's private key later cannot decrypt recorded traffic. A bigger RSA key still protects only key exchange without ephemerality, chain length is about trust not secrecy, and HTTP exposes everything in plaintext.

q: A company deploys one wildcard certificate across 50 services, all sharing the same private key. A single edge server is compromised and the key is stolen. What is the consequence?
options: Nothing — wildcard certificates cannot be stolen
All 50 services are compromised at once, since one key decrypts and impersonates every one of them
Only the edge server is affected; other services use different keys
Browsers automatically distrust the company
explain: Sharing one private key across 50 services means a single theft compromises every service's confidentiality and identity — maximum blast radius. Wildcard keys are files like any other and can absolutely be stolen, the services share the key by design, and browsers do not auto-distrust without revocation.

q: A company runs hundreds of internal services needing TLS. Public certificates for internal-only names are expensive and publish the names in public transparency logs. Which issues trusted certificates for internal use without public exposure?
options: HTTP for all internal traffic
Self-signed certificates on each service
An internal private CA whose root is distributed to company devices
Disabling certificate validation in clients
explain: A private CA issues internally trusted certificates for any internal name at no per-cert cost and without public logging, with trust anchored by distributing the root. HTTP abandons encryption, self-signed certs trigger warnings and multiply management, and disabling validation removes the authentication TLS is for.

q: A penetration test shows the company's web application is vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF). The tester used it to query the instance metadata service and steal the VM's IAM credentials. Which change makes credential theft via the metadata service far harder?
options: Leaving the metadata service open for convenience
Using longer IAM access keys
Blocking all outbound traffic
Enforcing IMDSv2, which requires a session token that simple SSRF requests cannot obtain
explain: IMDSv2 requires a PUT request to obtain a session token before metadata is served, which basic SSRF payloads cannot perform — closing the credential-theft path. Leaving IMDSv1 open preserves the vulnerability, key length is irrelevant once keys are stolen, and blocking all outbound traffic breaks the application.

q: A SaaS vendor needs an IAM role in the customer's account. The role's trust policy allows the vendor's account to assume it — but any of the vendor's other customers who learn the role ARN could assume it too. Which condition restricts assumption to the intended customer?
options: An external ID condition — a secret value only the intended customer and vendor know
Making the role name public
A longer role ARN
Allowing all accounts to assume the role
explain: The external ID acts as a shared secret in the trust policy, so only a caller presenting the correct value — the intended customer relationship — can assume the role, defeating the confused-deputy problem. Public names and longer ARNs are guessable or discoverable, and open trust is the vulnerability itself.

q: A developer with full administrative rights in a workload account starts launching expensive GPU instances in an unapproved region, violating company policy. IAM policies cannot restrain an administrator. Which organization-level control blocks this?
options: An IAM policy attached to the developer's user
A service control policy (SCP) denying the GPU instance family in unapproved regions at the OU level
A stronger password policy for administrators
A polite email asking the developer to stop
explain: SCPs apply above account administrators, so they can deny instance families or regions no matter what the account's own IAM policies allow — the only guardrail that binds admins. An IAM policy is the classic trap because admins can edit their own policies, passwords authenticate without authorizing, and emails are not controls.

q: An attacker exploited a containerized application and wrote malware to the container's filesystem for persistence. Which hardening setting makes the container's root filesystem immutable, blocking this persistence technique?
options: Using larger container images
Running the container as root
A read-only root filesystem, with writable volumes mounted only where needed
Running more replicas
explain: A read-only root filesystem prevents any writes outside explicitly mounted writable volumes, so malware cannot persist itself on the filesystem. Larger images add attack surface, running as root worsens the compromise, and more replicas just multiply the infected copies.

q: A containerized service must bind to port 443, which traditionally requires root — but the team removed root after a breakout incident. Which Linux mechanism grants ONLY the low-port binding privilege without full root?
options: Running the container as root again
Privileged mode
Adding the process to the sudoers file
Linux capabilities — granting CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE alone
explain: Capabilities split root's powers into discrete units, so CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE permits low-port binding while every other privilege stays dropped. Restoring root or privileged mode reopens the breakout risk, and sudoers grants broad command execution rather than one kernel privilege.

q: A multi-tenant cluster must guarantee no pod can run privileged, use host namespaces, or mount host paths. Which built-in Kubernetes mechanism enforces these restrictions cluster-wide?
options: Pod Security Standards (baseline/restricted), enforced via the Pod Security admission controller
NetworkPolicies
RBAC roles alone
A documented agreement with developers
explain: Pod Security Standards define baseline and restricted profiles covering privileged mode, host namespaces, and host paths, enforced automatically at admission. NetworkPolicies control traffic rather than pod privileges, RBAC governs API access rather than pod specs, and documentation does not enforce anything.

q: The platform team must enforce custom rules on every Kubernetes deployment — for example, all images must come from the approved registry and every pod must set resource limits. Which evaluates these policies at object-creation time and rejects violators?
options: kubectl describe after deployment
Admission controllers such as OPA/Gatekeeper evaluating policy-as-code on each request
Reading application logs
Quarterly manual audits
explain: Validating admission controllers intercept every create/update request and deny objects violating policy, preventing bad workloads from ever running. Post-deploy inspection finds violations after the fact, logs do not enforce policy, and quarterly audits leave months of exposure.

q: During the design phase, architects systematically ask six questions about each component: can it be spoofed, tampered with, repudiated, disclosed, denied service, or escalated in privilege? Which threat-modeling framework structures exactly these questions?
options: DREAD scoring
The cyber kill chain
The waterfall model
STRIDE — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege
explain: STRIDE is the mnemonic for exactly these six threat categories, making design reviews systematic rather than ad hoc. DREAD scores already-identified threats, the kill chain describes attack stages rather than design questions, and waterfall is a delivery methodology, not a threat model.

q: The SOC wants to map observed adversary behaviors — initial access, persistence, lateral movement — to a shared catalog of real-world tactics and techniques so detections and reports use common language. Which framework provides this?
options: STRIDE
CIS Benchmarks
MITRE ATT&CK, cataloging adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures
The OSI model
explain: MITRE ATT&CK organizes real adversary behaviors into tactics and techniques, giving defenders a common vocabulary for mapping detections and gaps. STRIDE is for design-time threat modeling, CIS Benchmarks are configuration baselines, and OSI describes network layers.

q: The security team plants fake cloud API keys in code repositories and internal wikis. The keys do nothing — but any use of them triggers an immediate alert. What are these deceptive credentials called, and what do they detect?
options: Production credentials with monitoring
Password vault entries
Backup encryption keys
Honeytokens (canary tokens) — they detect unauthorized access and repository compromise
explain: Honeytokens are fake secrets whose only purpose is to be tripped: any use proves an attacker is rummaging through repos or wikis. Real production credentials would grant actual access, vault entries are legitimate secrets, and backup keys serve recovery rather than detection.

q: Analysts handle phishing alerts by repeating the same 20 steps: isolate the host, block the sender, reset credentials, open a ticket. Which platform codifies these playbooks and executes the routine steps automatically?
options: A SIEM, which only collects and correlates alerts
SOAR — security orchestration, automation, and response
Email forwarding rules
A shared spreadsheet checklist
explain: SOAR platforms encode response playbooks and execute the repetitive containment actions automatically, shrinking response time from hours to minutes. A SIEM detects and correlates but does not act, email rules cannot isolate hosts, and spreadsheets guide humans without automating anything.

q: Attackers try three common passwords against 10,000 user accounts — staying under account-lockout thresholds — instead of hammering one account. Which attack is this, and which controls best blunt it?
options: Credential stuffing, which tests stolen password lists against one account at a time
A brute-force attack against a single account
Password spraying — defeated by MFA and impossible-travel or velocity anomaly detection
Phishing, which tricks users into revealing passwords
explain: Password spraying inverts brute force: few passwords across many accounts to dodge lockouts, and MFA plus anomaly detection are the effective counters. Credential stuffing replays breached username-password pairs rather than common guesses, single-account brute force trips lockouts, and phishing is a different attack entirely.

q: An API endpoint returns the order at /api/orders/4821 for any authenticated user — changing the number returns other customers' orders with no further check. Which API vulnerability is this?
options: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
SQL injection
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
BOLA/IDOR — broken object-level authorization: the API never verifies the requester owns the object
explain: BOLA means the API authenticates the user but never authorizes access to the specific object, so predictable IDs expose everyone's data. XSS injects scripts into pages, SQL injection targets the database layer, and CSRF tricks a victim's browser — none describe missing per-object checks.

q: A mobile app uses the OAuth authorization code flow, but as a public client it cannot safely store a client secret. Which extension protects the authorization code from interception on the device?
options: PKCE — the app proves it initiated the flow with a code verifier only it knows
The implicit flow, which returns tokens directly
The resource-owner password grant
A longer access token lifetime
explain: PKCE binds the authorization request to a secret verifier held by the app, so an intercepted authorization code is useless without it — designed exactly for public clients. The implicit flow is deprecated and less secure, the password grant exposes user credentials to the app, and token lifetime does not protect code interception.

q: An enterprise ships quarterly releases, maintains supported older versions, and needs a formal hotfix path for production issues. Short-lived trunk-based branches feel chaotic for this cadence. Which branching model provides dedicated release and hotfix branches?
options: GitFlow, with develop, release, and hotfix branches
Pushing everything straight to main
No branches — everyone edits the same files
Emailing code patches
explain: GitFlow's release branches isolate stabilization and its hotfix branches patch production without disturbing ongoing development — matching a quarterly, supported-versions cadence. Pushing to main offers no isolation, branchless editing guarantees conflicts, and email patches abandon version control entirely.

q: Misconfigured storage buckets and open security groups keep reaching production through infrastructure templates. Which pipeline check catches these misconfigurations before the template is ever applied?
options: A yearly manual architecture review
IaC static analysis (policy-as-code scanning) in the pipeline
Waiting for the CSPM tool to flag production
Trusting developers to read the security guide
explain: IaC scanning evaluates templates against security policies on every pull request, blocking misconfigurations before they become real infrastructure. Yearly reviews are far too late, CSPM only sees what already deployed, and trust is not a control.

q: Legal discovers a GPL-licensed library inside a commercial SaaS product, creating a compliance crisis. Which automated pipeline check would have flagged the license risk when the dependency was added?
options: Unit tests
Performance tests
Software composition analysis including license scanning
Code formatting checks
explain: SCA inventories every dependency and flags licenses incompatible with the product's commercial terms at the moment of introduction. Unit and performance tests verify behavior rather than legal terms, and formatting checks are cosmetic.

q: The end-to-end suite takes three hours running serially, and developers avoid running it. The tests are independent of each other. Which technique splits the suite across many parallel agents to finish in minutes?
options: Deleting half the tests
A single larger build machine
Skipping tests on Fridays
Test sharding — partitioning tests across parallel runners
explain: Sharding divides independent tests across many agents running simultaneously, collapsing hours into minutes without losing coverage. Deleting tests sacrifices quality, one bigger machine still runs serially, and skipping tests on a schedule is not engineering.

q: Database schema changes are applied by hand before deployments, causing drift between environments and occasional outages from forgotten steps. Which manages schema changes as safely as application code?
options: Versioned migration scripts, reviewed and applied automatically by the pipeline
A DBA running SQL by hand from memory
Never changing the schema again
Sharing one admin login for all changes
explain: Versioned migrations make schema changes repeatable, reviewable, and automatically applied in order across environments — the same discipline as code. Hand-run SQL is the drift source, freezing the schema blocks the product, and shared logins destroy accountability.

q: New-hire onboarding takes three days of installing toolchains, and 'works on my machine' bugs persist because every laptop differs. Which gives every developer an identical, ready-to-code environment in minutes?
options: A 40-page setup wiki
Devcontainers — containerized, version-controlled development environments
Faster laptops
One shared development server everyone SSHes into
explain: Devcontainers define the entire toolchain as code, so every developer — and CI — gets the identical environment instantly. Wikis document the manual pain without removing it, faster hardware does not standardize software, and shared servers create contention and snowflake state.

q: Developers wait two weeks for operations tickets to provision databases, storage buckets, and pipeline access for every new service. Which platform-engineering approach gives them approved, self-service provisioning in minutes?
options: Hiring more operations engineers to work the ticket queue faster
Giving every developer full cloud administrator rights
An internal developer platform with golden paths — supported self-service templates and services
A wiki explaining how to file tickets more clearly
explain: An internal developer platform with golden paths makes the blessed, secure way self-service, collapsing two weeks of tickets into minutes while keeping guardrails. More headcount scales the queue rather than removing it, full admin rights abandon least privilege, and wiki-documented tickets are still tickets.

q: A monorepo's CI rebuilds every component from scratch on each run, even when only one service changed — wasting hours daily. Which shares compiled build outputs across developers and CI so unchanged components are never rebuilt?
options: Deleting the build cache to save disk
Running builds on slower machines
Building everything twice for safety
A remote build cache, storing and reusing immutable build artifacts by content hash
explain: A remote cache keyed by content hash lets any developer or CI agent reuse already-built outputs, skipping redundant work across the whole organization. Deleting the cache guarantees full rebuilds, slower machines worsen the waste, and double-building doubles it.

q: A team deploys a rewritten pricing engine inside the existing service behind a feature flag. The new code processes real production requests, but responses still come from the old logic while the team compares outputs. Which technique is this?
options: A dark launch — new code executes on live traffic behind a flag, results compared silently
A big-bang cutover at midnight
Testing only in staging
Emailing customers to try a beta
explain: Dark launches execute new code against real production traffic while users see only the old results, validating behavior with zero user impact. Big-bang cutovers risk everyone at once, staging lacks production's reality, and beta emails reach too few users for statistical confidence.

q: Security findings consistently arrive weeks after code is written, when fixes require rework across merged features. Which approach moves security feedback to the moment code is committed?
options: An annual penetration test
Shift-left security — scanning and policy checks inside the development pipeline
Adding more firewalls in production
Accepting the findings as technical debt
explain: Shift-left embeds SAST, secret, dependency, and IaC scanning into pull requests, so developers fix issues in minutes while the code is fresh. Annual tests find problems a year late, firewalls do not fix code flaws, and accepting debt normalizes the delay.

q: User stories are vague, untestable, and routinely spill across sprints. Which mnemonic describes well-formed stories the team can actually commit to?
options: SMART goals
DRY code
INVEST — Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
YAGNI
explain: INVEST is the standard checklist for story quality: each letter targets exactly the vagueness causing the spillover. SMART describes goals rather than stories, DRY is about code duplication, and YAGNI advises against overbuilding — none define story structure.

q: Sprint planning sessions drag for hours because backlog items arrive unestimated, unclear, and too large. Which recurring ceremony prepares and sizes backlog items BEFORE planning?
options: The sprint retrospective
The daily standup
The sprint demo
Backlog refinement (grooming)
explain: Refinement sessions clarify, split, and estimate upcoming stories so planning starts from ready work instead of debating unknowns. Retrospectives improve process, standups synchronize daily work, and demos review finished increments — none prepare the backlog.

q: A critical, thorny production bug has resisted two solo engineers for a day. The team decides to attack it together at one screen, rotating the keyboard. Which practice is this?
options: Mob programming — the whole team swarming one problem in real time
Working solo in parallel
Handing the ticket to another team
Waiting for the bug to reproduce itself
explain: Mob programming concentrates the team's full context on one hard problem with instant review, often cracking bugs that defeat solo efforts. Parallel solo work duplicates the same stuck approach, handoffs lose context, and waiting is not a strategy.

q: Production servers accumulate undocumented tweaks over months until no one can reproduce them, and rebuilds are feared. Which practice regularly destroys and recreates servers from code so they never drift?
options: Treating servers as beloved pets
Phoenix servers — scheduled rebirth from automation, rising clean each time
Never rebooting, to avoid surprises
Documenting tweaks in a wiki after the fact
explain: Phoenix servers are periodically rebuilt from version-controlled automation, which proves the automation works and prevents drift from accumulating. Pet servers are the anti-pattern described, never rebooting hides rot, and after-the-fact documentation cannot reproduce a server.

q: A new feature must be visible only to internal employees and a beta customer cohort before general availability — not to 5% of random traffic. Which controls precisely WHO sees the feature?
options: A canary deployment to random users
A big-bang release to everyone
Feature flag targeting rules based on user attributes and cohorts
Deploying a separate application for beta users
explain: Targeting rules evaluate user attributes to show the feature exactly to employees and the beta cohort, independent of deployment. Canary percentages are random rather than cohort-based, big-bang exposes everyone, and a separate app doubles the operational burden.

q: Leadership tracks DORA metrics but worries they miss developer experience, satisfaction, and collaboration quality. Which framework complements delivery metrics with satisfaction, performance, activity, communication, and efficiency dimensions?
options: Counting lines of code per developer
Story points completed
More DORA dashboards
The SPACE framework — Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication, Efficiency
explain: SPACE explicitly measures the human and collaborative dimensions DORA omits, giving a balanced view of developer productivity. Lines of code and story points are easily gamed vanity metrics, and more DORA dashboards measure the same four dimensions again.

q: A Kubernetes node reports NotReady. Its pods show as running but are unreachable, and new pods briefly get scheduled to it. What should be checked FIRST?
options: The kubelet, container runtime, and node network health on the affected node
Deleting all pods in the cluster
Rebuilding the entire cluster
The application's source code
explain: NotReady means the node stopped reporting to the control plane — the kubelet, runtime, or node networking is the fault domain, so investigation starts there. Mass pod deletion and cluster rebuilds are destructive overreactions, and application code does not make nodes stop heartbeating.

q: A Kubernetes namespace has been stuck in Terminating for six hours. The resources inside appear mostly gone. What commonly blocks namespace deletion from completing?
options: Too many running pods
Finalizers on resources whose owning controller is no longer running to remove them
A DNS outage
Insufficient storage
explain: Finalizers require a controller to perform cleanup before deletion completes; if that controller is gone, the finalizer never clears and deletion hangs forever. Running pods would show in the namespace, DNS does not gate deletion, and storage pressure presents differently.

q: During node maintenance, kubectl drain hangs indefinitely on one node while others drain fine. The pending pods belong to a deployment protected by a strict PodDisruptionBudget. What is blocking the drain?
options: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
Pod labels
The PodDisruptionBudget — evicting another pod would violate the minimum-available guarantee
Node taints
explain: Drain performs voluntary evictions, which the PDB can veto when evicting would breach min-available — the drain waits rather than violating availability. HPA adjusts replica counts rather than blocking evictions, labels do not gate drains, and taints repel scheduling rather than hanging evictions.

q: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is configured but never adds replicas during clear CPU spikes, while a manually scaled deployment handles the load fine. Which is the MOST common root cause?
options: Too many replicas configured
The wrong container image
A DNS misconfiguration
Missing resource requests on the pods or a broken metrics server, so HPA has no data to decide on
explain: HPA computes utilization against resource requests using metrics-server data — without requests set or with metrics missing, it cannot trigger and stays frozen. Excess replicas would over- rather than under-scale, the image does not gate scaling decisions, and DNS is unrelated to autoscaling.

q: An order page loads in 50ms for the order header, then fires 400 individual queries to fetch line items one by one, taking 8 seconds total. Monitoring shows no slow single query. Which anti-pattern is this, and what is the fix?
options: N+1 queries — fetch the items with a join or eager load instead of one query per row
A missing index
An undersized database
Network latency to the database
explain: N+1 issues come from query count, not query speed: 400 round trips dominate even though each is fast, and a single join collapses them into one. No index fixes 400 round trips, the database is idle between queries rather than undersized, and latency per query is fine — it is the count that kills.

q: When a payment dependency slows down, every client retries aggressively, multiplying the load and turning a slowdown into a full cascading outage. Which bounds the total retry harm clients can cause?
options: Retrying faster and more often
Retry budgets with exponential backoff and jitter, capping retries as a fraction of traffic
Removing all timeouts so requests eventually succeed
Adding more client instances
explain: Retry budgets cap retries at a small fraction of normal traffic with backoff and jitter, so a struggling dependency is not buried by its own clients' retries. Faster retries amplify the storm, no timeouts let threads pile up indefinitely, and more clients multiply the retry sources.

q: Users report intermittent slowness to a cloud application. An mtr report shows clean latency for hops 1-3, then 15% packet loss starting at hop 4 that continues through every later hop to the destination. Where is the problem?
options: The destination server
The user's local router at hop 1
At or just after hop 4 — loss starting at one hop and persisting downstream implicates that hop or its link
DNS resolution
explain: When loss begins at hop 4 and every subsequent hop shows it, the later hops are merely reporting the same dropped packets — the fault lies at hop 4 or the link feeding it. The destination cannot cause loss measured upstream of it, hop 1 is clean, and DNS never appears in per-hop loss data.

q: A NAT gateway drops new connections under heavy load while CPU and memory look healthy. Logs mention table-full errors from the connection tracker. Which resource is exhausted?
options: The route table
The ARP cache
The DNS cache
The conntrack table — every connection consumes an entry, and the table has a fixed maximum
explain: Connection tracking stores state for every flow through the gateway in a fixed-size table; when it fills, new connections are dropped regardless of CPU or memory headroom. Route tables, ARP, and DNS caches are unrelated to per-connection state exhaustion.

q: A certificate is valid, unexpired, and chains to a trusted root — yet browsers show a name-mismatch warning for shop.example.com while www.example.com works fine. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: shop.example.com is missing from the certificate's Subject Alternative Name (SAN) list
The certificate is expired
The private key is too short
The site is served over HTTP
explain: Browsers validate the hostname against the SAN list; a name absent from the list triggers a mismatch warning even when everything else about the certificate is perfect. Expiry would warn on all names, key length does not cause name errors, and HTTP would not present a certificate at all.

q: A page loads over HTTPS, but browsers block several images and scripts with warnings, leaving the page broken. The certificate is valid. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: An expired certificate
Mixed content — the page loads HTTP subresources that browsers block on a secure page
A DNS misconfiguration
A slow origin server
explain: Browsers block active HTTP subresources on HTTPS pages as mixed content, breaking exactly the images and scripts described while the certificate itself is fine. Expiry would warn on the page load itself, DNS would prevent loading entirely, and slowness does not trigger blocking warnings.

q: Long-running report requests fail at exactly 60 seconds when accessed through the load balancer, but succeed when sent directly to the backend. Backend logs show the request was still processing. Which setting is the culprit?
options: The backend crashing at 60 seconds
A DNS TTL of 60 seconds
The load balancer's idle timeout, closing connections before the backend responds
A firewall blocking the report endpoint
explain: A load balancer idle timeout severs connections silent longer than the threshold — the exact-60-second failure through the LB but not direct points squarely at it. A backend crash would fail direct requests too, DNS TTL does not sever established connections, and a firewall block would fail fast rather than at 60 seconds.

q: A site-to-site VPN will not establish. Logs show IKE phase 1 completing successfully, but phase 2 fails repeatedly. The pre-shared key is confirmed correct. What is MOST likely mismatched?
options: The pre-shared key
The peer IP addresses
Dead peer detection timers
Phase 2 IPsec parameters — encryption, integrity, PFS group, or lifetimes
explain: Phase 1 authenticates the peers (PSK confirmed working), while phase 2 negotiates the actual IPsec SAs — failure here means the transform sets, PFS groups, or lifetimes disagree. The PSK is proven by phase 1 success, peer IPs are needed for phase 1 itself, and DPD timers affect liveness rather than negotiation.

q: Legitimate company emails land in recipients' spam folders, while attackers successfully send spoofed emails appearing to come from the company's domain. Which set of DNS records authenticates legitimate senders and tells receivers how to handle failures?
options: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC working together
MX records alone
A records for the mail server
Removing all DNS records
explain: SPF authorizes sending servers, DKIM cryptographically signs messages, and DMARC ties them together with a handling policy — the complete anti-spoofing trio. MX records only direct inbound mail, A records merely resolve names, and removing records breaks mail entirely.

q: The same class of outage recurs every few months. Each incident is fixed at the symptom level — a service is restarted, a disk is cleared — but nothing changes structurally. Which technique drives the investigation past symptoms to the systemic root cause?
options: Rebooting more quickly next time
The Five Whys — repeatedly asking why until reaching the process or design flaw
Assigning blame to whoever was on call
Adding more dashboards
explain: The Five Whys iteratively peels symptom layers until the systemic cause — the missing automation, the design flaw — is exposed and fixable. Faster reboots optimize the symptom response, blame ends learning, and dashboards observe without explaining.

q: A Java application stops responding but CPU sits near idle — threads appear stuck waiting rather than spinning. GC logs are clean. Which diagnostic reveals what every thread is currently doing?
options: A heap dump
Restarting the application
A thread dump, showing each thread's stack trace and lock state
Increasing the heap size
explain: A thread dump captures every thread's stack trace and monitor state at a moment in time, exposing deadlocks and threads blocked on locks or I/O — matching the hung-but-idle symptom. Heap dumps show memory contents rather than thread activity, restarts destroy the evidence, and heap size is irrelevant with clean GC.

q: A database stored procedure runs in milliseconds for most parameter values but takes minutes for a few specific ones. The cached execution plan was compiled for an atypical parameter value. Which phenomenon is this, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: A missing index
Lock contention
Disk failure
Parameter sniffing — mitigate with recompile hints or optimize-for-unknown plan guides
explain: Parameter sniffing reuses a plan optimized for the first-seen parameter value, which performs terribly for values with different selectivity — the classic fast-for-some, slow-for-others pattern. A missing index would be slow for all values, lock contention shows blocking rather than plan choice, and disk failure does not vary by parameter.

q: An architect evaluates a multi-region key-value store. Beyond the familiar partition trade-off between availability and consistency, she notes the system also trades request latency against consistency while the network is perfectly healthy. Which theorem captures both trade-offs?
options: The CAP theorem, which already covers both the partition and the healthy-network cases
PACELC, which states that during a Partition there is an Availability-Consistency trade-off, and Elsewhere a Latency-Consistency trade-off
The Byzantine Generals Problem, which governs all distributed consistency decisions
Amdahl's law, which limits the speedup from adding database nodes
explain: PACELC extends CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability vs Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose Latency vs Consistency. CAP alone only addresses behavior during partitions. The Byzantine Generals Problem concerns faulty/malicious nodes, and Amdahl's law concerns parallel speedup — neither describes this trade-off.

q: A cloud application serves two kinds of requests through one load balancer: quick static-asset requests and long-running report-generation requests that hold connections for minutes. With round-robin distribution, some servers accumulate many long requests and slow down while others sit idle. Which load-balancing algorithm BEST evens out the load?
options: Round robin with shorter health-check intervals
Least connections, which routes each new request to the server with the fewest active connections
IP-hash stickiness based on the client's source address
Static weights assigned by each server's CPU size at deploy time
explain: Least-connections routing accounts for connection duration, so servers holding long report requests receive fewer new ones. Round robin ignores how long connections last, and shorter health checks do not change distribution. IP hashing can worsen imbalance by pinning heavy clients, and static deploy-time weights go stale as conditions change.

q: A company runs a global API edge service from five regions. It wants every user worldwide to reach the nearest healthy region automatically, with failover handled at the routing layer instead of waiting out DNS TTL caching. Which technique advertises the same IP address from all five regions so internet routing delivers each client to the closest one?
options: Anycast
Geolocation DNS records
Round-robin DNS
NAT traversal
explain: Anycast announces the same IP prefix from multiple sites, and BGP routing naturally delivers each client to the topologically nearest healthy announcement, with fast failover. Geolocation DNS depends on resolver-location accuracy and still suffers TTL caching delays. Round-robin DNS ignores geography entirely, and NAT traversal is an unrelated connectivity technique.

q: A team runs dozens of microservices written in three languages. They need uniform log shipping, metrics collection, and mutual TLS for every service, but they cannot modify each service's code. Which pattern deploys a helper container alongside each application container in the same pod to provide these cross-cutting concerns?
options: An init container that configures the network and then exits
A DaemonSet that runs one agent per cluster node
A sidecar container sharing the pod's lifecycle and network namespace
Embedding the agents as shared libraries compiled into each service
explain: A sidecar runs alongside the application container in the same pod, sharing its network namespace, so it can add logging, metrics, and mTLS with zero code changes. Init containers run to completion before the app starts, so they cannot serve ongoing traffic. DaemonSets are per-node rather than per-pod, and embedding libraries requires the code changes the team cannot make.

q: An HPC team runs latency-sensitive simulations on cloud VMs. Virtualized networking adds jitter because every packet traverses the hypervisor's virtual switch. Which feature gives the VM's network interface near-bare-metal performance by bypassing the hypervisor for the data path?
options: Enabling jumbo frames on the virtual switch
SR-IOV (single-root I/O virtualization), which maps virtual functions of the physical NIC directly into the guest
Placing the instances in the same subnet
Increasing the MTU on the virtual switch
explain: SR-IOV (sold as enhanced networking) lets the guest drive the physical NIC's virtual functions directly, removing the hypervisor from the packet path and cutting latency and jitter. Jumbo frames improve bulk throughput, not hypervisor bypass. Same-subnet placement does not remove the virtual switch, and an MTU tweak is marginal.

q: A company runs a Hadoop/HDFS cluster where each rack must hold a complete set of data block replicas, so losing a whole rack never loses data. The scheduler must also know which nodes share a rack to place replicas correctly. Which placement strategy spreads instances across logical partitions such as racks, with awareness of the partition topology?
options: Partition placement groups, which distribute instances across logical partitions like racks
Cluster placement groups, which pack instances as tightly together as possible
Spread placement across distinct physical hosts
Availability zone placement
explain: Partition placement groups spread instances across logical partitions (racks) and expose the topology so replica-aware software like HDFS places copies correctly. Cluster placement does the opposite — it packs instances tightly for low latency. Spread placement separates hosts but is not rack-topology-aware, and availability zones are a coarser boundary than racks.

q: A company lifts its monolithic VM-based application to cloud VMs with no architectural changes, then calls it 'cloud-native' in marketing. An architect objects. Which statement BEST captures the real distinction?
options: Both terms mean the same thing, so the architect is wrong
