q: A database's read traffic has tripled. An engineer enables the managed database's Multi-AZ option expecting read queries to spread across both copies. Reads do not improve. Why?
options: Read replicas only accelerate write traffic.
Multi-AZ is a high-availability failover copy, not a scaling mechanism — the standby serves no production reads; read replicas are the feature that scales read traffic.
Multi-AZ requires a special database driver the application lacks.
The standby copy was placed in the wrong availability zone.
explain: Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby for automatic failover — it absorbs no production reads by design, which is the classic exam trap. Horizontal read scaling is what read replicas are for. The distractors invent driver requirements, invert the replica's purpose, and misdiagnose placement as the cause.

q: A social app stores profiles in a geo-replicated database. Users complain that after updating their profile, the page sometimes shows the old data for several seconds. Which consistency model does the application need?
options: Read-your-writes consistency: a session always sees its own prior writes, even while other users' updates still propagate with a lag.
A longer cache TTL on profile pages.
Strong global consistency for every read worldwide.
Eventual consistency with no session guarantees.
explain: Read-your-writes is the targeted fix: it guarantees the writer's own session sees fresh data — via session affinity or version tracking — without paying global-consensus latency on every read. Full strong consistency is overkill for this symptom, raw eventual consistency is the broken status quo, and longer TTLs deepen the staleness.

q: A team carves a /28 subnet for an auto-scaling web tier, calculating 16 addresses. Instances fail to launch once 11 are running. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Auto-scaling groups cannot exceed 10 instances.
The instances exhausted the account's CPU quota.
A /28 provides 28 usable addresses, so the math was right.
The cloud platform reserves several addresses in every subnet (network, broadcast, router, DNS), so a /28 yields only 11 usable addresses — the subnet is simply too small.
explain: Cloud subnets reserve addresses (typically network, broadcast, gateway, and DNS), leaving a /28 with 11 usable — capacity planning must subtract reservations. The distractors invent an ASG limit, blame CPU quota, and confuse the '/28' prefix length with '28 addresses.'

q: An enterprise has exhausted private IPv4 space: hundreds of peered VPCs and on-premises networks collide on 10.0.0.0/8, and renumbering is impractical. Which strategy BEST resolves the exhaustion long-term?
options: Adopt IPv6 (dual-stack) for new networks, gaining effectively unlimited address space and eliminating NAT and overlap workarounds.
Deploy NAT everywhere to reuse the same ranges.
Carve 10.0.0.0/8 into smaller subnets.
Buy public IPv4 addresses for internal use.
explain: IPv6's vast space ends exhaustion and overlap games permanently, and dual-stack lets adoption proceed incrementally. Subdividing 10/8 cannot create addresses that do not exist; NAT hides addresses but does not resolve routing collisions between identical ranges; buying public IPv4 for internal use is costly and pointless.

q: A fleet of 50,000 battery-powered sensors on flaky cellular links must publish small readings every minute. HTTP polling from each device drains batteries and drops messages. Which protocol is DESIGNED for this pattern?
options: MQTT — a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol with tiny headers, persistent sessions, and quality-of-service levels built for constrained, unreliable devices.
GraphQL over WebSockets.
FTP for scheduled file uploads.
SMTP with batched messages.
explain: MQTT was built for exactly this: minimal bandwidth, brokered pub/sub so devices never poll, and QoS levels for delivery assurance over lossy links. FTP and SMTP are file/mail transfer protocols, and GraphQL-over-WebSockets adds overhead suited to rich client apps, not constrained sensors.

q: A company stores regulated data in object storage. It wants encryption at rest with provider-managed infrastructure BUT with its own control over key rotation, auditing, and instant revocation. Which option fits?
options: TLS in transit only.
Client-side encryption with keys stored in application config files.
Server-side encryption with KMS-managed keys (SSE-KMS): the provider handles the crypto infrastructure while the customer controls the key's rotation, access policy, audit trail, and disablement.
SSE-S3 with provider-managed keys.
explain: SSE-KMS splits duties correctly: the provider runs the encryption while the customer owns the key lifecycle — rotation schedules, access policy, logged usage, and one-click disable that renders data unreadable. SSE-S3 gives no key control; config-file keys are unmanageable and leak-prone; TLS protects only data in flight.

q: A company must exit its datacenter in 90 days. Its monolith cannot be rewritten in time, but leadership also wants cloud-native benefits eventually. Which migration sequencing is MOST realistic?
options: Rehost (lift-and-shift) now to meet the deadline, then replatform and refactor incrementally once running in the cloud.
Lift-and-shift and declare the migration complete.
Rewrite everything as microservices before the move.
Stay in the datacenter until the rewrite is complete.
explain: Rehost buys speed when the deadline dominates; replatforming afterward captures elasticity and managed services without big-bang risk. A full rewrite first blows the 90-day constraint; waiting keeps the datacenter; stopping at lift-and-shift abandons the optimization phase the business asked for.

q: Three microservices share one relational database for 'simplicity.' Now every schema change requires all three teams to coordinate deploys, and one team's heavy report locks tables the others need. Which data pattern fixes the coupling?
options: A bigger shared database server.
A larger database connection pool.
One database per developer.
Database per service: each microservice owns its private data store and exposes data only through its API, so teams change schemas and deploy independently.
explain: Database-per-service enforces the bounded context at the data layer: no shared tables means no cross-team schema coordination and no cross-service lock contention. A bigger box keeps the coupling, more connections do not address schema coordination, and per-developer databases are a parody of the pattern.

q: A product catalog's search uses SQL LIKE '%keyword%' queries. Past 10 million rows, searches slow to seconds and relevance ranking is impossible. Which technology is PURPOSE-BUILT for this workload?
options: More read replicas of the relational database.
Caching the LIKE query results.
A full-text search engine (inverted index): tokenizes text, ranks by relevance, and answers keyword queries in milliseconds at scale.
A longer query timeout for the LIKE searches.
explain: Inverted indexes are the data structure search is built on — tokenization, stemming, and relevance scoring that LIKE can never provide. Read replicas multiply the same slow scan, longer timeouts normalize bad UX, and result caching fails against the combinatorial space of ad-hoc keyword queries.

q: A streaming vendor claims its platform delivers 'exactly-once processing' to consumers. The architect remains skeptical. What is the technically accurate view?
options: At-most-once delivery is safer because it avoids duplicates.
Exactly-once is guaranteed if the broker is configured for it.
Idempotency is only needed for at-most-once systems.

True exactly-once delivery across a distributed system is effectively impossible; the honest implementation is at-least-once delivery combined with idempotent consumers, which yields exactly-once effects.
explain: Networks can always duplicate or ambiguously fail a delivery, so exactly-once delivery cannot be guaranteed — but idempotent processing makes redelivery harmless, producing exactly-once outcomes. Broker settings cannot repeal distributed-systems physics; at-most-once silently drops messages; and idempotency is the companion of at-least-once, not at-most-once.

q: An order workflow spans five microservices. The team debates two designs: a central workflow service commanding each step, versus services reacting to each other's events with no central controller. What is this design decision called?
options: Monolith versus microservices.
The competing-consumers pattern.
Synchronous versus asynchronous communication.
Orchestration (central conductor) versus choreography (decentralized event reactions) — a trade-off between centralized visibility and loose coupling.
explain: Orchestration centralizes workflow logic for visibility and control at the cost of coupling to the conductor; choreography keeps services decoupled via events at the cost of harder-to-trace flows. Sync/async is an orthogonal transport choice; monolith/microservices is a different decomposition question; competing consumers is about scaling queue workers.

q: A company serves a mobile app, a web app, and a partner API from the same backend. The mobile app needs tiny aggregated payloads, the web app needs rich data, and partners need a stable subset — one general API serves all three badly. Which pattern fits?
options: A single GraphQL schema with no per-client ownership.
Direct database access for each client.
Backend-for-Frontend (BFF): a dedicated API layer per client type that aggregates and shapes backend responses to each client's needs.
One more generic REST endpoint for everyone.
explain: BFF gives each client an API shaped to its needs and owned alongside it, so mobile payload size and partner stability evolve independently. Another generic endpoint repeats the compromise, direct DB access abandons service boundaries, and one shared GraphQL schema without per-client ownership just moves the tug-of-war.

q: Analysts wait 24 hours for the nightly ETL batch before querying today's transactions, and the ETL jobs keep breaking on schema changes. Which modern integration approach removes the batch pipeline?
options: More frequent batch jobs.
Manual CSV exports for analysts.
Zero-ETL: the database replicates changes directly into the analytics engine, so fresh data is queryable without a batch pipeline to maintain.
A bigger ETL server.
explain: Zero-ETL eliminates the pipeline as a thing to build, break, and babysit — replication keeps analytics fresh continuously. Bigger or more frequent batches preserve the failure-prone middle layer; CSV exports are a regression to manual toil.

q: After a supply-chain attack, leadership demands proof that every production artifact was built from a specific reviewed commit on trusted infrastructure — not tampered with afterward. Which framework defines these build-integrity levels?
options: DORA metrics.
SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts): grades builds on provenance, requiring hermetic, isolated builds that produce signed, verifiable provenance linking each artifact to its source.
The twelve-factor app methodology.
Semantic versioning.
explain: SLSA specifically addresses 'was this artifact built correctly from the right source' via provenance requirements at increasing levels. DORA measures delivery speed and stability, semver numbers releases, and twelve-factor guides application design — none attest to build integrity.

q: A team's Kubernetes-based CI cannot mount the Docker socket (a known container-escape risk), so image builds fail. Which tool builds container images inside Kubernetes without a Docker daemon?
options: Kaniko (or similar daemonless builders): builds images from a Dockerfile in userspace without requiring the Docker socket or privileged mode.
Building images on developers' laptops and pushing them.
Skipping image builds and deploying raw source code.
Mounting the Docker socket anyway with a warning comment.
explain: Daemonless builders execute Dockerfile instructions in userspace, fitting locked-down CI where the Docker socket is forbidden. Socket mounting reintroduces the escape risk, laptop builds are unauditable, and deploying raw source discards the immutable-artifact model.

q: A feature-flag flip in a ConfigMap takes effect only after someone manually restarts the Deployment -- and twice the on-call forgot, leaving stale flags in production. Which Kustomize feature makes config changes roll automatically?
options: A runbook reminding on-call to restart the Deployment.
Baking flags into the container image.
Mounting flags via hostPath volumes.
configMapGenerator with content hashing: the generated ConfigMap name includes a hash of its contents, so any change alters the pod spec and triggers a rolling update.
explain: Hash-suffixed ConfigMaps turn content changes into spec changes, which the Deployment controller rolls automatically -- no human step to forget. Runbooks rely on memory, hostPath breaks the container model, and image-baked flags force rebuilds per toggle.

q: A GitOps-managed queue worker needs its message queue to exist before the workers start, but the GitOps tool syncs alphabetically and the workers crash-loop on the missing queue. Which mechanism enforces the ordering?
options: Letting the workers crash-loop until the queue appears.
Creating the queue by hand before every deploy.
Sync waves (or PreSync hooks): assign the queue resource an earlier wave so GitOps creates it and waits before syncing the workers.
Removing the queue from version control.
explain: Sync waves make ordering declarative and enforced -- the pipeline cannot start dependents until earlier waves succeed. Manual creation is forgotten under pressure, crash-looping is the current outage, and unversioned resources reintroduce drift.

q: A team deletes a Kubernetes Service manifest from Git, but the Service keeps running in the cluster for weeks, still receiving traffic and confusing debugging. What GitOps setting prevents this drift?
options: Restarting the GitOps agent every night.
Never deleting manifests from Git.
Enable pruning (sync with prune): the GitOps agent deletes cluster resources that no longer exist in Git, keeping live state converged.
Deleting resources by hand after every Git change.
explain: Pruning closes the loop: Git is the source of truth for existence, not just content. Manual deletion is forgotten, never-deleting rots the repo, and agent restarts do not change reconciliation semantics.

q: A team must add an index to a 500-million-row production table. A naive ALTER TABLE would lock writes for an hour. Which online-schema-change approach avoids the long lock?
options: Running the ALTER TABLE during peak traffic.
An online schema-change tool (gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change): copies the table in the background, replays ongoing writes via the binary log, then swaps tables in a brief atomic cutover.
Adding the index to a backup copy of the database.
Dropping the table and recreating it with the index.
explain: Online schema-change tools decouple the heavy copy from the cutover: background copy plus binlog replay means only a seconds-long atomic swap blocks writes. Peak-hour ALTERs, drop-recreate, and backup-only changes are downtime, data loss, or no-ops respectively.

q: Every dependency update requires a developer to hand-edit image tags in Git, and updates lag for weeks. Which GitOps automation keeps image tags current without manual commits?
options: Flux image automation: policies scan the registry and automatically commit updated image tags to Git when new versions match the policy.
Disabling dependency updates entirely.
Deploying the ':latest' tag and skipping Git.
A developer editing tags every Friday.
explain: Image automation keeps Git as the source of truth while removing the human from the tag-update loop — policy-gated, auditable commits. ':latest' destroys traceability, manual Fridays preserve the lag, and freezing updates stockpiles CVEs.

q: A startup with five services finds Helm chart maintenance outweighs its benefits -- they only ever change replica counts and image tags per environment. Which lighter-weight tool fits?
options: Copy-pasting full manifests per environment.
Writing a custom Helm chart per service.
Editing YAML by hand in production.
Kustomize: base manifests plus per-environment overlays for simple patches, with no chart scaffolding or templating to maintain.
explain: Kustomize matches the actual need -- small per-environment patches -- without chart overhead. Custom charts add the maintenance being escaped, copying manifests recreates drift, and hand-editing production is uncontrolled.

q: A Helm upgrade succeeds, but the new application version crashes because it expects a CustomResourceDefinition version the cluster does not have. The chart included the updated CRD. Why did Helm not install it?
options: CRDs update automatically alongside the application.
The cluster rejected the new CRD.
Helm does not upgrade CRDs on 'helm upgrade' — CRDs are installed once at install time and must be managed separately from the release lifecycle.
Helm upgrades are atomic by default, which skips CRDs.
explain: Helm deliberately treats CRDs as cluster-scoped singletons outside the release lifecycle, so upgrades skip them — teams must apply CRD changes explicitly. The cluster never saw the new CRD, atomicity is a different feature, and 'automatic' is precisely the false belief that caused the crash.

q: A new PCI-scoped service needs per-pod database credentials that expire every hour, and developers must never handle passwords. Which pattern delivers this without application code changes?
options: The same credentials as the non-PCI services.
One shared password in a Kubernetes Secret.
Hardcoded passwords rotated by developers.
Vault Agent injector sidecar: injects dynamically generated, short-lived credentials into each pod at startup and rotates them automatically.
explain: The injector gives every pod its own short-lived lease -- compromise windows shrink to the hour and rotation is automatic, with no code changes. Shared secrets, manual rotation, and credential reuse across scopes all violate the PCI requirement.

q: A Terraform module creates subnets with 'count', but removing the middle subnet from the list forces Terraform to recreate every later subnet — causing an outage. Which construct avoids this?
options: A larger count value.
Splitting the subnets into two separate Terraform projects.
for_each with stable keys: resources are addressed by their map key, so removing one entry destroys only that resource instead of shifting every index.
Creating subnets by hand in the console.
explain: count addresses resources by position, so list edits cascade; for_each addresses by key, so edits are surgical. Bigger counts, project splits, and manual creation all dodge the actual addressing flaw.

q: An Ansible playbook restarts the web tier across 200 servers at once, causing a full outage during every deploy. Which playbook feature rolls the restart in safe batches?
options: Disabling the load balancer health checks during the run.
Running the playbook faster to shorten the outage.
serial (with health checks): run the play against a limited batch of hosts at a time, verifying each batch before proceeding.
Restarting every server twice for safety.
explain: serial bounds the blast radius of each wave and gates progress on batch health — the rolling-restart pattern. Speed, repetition, and disabled checks all amplify rather than contain the outage.

q: A platform team supports 20 application teams. Each team's Ingress annotations conflict, vendor-specific hacks spread, and upgrades break routing. Which Kubernetes API gives them a standardized, role-separated routing model?
options: A shared document of approved Ingress annotations.
One cloud load balancer per team.
NodePort services with manual DNS entries.
The Gateway API (Gateway + HTTPRoute): a standardized, expressive routing API with clear role boundaries, replacing annotation-driven Ingress.
explain: Gateway API was designed for exactly this: first-class route objects and role separation (infrastructure vs application teams) instead of annotation soup. NodePorts abandon L7 routing, per-team LBs multiply cost, and documenting the hacks standardizes the mess.

q: A team builds container images on ARM-based laptops, but production runs x86 nodes — and some edge nodes are ARM. Images fail with 'exec format error' on mismatched nodes. What is the robust fix?
options: Run production through QEMU emulation.
Build multi-architecture images (manifest lists) containing both ARM64 and AMD64 variants, so each node pulls its native architecture automatically.
Build separate tags like 'app-arm' and 'app-x86'.
Force everyone to develop on x86 laptops.
explain: Multi-arch manifests let the registry serve the right binary per node transparently — one tag, correct architecture everywhere. Mandating laptop architectures ignores the edge fleet; emulation sacrifices performance and reliability; split tags push architecture awareness into every deployment.

q: A Helm upgrade introduces a regression. The team needs the failed release to roll itself back automatically instead of leaving the cluster half-upgraded while someone notices. Which upgrade flag provides this?
options: --atomic: automatically rolls back to the previous release if the upgrade fails, cleaning up partial state.
Deleting the release and reinstalling it.
--force, which recreates resources.
--dry-run, which previews the changes.
explain: --atomic couples upgrade success to automatic rollback, so a failed release never lingers half-applied. Dry-run only previews, --force pushes through problems destructively, and delete/reinstall is manual toil that discards release history.

q: A build pipeline needs a private package-registry token during the Docker build, but baking it into a layer would leak it to anyone who pulls the image. How should the build consume the secret?
options: Embed the token in the application code.
COPY the token file in, then delete it in the next layer.
BuildKit secret mounts (--secret): expose the secret as a temporary file during that single build step; it never lands in any image layer.
Pass the token as a build ARG, then unset it in a later step.
explain: Secret mounts exist precisely because layers are forever — the secret is visible only to the running build step. ARGs linger in image history, deleted-in-later-layer files persist in earlier layers, and code-embedded tokens leak through version control as well.

q: Every pull request needs an isolated full-stack environment for testing, including a realistic database — but provisioning full database copies per PR takes hours. Which approach gives each PR a fast, isolated database?
options: An empty database per pull request.
One shared database for all pull requests.
Testing against the production database directly.
Database branching (copy-on-write clones): each PR gets an instant, isolated, writable clone of production-like data that shares unchanged pages with the parent.
explain: Copy-on-write branching makes per-PR databases instant and isolated — writes go to the branch while reads share the parent's pages. Shared databases cause cross-test interference, empty databases hide data-dependent bugs, and testing on production risks real data.

q: Weekly full backups no longer fit in the backup window, but the team fears long incremental chains after a painful 30-incremental restore. Which technology keeps incrementals fast AND restores simple?
options: Full backups every night.
Incrementals without any change tracking.
Skipping backups on weekends.
Changed-block tracking (CBT): the platform tracks exactly which blocks changed, so incrementals copy only deltas and synthetic fulls can be assembled without re-reading everything.
explain: CBT attacks both problems: block-level change maps make incrementals quick to create, and synthetic-full assembly avoids marathon restore chains. Nightly fulls cannot fit the window, untracked incrementals are slow to scan and chain, and skipping weekends just creates coverage gaps.

q: A team pages on high CPU, full disks, and saturated queues — yet users experience outages the dashboards never flagged, while engineers get paged for resource spikes users never felt. According to SRE practice, what should alerts target?
options: Every resource metric, paged immediately.
Symptoms (user-facing pain: latency, error rate, availability), not causes — page when users hurt, and use resource metrics for diagnosis and tickets.
Only disk space, the most common failure.
Nothing — wait for users to complain.
explain: Symptom-based alerting aligns paging with user impact: causes are for dashboards and diagnosis, symptoms are for waking people up. Paging on every cause creates the fatigue described, silence abandons the team, and single-metric focus misses everything else.

q: A nightly batch pipeline has no 'requests' — it runs jobs. The team tries to apply RED (rate/errors/duration of requests) and it does not fit. Which signals suit a batch workload?
options: RED metrics applied the same way as the API.
Job-oriented signals: runs completed versus failed, run duration against historical baseline, data freshness (how stale the output is), and output record counts.
No monitoring — batches either work or they do not.
Only CPU utilization of the worker nodes.
explain: Batch health is about job outcomes and data freshness, not request rates — a 'successful' run that produced zero records or day-old data is a failure RED cannot see. Forcing request metrics, watching only CPU, or skipping monitoring all miss the pipeline's actual contract.

q: A critical kernel CVE is announced, but the fleet cannot tolerate the reboot window a normal patch requires — uptime SLAs are strict. Which technology applies the kernel fix without rebooting?
options: Ignoring the CVE until the next maintenance window.
Kernel livepatching: loads the patched code into the running kernel, fixing the CVE with zero downtime for supported patch classes.
Recompiling the kernel by hand on each host.
Rebooting the entire fleet at once anyway.
explain: Livepatch is designed for exactly this: critical kernel fixes without the reboot, buying time until the next scheduled window. Mass reboots violate the SLA, waiting leaves the CVE exploitable, and hand-compiled kernels still require reboots to take effect.

q: A team wants to discover hidden weaknesses with fault injection, but leadership fears chaos experiments will cause a real customer-facing outage. Which safeguard makes production chaos responsible?
options: Running chaos in production with no limits.
Running chaos only in the CEO's demo environment.
Strict blast-radius controls: run during business hours with automatic abort on SLO breach, limited to a small percentage of traffic or a single zone, with a one-click halt.
Never running chaos experiments at all.
explain: Blast-radius discipline — bounded scope, steady-state monitoring, automatic halt — is what separates chaos engineering from sabotage. Unlimited production fault injection is reckless; avoiding it entirely leaves weaknesses for real incidents to find; demo environments do not resemble production.

q: A company bought standard reserved instances, but six months later the workload moves to a new instance family the reservations do not cover — and the reservations sit unused. Which commitment type would have allowed the change?
options: Even longer standard reservations.
Standard reservations with no exchange option.
Convertible reservations (or flexible savings plans): allow exchanging the commitment for a different instance family, size, or region as needs evolve.
On-demand pricing for everything.
explain: Convertible commitments trade a slightly smaller discount for flexibility — the right call when instance families are likely to shift. Standard reservations lock the shape, all-on-demand abandons savings, and longer terms magnify the mistake.

q: A backup verification script LISTs millions of objects and issues a HEAD per object nightly. Storage is cheap, but the object-storage bill tripled. What is the team paying for?
options: API request costs: object storage charges per thousand requests, so millions of LIST/HEAD calls dominate the bill even though the bytes stored are cheap.
Data transfer out to the internet.
The storage capacity in bytes.
A billing error that should be disputed.
explain: Object-storage economics have two axes — bytes and requests — and request-heavy patterns like per-object HEADs can dwarf capacity charges. The bytes did not triple, nothing left the region, and the bill reflects documented per-request pricing.

q: A team enables VPC flow logs on every subnet 'for security,' then gets a shocking ingestion bill — most logs are never queried. Which approach keeps the security value while controlling cost?
options: Disable flow logs entirely.
Log everything forever.
Scope and sample: log only sensitive subnets (or sample a percentage), set aggressive retention, and aggregate before long-term storage.
Enable logging only after an incident is declared.
explain: Flow-log value is concentrated: sensitive subnets and recent windows matter most, so scoping plus short hot retention preserves forensics at a fraction of the cost. Disabling loses the capability, log-everything-forever is the bill shock, and post-incident enabling cannot retroactively capture evidence.

q: The cloud bill keeps growing though no new projects launched. Investigation finds unattached elastic IPs, load balancers with no targets, and NAT gateways serving deleted subnets. Which practice prevents this recurring waste?
options: Deleting resources at random to save money.
Manual quarterly audits of the console.
Continuous idle-resource hygiene: automated discovery of unattached or unused resources with owner tagging and scheduled reclamation.
Bigger budgets to absorb the waste.
explain: Cloud waste is continuous, so the control must be continuous: automated detection plus ownership data makes reclamation safe and routine. Bigger budgets fund the leak, quarterly audits let waste compound for months, and random deletion is reckless.

q: Compliance requires one year of searchable security logs, but keeping a year in hot searchable storage costs a fortune. Which retention design meets the requirement affordably?
options: Keeping logs only on local disks.
One year of hot storage for everything.
Deleting logs after 30 days.
Tiered retention: recent logs in hot searchable storage, older logs aged automatically to cheap archival tiers, with only aggregated metrics kept hot long-term.
explain: Tiering matches cost to access pattern -- investigations query recent data, compliance needs the archive -- satisfying the year-long requirement without year-long hot prices. All-hot is the fortune, 30-day deletion violates the requirement, and local disks are neither searchable nor durable.

q: A startup's cloud bill doubles every quarter. The board asks for a durable framework for cost accountability, not a one-time audit. Which FinOps lifecycle should the company adopt?
options: Freeze all cloud spending for a quarter.
Buy reserved capacity for everything immediately.
Move all workloads back on-premises.
Inform (visibility and allocation), Optimize (rightsizing, commitments, waste removal), Operate (continuous governance and accountability).
explain: FinOps is a continuous loop: you cannot optimize what you cannot see (inform), savings follow understanding (optimize), and without governance costs rebound (operate). Blanket reservations risk massive waste, repatriation is a major decision needing data, and spending freezes just defer the problem.

q: Finance sees the company pays for 100 reserved compute units but only 60 are ever used, while a separate workload pays full on-demand rates. Which two metrics untangle this misalignment?
options: Average CPU utilization.

Coverage (what share of usage sits under commitment) and utilization (what share of commitments is actually used) -- low utilization with low coverage means commitments were bought for the wrong shapes.
The number of running instances.
Total monthly spend.
explain: Utilization exposes wasted commitments; coverage exposes uncommitted spend -- together they reveal the mismatch. Totals, instance counts, and CPU averages cannot show whether commitments match real usage.

q: A team's CI runners sit idle 70% of the time but must handle bursts at merge rush hour. On-demand runners cost a fortune for mostly-idle capacity. Which purchasing option fits this intermittent, fault-tolerant workload?
options: Three-year reservations for the runner fleet.
Bigger on-demand instances.
Dedicated hosts for the runners.
Spot (preemptible) instances for runners: CI jobs can retry on interruption, and the deep discount matches the intermittent pattern.
explain: CI is the textbook spot workload — interruptible, retryable, bursty — converting idle waste into cheap elastic capacity. Reservations lock in peak pricing for mostly-idle boxes, dedicated hosts are the premium tier, and bigger on-demand instances just scale the waste.

q: Thousands of old AMIs accumulate over years; each references snapshots that cost money monthly, and nobody knows which images are still needed. Which lifecycle control fixes this?
options: Stop building new AMIs entirely.
AMI lifecycle policies: tag AMIs with creation dates and automatically deregister (and delete associated snapshots) those past the retention window.
Delete AMIs manually when someone remembers.
Keep every AMI forever, just in case.
explain: Lifecycle policies make retention a rule instead of a memory — expired AMIs and their snapshots are reclaimed automatically. Keep-forever is the bill, manual cleanup does not happen reliably, and halting new images breaks the golden-image pipeline.

q: Development VMs sit idle every night and weekend, burning compute spend. Stopping them loses in-memory state developers want preserved, and start/stop scripts keep breaking. Which feature preserves RAM state while stopping the billing?
options: Snapshotting the disks nightly.
Leaving the VMs running.
Terminating the VMs every night.
Hibernation: saves RAM to disk and stops the instance — compute billing halts while the exact in-memory state resumes on start.
explain: Hibernation is stop-with-memory: the OS state including RAM is persisted, billing stops, and resume restores the session. Termination loses everything, always-on pays for idle, and disk snapshots do not capture RAM and need manual restore choreography.

q: After a deployment, error rates climb — but nobody can tell whether the deploy caused it or it started earlier, because dashboards show no deploy events. Which observability practice closes this gap?
options: Reconstructing the timeline from memory.
Deployment markers (annotations): automatically record every deployment as an event overlaid on dashboards, correlating changes with metric shifts.
Building more dashboards.
Rolling back every deploy on suspicion.
explain: Markers turn 'did the deploy cause this?' into a visual fact — the event line sits exactly where metrics moved. Memory is unreliable, more dashboards lack the event dimension, and suspicion-driven rollbacks create churn without diagnosis.

q: A team enables CloudTrail data events on a busy object-storage bucket 'for complete auditing' and the logging bill explodes — management events were pennies. What distinguishes the two?
options: Management events already cover object reads.
Data events log every object-level API call (each GET/PUT), so high-traffic buckets generate millions of events; management events log only control-plane actions and are far fewer.
Data events are free; only storage costs apply.
The only fix is disabling all logging.
explain: The cost difference is volume: data-plane calls scale with traffic while control-plane calls scale with humans. Assuming data events are free, expecting management events to cover reads, or disabling logging all miss the actual trade-off — scope data events to sensitive buckets.

q: Microservices authenticate to each other with static API keys committed in config files. Keys never rotate, and one leaked in a log last quarter. Which modern pattern replaces static keys?
options: Longer, more complex static API keys.
Short-lived OAuth 2.0 client-credentials tokens (or workload identity): services authenticate and receive minutes-long tokens automatically, so there is no static secret to leak.
Disabling authentication between services.
One shared API key across all services.
explain: Short-lived tokens eliminate the standing secret — theft windows shrink to minutes and rotation is automatic. Complex static keys, shared keys, and no auth all preserve or worsen the standing-secret problem.

q: After a competitor's domain was spoofed with a fraudulently issued certificate, a domain owner wants to ensure only its contracted CA can ever issue certificates for its domains. Which DNS control does this?
options: DNSSEC alone.
Wildcard certificates for all subdomains.
CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) DNS records, which declare the only certificate authorities permitted to issue certificates for the domain.
Longer certificate validity periods.
explain: CAA whitelists issuing CAs; compliant CAs must refuse issuance they are not authorized for. Longer validity extends attacker utility, wildcards widen scope, and DNSSEC authenticates DNS data but does not constrain CA issuance.

q: After a rogue-certificate incident, the team wants early warning the next time ANY publicly trusted certificate is issued for its domains — even by an unexpected CA. Which mechanism provides this?
options: Pinning certificates in mobile apps.
Checking certificate expiry dates monthly.
Using only one CA forever.
Certificate Transparency (CT) log monitoring: all public CAs must log issuance to public, append-only logs that the team can watch for its domains.
explain: CT makes secret issuance impossible — every public certificate is logged, so monitoring the logs detects rogue issuance within hours. Expiry checks, pinning, and CA loyalty all miss certificates issued elsewhere.

q: An API accepts bearer tokens, and the team worries that a stolen token can be replayed from anywhere. Which mechanism binds a token to the client that legitimately holds it?
options: DPoP (Demonstrating Proof of Possession) / sender-constrained tokens: the client proves possession of a private key on each request, so a stolen token alone is useless elsewhere.
One token shared by all clients.
Longer bearer tokens.
Sending tokens over plain HTTP.
explain: Proof-of-possession turns 'who has the token' into 'who has the key' — replay from another machine fails the signature check. Longer tokens, plaintext transport, and shared tokens all keep or worsen bearer replayability.

q: A data pipeline running on Kubernetes needs to read from a cloud storage bucket. The platform team refuses to distribute long-lived access keys to application teams. How should the pipeline authenticate?
options: A shared access key in a Kubernetes Secret.
With IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA): the pod receives short-lived credentials via OIDC federation -- no long-lived keys to distribute, leak, or rotate.
The node's IAM role, shared by all pods.
Hardcoded keys in the container image.
explain: IRSA eliminates static credentials: the cloud mints short-lived tokens bound to the service account's identity. Shared secrets relocate the same long-lived key, node-role sharing violates least privilege across every pod on the node, and image-baked keys leak to anyone who pulls the image.

q: A build pipeline installs dependencies with floating version ranges. An attacker publishes a malicious package with the same name as the company's private package — but a higher version — on the public registry. Which attack is this, and what stops it?
options: A zero-day — prevented by faster patching.
A license violation — prevented by legal review.
Typosquatting — prevented by code review.
Dependency confusion: the resolver picks the higher-versioned public package. Stop it with scoped registries, explicit registry priority for private names, or version pinning and lockfiles.
explain: Dependency confusion exploits resolver precedence: public registries outrank private ones for the same name at higher versions. The fixes are resolver-level (scope, priority, pinning), not human review — typosquatting is a different attack, this is not a zero-day, and licensing is unrelated.

q: A legacy application cannot be patched — the vendor is defunct and the system cannot tolerate downtime — but it has a known exploitable vulnerability. Which compensating control shields it until decommission?
options: Virtual patching: deploy IPS/WAF rules that block exploitation of the specific vulnerability at the network or application layer without touching the host.
Accept the risk and do nothing.
Reboot the system weekly.
Disconnect the system from the network permanently.
explain: Virtual patching is the textbook compensating control for unpatchable systems — exploit signatures blocked upstream buy time safely. Disconnection may be impossible for a working system, pure risk acceptance ignores the known exploit, and reboots change nothing about the vulnerability.

q: A company decommissions SSDs that held customer data. The team debates: overwrite, degauss, or destroy. According to NIST 800-88, which factor decides the right sanitization level?
options: One overwrite pass works for all media types.
Deleting the files is sufficient.

The data's confidentiality level matched against the media type — Clear, Purge, or Destroy — noting that degaussing does not work on SSDs (no magnetic storage), so cryptographic erase or physical destruction applies.
Always degauss every drive.
explain: 800-88 ties the method to data sensitivity and media physics: SSDs need crypto-erase or destruction because overwrites cannot reach wear-leveled blocks and magnets cannot touch flash. Blanket degaussing, file deletion, and single-pass overwrites all fail on modern media.

q: A compliance framework requires mandatory access control on all container hosts, but seccomp is blocked by the hardened kernel configuration. Which alternative confines container processes?
options: Building a bigger container image.
Running all containers as root.
Disabling the compliance requirement.
An AppArmor (or SELinux) MAC profile: confines the container to only the files, capabilities, and operations it needs.
explain: MAC profiles provide least-privilege confinement at the kernel interface independent of seccomp. Running as root amplifies breakouts, waiving the requirement abandons compliance, and image size is irrelevant.

q: A cluster audit finds the kubelet API accepts anonymous requests, exposing pod logs and exec endpoints to anyone who reaches the node network. What is the correct hardening?
options: Leave anonymous access enabled for debugging convenience.
Disable anonymous kubelet access and require authentication and authorization (client certificates or bearer tokens) for all kubelet API requests.
Delete the kubelet from every node.
Expose the kubelets directly to the internet for easier debugging.
explain: The kubelet API is a privileged control surface — anonymous access hands exec and logs to anyone on the network. Internet exposure, convenience exceptions, and deleting the kubelet are all worse than the finding.

q: A community site's user profiles suffer stored XSS: an attacker's script saved in a profile bio executes in every visitor's browser, spreading like a worm. Input validation exists but is bypassed with encoding tricks. Which defense-in-depth header limits the damage?
options: Compressing profile pages.
A longer session timeout.
Content Security Policy (CSP): restricts which sources may execute scripts, so the injected inline scripts are blocked by the browser.
Disabling user profiles entirely.
explain: CSP is the safety net for imperfect validation -- the browser refuses to run scripts from unapproved sources, halting the worm. Session timeouts and compression are unrelated; disabling profiles destroys the product instead of securing it.

q: An attacker sets a victim's session cookie to a known value before login; after the victim authenticates, the attacker uses the same session ID. Which control defeats this session-fixation attack?
options: Putting session IDs in the URL.
Regenerate the session ID upon successful authentication, so any pre-set identifier becomes invalid the moment privileges attach.
Sessions that never expire.
Longer session IDs.
explain: Regeneration breaks the attack's core assumption — that the pre-login session survives login. ID length is irrelevant when the attacker supplies the value, URL sessions leak and are fixable the same way, and immortal sessions only help the attacker.

q: Browsers must check whether a server's certificate was revoked, but direct OCSP queries leak browsing behavior to the CA and add latency. Which TLS feature solves both problems?
options: Disabling revocation checks.
OCSP stapling: the server periodically fetches a signed OCSP response and 'staples' it to the handshake, so clients verify revocation without contacting the CA.
Certificate pinning.
Longer certificate lifetimes.
explain: Stapling preserves revocation checking while removing the privacy leak and extra round trip — the response comes from the server, signed and fresh. Disabling checks abandons revocation, longer lifetimes extend exposure, and pinning addresses trust anchors rather than revocation status.

q: A company encrypts petabytes with envelope encryption. Auditors ask: who used which data keys, and when? Which capability answers this without custom instrumentation?
options: KMS-backed keys log every encrypt and decrypt API call to the cloud audit trail, giving a complete, tamper-evident record of key usage.
The encryption keys record their own usage.
Application logs of file access.
Asking developers who accessed the data.
explain: Centralized KMS turns key operations into auditable API events — who, which key, when — automatically. Application logs track files not keys, human attestation is not evidence, and cryptographic keys have no logging capability.

q: Malware on a VM beacons to an external command-and-control domain over DNS. The team cannot clean the host immediately. Which network control neuters the beaconing without touching the host?
options: DNS sinkholing: resolve the malicious domain to a controlled dead-end IP at the DNS layer, cutting the C2 channel while logging which hosts query it.
Deleting the malware's files by hand.
Blocking all outbound DNS.
Ignoring it until the next patch window.
explain: Sinkholing severs command-and-control at the choke point the malware must use, and the sinkhole logs identify every infected host. Blanket DNS blocks break the business, manual deletion is unavailable and incomplete, and waiting leaves the channel open.

q: A security review finds production container images contain hardcoded API keys — and worse, the keys persist in older image layers even after being 'removed' in a later Dockerfile step. What is the correct remediation?
options: Remove secrets from the build entirely (inject at runtime via a secrets manager); rebuild from a clean base, rotate all exposed keys, and scan registries for the tainted images.
Keep the keys but make the registry private.
Delete the key in a later Dockerfile layer.
Rotate the keys next quarter.
explain: Layer history is immutable — 'removing' a secret later leaves it in earlier layers, so only clean rebuilds plus immediate rotation work, with runtime injection preventing recurrence. Later-layer deletion is the exact misconception, private registries still distribute the layers, and delayed rotation leaves known-compromised keys active.

q: A security scan flags containers running as root. The only privileged operation the app needs is binding to port 443. How should the team remove root without breaking the service?
options: Grant only the NET_BIND_SERVICE capability (or remap to an unprivileged port behind the load balancer) instead of running as full root.
Keep running as root; the scan is informational.
Make the application binary setuid root.
Set allowPrivilegeEscalation to true.
explain: Linux capabilities grant just the needed privilege -- binding low ports -- without full root. Ignoring the scan, enabling privilege escalation, or setuid binaries all preserve or reopen the escalation paths.

q: Before a sprint, the product owner, developer, and tester meet to walk through concrete examples of how a prorated refund should behave, capturing them as automated tests that will gate the story. Which collaborative practice is this?
options: ATDD (Acceptance Test-Driven Development), often run as a 'three amigos' workshop: the whole team agrees on executable acceptance criteria before building.
TDD at the unit level by the developer alone.
Exploratory testing after the feature ships.
A sprint retrospective.
explain: ATDD's hallmark is the whole team defining acceptance through concrete examples before implementation -- alignment on 'done' up front. Solo TDD works at the unit level, exploratory testing is unscripted post-hoc investigation, and retrospectives review the process, not acceptance criteria.

q: A ticket vendor must survive an onsale stampede: 10x normal traffic for 20 minutes when a popular concert goes on sale. The goal is not just handling the rush but learning how the system degrades past capacity. Which test type fits?
options: Soak testing for 72 hours at normal load.
A/B testing the checkout page design.
Load testing at the expected daily peak.
Spike testing: sudden extreme load to observe failure modes and recovery behavior beyond expected peaks.
explain: Spike testing deliberately exceeds capacity to characterize how the system breaks and recovers -- the onsale question is about degradation past the limit. Expected-peak testing validates the forecast, soak testing hunts slow leaks at normal load, and A/B testing optimizes design, not resilience.

q: A fintech's auditor asks how security is assured in every sprint, not just at release time. The team points to its Definition of Done. What belongs in it?
options: Security completion criteria: secret scanning, dependency vulnerability checks, and threat-model review where applicable -- a story is not done until these pass.
Skipping security for internal tools.
One annual penetration test.
A promise to do security 'later'.
explain: Putting security in the Definition of Done makes it a per-increment completion criterion -- auditable every sprint. 'Later' is the current rework loop, annual tests are too rare, and internal tools are attacked too.

q: A DAST scan reports 200 findings with no code locations, so developers cannot find the vulnerable lines; SAST alone floods them with false positives. Which technique gives runtime-verified findings mapped to exact code?
options: Manual penetration testing once a year.
Running more DAST scans.
IAST (Interactive Application Security Testing): agents inside the running app observe code execution during tests, pinpointing vulnerable lines actually exercised.
A web application firewall.
explain: IAST combines runtime proof with code visibility -- findings point at the exact lines executed under test, cutting both DAST's vagueness and SAST's noise. More DAST repeats the location problem, annual pentests are too rare, and WAFs protect rather than locate.

q: Every team picks different databases, queues, and CI tools; the company now operates 40 overlapping technologies nobody fully understands. Which practice guides technology choices without banning experimentation?
options: A technology radar: the organization publishes which tools to adopt, trial, assess, or hold — guiding choices while leaving room for evaluated experiments.
Standardizing on whatever the loudest team uses.
Letting every team choose freely forever.
Banning all new tools immediately.
explain: A radar creates shared direction with explicit experimentation lanes — teams innovate inside the 'trial' ring instead of fragmenting the stack. Unbounded choice produced the sprawl, blanket bans kill learning, and loudest-wins is not an engineering strategy.

q: A platform team spent six months building a service catalog nobody uses; product teams say it solves problems they do not have. According to platform engineering principles, what went wrong?
options: They should have spent twelve months on it.
Catalogs should be built in secret, then launched.
Product teams are ungrateful.
They built a 'thick' platform from guesses instead of the thinnest viable platform: start from validated user needs and grow incrementally with feedback.
explain: The thinnest viable platform treats the platform as a product -- solve real, validated pain first. More time, blaming users, or secrecy all skip the validation that was missing.

q: A platform team debates building a bespoke CI system versus adopting a managed one. Engineering time is scarce and CI is not the company's product. Which principle guides this decision?
options: Always build everything in-house.
Outsource all engineering.
Let each team run its own CI scripts.
Buy over build for undifferentiated heavy lifting: adopt the managed CI and focus scarce engineering on the product — build only where it differentiates.
explain: Build-vs-buy is about focus: CI is table stakes, not differentiation, so buying it back buys engineering time for the product. In-house everything, fragmented scripts, and total outsourcing all misallocate the scarce resource.

q: A new team argues daily about code review turnaround, meeting etiquette, and who is on point for incidents. Velocity suffers from the meta-conflict. Which agile practice resolves this explicitly?
options: Reorganizing the team.
The manager dictating all team norms.
Working agreements: the team collaboratively writes down its norms (review SLAs, communication channels, on-call expectations) and revisits them in retrospectives.
Ignoring the friction and hoping it fades.
explain: Working agreements make implicit expectations explicit and team-owned, so violations are discussable rather than personal. Dictated norms lack buy-in, hoping fails, and reorgs relocate the same undiscussed friction.

q: Developers complain CI is 'slow sometimes' but the platform team has no data — just anecdotes. Which practice turns platform quality into something measurable and accountable?
options: Adding more CI servers without any targets.
Define SLOs for the platform itself (for example, 95% of builds start within 2 minutes, plus pipeline success rate), with error budgets that prioritize platform work.
Asking developers to be patient.
Measuring only developer headcount.
explain: Platform SLOs apply the same reliability discipline inward — user-developers get quantified promises and the team gets error-budget-driven priorities. Patience, blind capacity, and headcount metrics all dodge accountability.

q: A product owner asks when a 200-point backlog will ship. Velocity-based math gives one date, but stakeholders have been burned by single-point estimates. Which forecasting technique communicates the uncertainty honestly?
options: The loudest engineer's gut feel.
Promising the earliest possible date.
Velocity divided by story points, stated as one date.
Monte Carlo forecasting: simulate thousands of possible futures from historical throughput data, producing date ranges with confidence levels.
explain: Monte Carlo turns throughput history into probability distributions — honest about uncertainty instead of hiding it in a single date. Point estimates pretend precision, gut feels are not data, and earliest-date promises optimize for disappointment.

q: Load tests against a 10-row database pass easily, but production with 10 million rows falls over -- volume-dependent bugs escape every release. The team needs realistic data volumes without using real customer PII. Which approach works?
options: Skip load testing for minor releases.
Copy production data as-is into staging.
Keep testing against the tiny database.
Data subsetting with masking: extract a representative slice of production data and mask or obfuscate the sensitive fields.
explain: Subsetting preserves production's shape and volume while masking removes the compliance risk -- catching the bugs that only appear at scale. Raw copies violate regulations, tiny databases hide the failures, and skipping testing ships blind.

q: A homepage JavaScript bundle doubled after a library upgrade, and page loads degraded -- discovered weeks later by accident. The team wants the pipeline to catch this automatically. Which gate fits?
options: Performance budgets in CI (for example, Lighthouse CI): fail builds exceeding size or timing thresholds, making regressions visible the day they land.
Asking developers to watch bundle sizes.
Upgrading the web servers.
Annual performance audits.
explain: CI performance budgets turn degradation into a build failure -- immediate and objective. Annual audits discover it months late, good intentions are unenforced, and server upgrades do not shrink client-side bundles.

q: Architecture principles ('no circular dependencies,' 'response times under 200ms') are documented but decay within months as code evolves. Which practice keeps architectural characteristics continuously verified?
options: Wiki documentation of the principles.
Trusting developers to remember the rules.
Annual architecture reviews.
Architecture fitness functions: automated tests that continuously verify architectural constraints — dependency rules, performance budgets, security policies — in the pipeline.
explain: Fitness functions make architecture executable: violations fail the build the day they are introduced, not the quarter they are discovered. Annual reviews, wikis, and memory all allow the same silent drift.

q: A team's refinement sessions end with items the team still cannot estimate -- unclear, untestable, too large -- so sprint planning becomes guesswork. Which artifact ensures only ready work enters planning?
options: A Definition of Ready: the agreed checklist (clear, estimated, small enough, testable) a backlog item must meet before sprint planning.
Skipping estimation entirely.
Longer refinement meetings.
A Definition of Done.
explain: The Definition of Ready gates intake quality so planning commits rather than clarifies. The Definition of Done governs the other end, longer meetings normalize the dysfunction, and skipping estimation removes the sizing signal entirely.

q: Two features compete for one team: a quick compliance fix needed urgently, and a large revenue feature. Gut feel favors the big revenue bet. Which prioritization model weighs value, urgency, and effort honestly?
options: Biggest revenue first, always.
Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF): prioritize by cost of delay divided by job size, sequencing the highest value-per-effort work first.
Whoever shouts loudest.
First-in, first-out ordering.
explain: WSJF makes the economics explicit -- the urgent small fix often outranks the big bet on cost-of-delay-per-effort. Revenue-only ordering ignores urgency and duration, FIFO ignores economics, and volume is not value.

q: A central DevOps team drowns in tickets while product teams never learn the tooling -- every deploy needs central help. Leadership wants the central team to teach rather than do. Which Team Topologies team type fits?
options: An enabling team: embedded specialists who coach product teams to build the capability themselves, then step back.
A bigger central team doing more tickets.
Dissolving the central team entirely.
A complicated-subsystem team owning the tooling forever.
explain: Enabling teams transfer capability rather than creating dependency -- they teach, unblock, and leave. A bigger ticket queue, permanent ownership, or dissolution all preserve the learned-helplessness problem.

q: New pods sit in Pending with 'insufficient IPs' on nodes that have plenty of CPU and memory free. The cluster uses a VPC-native CNI where each pod consumes a subnet IP. What is the constraint?
options: Increase the pods' memory limits.
The pods need more CPU requests.
Per-instance network-interface and IP limits: each node type supports a fixed number of pods, and the subnet itself may be exhausted — add nodes, use prefix delegation, or expand subnet capacity.
The Kubernetes scheduler is broken.
explain: VPC-native pod networking ties pod capacity to ENI/IP quotas per instance type — a hard ceiling independent of CPU and RAM. More CPU requests, scheduler blame, or memory tweaks all miss the networking constraint.

q: A web server suddenly exhausts its connection capacity though traffic volume looks normal. Logs show a flood of HTTP/2 requests, each immediately canceled with RST_STREAM. Which attack pattern is this?
options: A slowloris attack.
A volumetric UDP flood.
A legitimate traffic spike.
HTTP/2 rapid reset (CVE-2023-44487): abusing stream cancellation to make the server do expensive setup work per request at negligible attacker cost.
explain: Rapid reset exploits the asymmetry between cheap client cancellations and expensive server-side stream setup — the signature is high RST_STREAM rates with normal bandwidth. Volumetric floods show bandwidth spikes, slowloris is the opposite tempo (holding connections open), and real users do not cancel every stream.

q: TLS handshakes to a site intermittently take several seconds, though the certificate is valid and the network is fast. Packet captures show clients stalling after receiving the certificate. What is the likely stall?
options: Revocation checking: clients blocking on slow or unreachable OCSP responders (or CRL downloads) before completing the handshake.
The certificate file is too large.
The cipher suite is too computationally strong.
HTTP/2 is disabled on the server.
explain: Post-certificate stalls are the signature of revocation lookups timing out — OCSP/CRL fetches block the handshake. Cipher strength does not add seconds, certificates are kilobytes, and the HTTP version negotiates after the handshake completes.

q: Long-lived WebSocket connections through the load balancer drop at exactly 60 seconds of inactivity, though the application is healthy. Which fix keeps idle connections alive?
options: Shortening the application's own timeouts.
Restarting the application servers.
Enable application-level keepalives (ping/pong frames): periodic traffic resets the load balancer's idle timer — or raise the LB idle timeout to exceed the application's.
Removing the load balancer.
explain: The 60-second guillotine is the LB's idle timeout doing its job — keepalives give it traffic to see, or a longer timeout matches the workload. Restarts, LB removal, and shorter timeouts all miss the idle-timer mechanism.

q: Legitimate company emails land in recipients' spam folders. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC all pass. The sending IPs have no PTR records. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: SPF needs an additional mechanism.
Missing reverse DNS (PTR): many receivers treat the absence of a matching PTR record as a spam signal, regardless of SPF/DKIM/DMARC.
DMARC should be removed.
The email content looks spammy.
explain: Receiving servers layer heuristics: valid SPF/DKIM/DMARC plus missing PTR still smells like a compromised host or snowshoe spam operation. The passing authentication results exonerate content and SPF/DKIM/DMARC configuration; the missing PTR is the remaining standard check.

q: A Kubernetes node starts evicting pods though CPU, memory, and disk all look healthy. The node runs hundreds of short-lived processes per pod. Which pressure condition is the kubelet reacting to?
options: Network saturation.
PID pressure: the node hit its process-ID limit, and the kubelet evicts pods to reclaim PIDs.
Memory pressure.
Disk pressure.
explain: Kubelets evict on three pressures — memory, disk, and PID — and PID exhaustion from process-spawning workloads is the classic overlooked one. The stem rules out memory and disk, and network saturation does not trigger eviction.

q: A three-node etcd cluster (Kubernetes control plane) shows intermittent leader elections and slow API responses, though CPU and network are fine. Metrics show high WAL fsync durations. What is the root-cause class?
options: A network partition between members.
Too many Kubernetes namespaces.
Too few etcd nodes for quorum.
Slow disk: etcd is fsync-latency-sensitive, and high fsync times destabilize consensus — move etcd to low-latency SSD storage.
explain: etcd's consensus depends on fast durable writes; slow disks cause missed heartbeats and leader churn regardless of CPU and network. Three nodes is the correct quorum size, the network is healthy, and namespace count does not affect WAL latency.

q: After enabling dual-stack IPv6, some clients cannot reach the application though IPv4 clients work fine. The service binds explicitly to 0.0.0.0. What is wrong?
options: The application binds IPv4-only (0.0.0.0); on a dual-stack host it must also bind [::] (or dual-bind) to accept IPv6 connections.
IPv6 is broken on the internet.
The firewall blocks all traffic.
DNS does not support IPv6.
explain: 0.0.0.0 is IPv4-any only — IPv6 SYN packets arrive at a host with nothing listening on v6. The network path and DNS are proven by clients reaching the host; the socket simply is not there.

q: WAL archiving works, but the primary database's disk fills every few weeks. A failed switchover test last month left a replication slot behind that nobody cleaned up. What is the mechanism filling the disk?
options: The archive command is too slow.
The orphaned replication slot: the primary retains WAL indefinitely for a slot that will never be consumed, so WAL accumulates unboundedly despite healthy archiving.
Normal transaction growth.
The disk needs defragmentation.
explain: Replication slots pin WAL until consumed -- a slot from the failed test never advances, so WAL grows without bound. Archiving works fine, growth is not organic, and defragmentation is irrelevant.

q: After migrating 50 million rows into a new partitioned table, the optimizer ignores the new partition indexes and scans everything -- queries that should take milliseconds take minutes. What should the administrator do FIRST?
options: Update the table statistics (ANALYZE): the planner is choosing full scans based on stale statistics from before the migration.
Increase the database server's memory.
Rewrite queries with optimizer hints.
Add more indexes to the new table.
explain: Bulk migrations invalidate row-count estimates, and the planner picks full scans when it believes tables are small -- fresh statistics restore index usage. More indexes, more RAM, or hints all dodge the stale-statistics root cause.

q: An API endpoint that returns 'all orders' worked fine for years but now times out; the orders table has grown 100x. The query itself is indexed and fast in small batches. What is the fundamental fix?
options: Add more indexes to the orders table.
Cache the full result set.
Paginate the endpoint (limit/offset or keyset pagination): bound every response instead of materializing the entire table.
Increase the API timeout.
explain: Unbounded result sets are a latent defect that data growth exposes — pagination bounds work per request regardless of table size. Indexes do not shrink the result, longer timeouts just delay the inevitable, and caching a gigantic payload moves the bottleneck.

q: A Kubernetes API server grows slower over weeks; etcd's database size keeps climbing though the object count is stable. What maintenance does etcd need?
options: Deleting random ConfigMaps.
Adding more etcd nodes.
Compaction and defragmentation: etcd retains old MVCC revisions; periodic compaction purges them and defrag reclaims the space, keeping the backend under quota.
Restarting etcd every week.
explain: etcd is multiversion: every update keeps old revisions until compacted, so steady churn inflates the backend even with constant object counts. More nodes copy the bloat, deleting objects misses the revision cause, and restarts do not compact.

q: New pods cannot be created in a cluster — kubectl hangs on apply — though existing pods run fine and the API server is healthy. A recently installed validating webhook is unreachable. What is happening?
options: The nodes are out of capacity.
etcd is full.
The failing validating admission webhook blocks pod creation: the API server waits on the unreachable webhook (fail-closed), so no new pods are admitted.
The scheduler is down.
explain: Validating webhooks run synchronously in the admission chain — an unreachable fail-closed webhook halts all matching creates. The scheduler, etcd, and node capacity all act later in the lifecycle than admission.

q: A forum's web server stops accepting new connections during a controversy. Netstat shows thousands of connections in ESTABLISHED state, each sending a byte every 20 seconds. CPU and memory are fine. What is happening?
options: Slow-client exhaustion (slowloris-style): connections held open by trickling data consume sockets and threads without doing work -- mitigate with read timeouts and connection limits.
A memory leak in the forum software.
A CPU-bound application bug.
The database is overloaded.
explain: Thousands of barely-active connections with idle CPU and memory is the signature of slow-client resource exhaustion. CPU, memory, and database theories all contradict the observed evidence.

q: gRPC services work with direct pod connections but fail through the Layer 7 load balancer, which was configured for generic TCP passthrough. What is the misconfiguration?
options: TCP is faster, so passthrough is the correct mode.
gRPC requires HTTP/2: the load balancer must terminate or route HTTP/2 (not raw TCP), with proper handling of HTTP/2 streams, trailers, and health checks.
The pods are unhealthy.
gRPC does not work in Kubernetes.
explain: gRPC is HTTP/2 with trailers and streaming semantics — a TCP-mode LB cannot do HTTP/2 health checks, routing, or trailer handling. Direct-pod success exonerates the pods, and raw TCP discards the protocol features gRPC depends on.

q: A pod fails immediately with 'exec format error' after the team rebuilt its image on new ARM-based CI runners; the image ran fine when built on the old x86 runners. The nodes are x86. What happened?
options: The registry corrupted the image.
Architecture mismatch: the image now contains ARM64 binaries that x86 nodes cannot execute — build multi-arch images or pin the build to the target architecture.
The application code has a bug.
x86 nodes cannot run containers.
explain: 'Exec format error' is the OS refusing a foreign-architecture binary — the CI change silently switched architectures. The code is identical, the registry is fine, and x86 nodes ran the old x86 image without issue.

q: A European bank runs its customer portal in eu-west-1 with cross-region replication to us-east-1 for disaster recovery. Its compliance team flags a data-residency violation. Which architecture resolves it?
options: There is no violation because the data is encrypted in transit
Replicate to a second EU region instead so customer data never leaves its legal jurisdiction
Treat Multi-AZ deployment as cross-region DR and disable replication
Move the primary region to us-east-1 to reduce latency
explain: Data residency governs where data physically rests — encryption in transit does not change that, so replicating PII to the US violates EU residency rules. A second EU region preserves jurisdictional compliance while still providing regional disaster recovery. Multi-AZ protects against zone failure, not region-wide events, and moving the primary to the US deepens the violation.

q: A fintech startup's ledger runs on an eventually consistent datastore with read replicas. Customers are occasionally double-charged when retries land on different replicas. Which architectural change fixes the root cause?
options: Add more read replicas to spread retry traffic
Use strongly consistent (conditional/transactional) writes for ledger entries
Cache balances at the edge to reduce replica lag
Enable Multi-AZ on the replicas for consistency
explain: Double-charging is a consistency defect: a retry must observe the first write, which requires strong consistency or conditional writes on the ledger. More replicas increase divergence, edge caching adds another stale layer, and Multi-AZ provides availability/failover — not read-after-write consistency.

q: A company runs 40 microservices needing mutual authentication, retries, and traffic splitting between services (east-west). The team proposes extending their API gateway to do it. Why is a service mesh the better fit?
options: A service mesh handles east-west mTLS and resilience via sidecars; the API gateway is for north-south client traffic
An API gateway natively provides sidecar-based mTLS between services
A WAF can replace both the gateway and the mesh
Network ACLs provide the same retries and traffic splitting
explain: Service-mesh sidecars own service-to-service concerns (identity, mTLS, retries, splitting); the API gateway faces external clients. Gateways do not inject sidecars, a WAF is perimeter request filtering without workload identity, and NACLs are stateless packet filters with no notion of retries or routing.

q: A retailer runs a steady baseline on-premises but traffic spikes 8x during holiday sales. Which hybrid pattern handles the spikes most cost-effectively?
options: Migrate everything to the cloud on reserved instances
Buy on-premises hardware sized for the holiday peak
Keep the baseline on-premises and burst peak traffic to the cloud
Run the baseline in the cloud on spot instances
explain: Cloud bursting matches elastic demand with elastic supply: the steady baseline stays on sunk-cost hardware while peaks consume pay-as-you-go cloud. Full migration on reservations over-provisions, peak-sized hardware idles most of the year, and spot instances risk interruption of the steady baseline workload.

q: An IoT platform receives 100,000 sensor messages per second in bursts, but its order-processing database degrades above 10,000 writes per second. Which pattern protects the database?
options: Vertically scale the database to 100,000 writes per second
Place a message queue between ingestion and processing to buffer bursts (load leveling)
Enable Multi-AZ on the database for write throughput
Add read replicas to absorb the writes
explain: A queue decouples ingest rate from processing rate, smoothing bursts into a pace the database sustains. Vertical scaling for peak is costly with hard ceilings, Multi-AZ is failover rather than throughput, and read replicas cannot accept writes.

q: When a user uploads a video, the platform must generate thumbnails, transcode three resolutions, and extract metadata — then notify the user only after all finish. Which pattern fits?
options: Publish one event that fans out to parallel workers, then fan in on completion before notifying
Chain the steps in one long sequential function
Poll the upload bucket from a single worker every minute
Run each step on a larger instance in sequence
explain: Fan-out parallelizes the independent tasks and fan-in gates the notification on all completing. A sequential chain wastes wall-clock time, polling adds latency and cost, and larger instances do not parallelize independent work.

q: A company needs ad-hoc machine learning over raw clickstream logs plus governed BI dashboards over cleaned sales data. Which storage architecture serves both?
options: A data warehouse for everything, including the raw logs
The OLTP order database, queried directly by analysts
Raw files on object storage with no catalog or schema
A data lake for raw data with schema-on-read, plus curated warehouse marts for BI
explain: The lake holds raw variety cheaply with schema-on-read for data science, while curated marts give BI performance and governance. Warehouse-only forces premature schemas onto raw data, direct OLTP queries risk production, and catalog-free files become an ungovernable data swamp.

q: A global SaaS app serves static marketing assets and personalized API responses from one origin region. Users in Asia report slow loads. Which caching design is correct?
options: Cache static assets at the CDN edge; serve personalized API responses from regional origins with minimal caching
Cache all API responses at the edge for one hour
Add more origins in the same region
Route all traffic through a VPN concentrator
explain: Static assets are safely cacheable at the edge; personalized responses must not be cached broadly or users see stale or other users' data — regional origins shorten the path instead. Same-region origins do not fix distance, and a VPN concentrator adds hops rather than removing them.

q: A company replicates 5 TB nightly between its data center and the cloud with strict latency requirements. Its site-to-site VPN shows variable throughput. Which connectivity change is appropriate?
options: A dedicated private connection (e.g., Direct Connect/ExpressRoute) for consistent throughput
Add a second VPN tunnel and bond them
Compress harder and keep the VPN
Send the data over the public internet with TLS
explain: Dedicated private links provide consistent bandwidth and SLA-backed performance. Bonded VPNs still traverse the variable public internet, compression does not fix throughput variance, and public internet with TLS lacks consistency guarantees.

q: An analytics cluster's storage grows 3x yearly while compute needs stay flat. The team keeps buying bigger combined nodes. Which architecture breaks this coupling?
options: Bigger combined nodes with faster disks
Multi-AZ deployment of the same nodes
Disaggregated storage on object storage with elastic, separately scaled compute
Read replicas of the analytics database
explain: Disaggregation lets storage and compute scale independently, so flat compute needs stop driving storage purchases. Bigger combined nodes re-couple the two and waste compute, Multi-AZ addresses availability rather than scaling economics, and read replicas serve read traffic, not storage growth.

q: A web tier stores user sessions in instance memory. Autoscaling works on scale-out, but users get logged out on scale-in. Which fix preserves autoscaling?
options: Externalize sessions to a shared store and make instances stateless
Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer
Disable scale-in during business hours
Use larger instances so fewer are needed
explain: Stateless instances plus a shared session store survive any instance churn. Sticky sessions break the moment the pinned instance terminates, disabling scale-in wastes money, and larger instances still die and take their in-memory sessions with them.

q: After ransomware encrypted a company's primary region including its same-account snapshots, which backup architecture would have preserved recovery?
options: More frequent snapshots in the same account and region
Multi-AZ deployment of the application
Versioning on the primary storage buckets
Immutable, cross-region, cross-account backups with separate credentials
explain: An attacker with account access deletes same-account backups, so recovery requires isolation: different account, different region, immutability, and separate credentials.
