Higher frequency does not help if backups are deletable, Multi-AZ is availability rather than backup, and same-account versioning is equally deletable.

q: Order placement must update inventory, charge the card, and notify shipping. Today the web app calls all three synchronously; when the shipping API is slow, checkouts time out. Which architecture decouples them?
options: A faster synchronous HTTP client with longer timeouts
A shared database that all three services poll
An event bus: checkout publishes 'order placed' and each service consumes independently
A bigger monolith with threads per downstream call
explain: An event bus decouples the services in time and failure domains — a slow consumer no longer blocks checkout. Longer timeouts preserve the coupling, shared-database polling couples schema and load, and monolith threads still fail together.

q: A team mandates 'only services that exist identically on all three clouds' to avoid lock-in. What is the chief architectural cost of this rule?
options: It eliminates all forms of lock-in
It reduces operational cost
It improves application latency
It forfeits differentiated managed services, forcing the team to rebuild undifferentiated work
explain: Lowest-common-denominator multi-cloud bans the best managed services on each platform, so the team re-implements databases, queues, and IAM itself. Operational and data-gravity lock-in remain regardless, self-management raises cost rather than lowering it, and latency is unaffected by the rule.

q: A global shopping cart must accept writes during a network partition between regions. Per the CAP theorem, which design stays available?
options: Block writes until the partition heals to keep carts consistent
Route all writes to a single region
Rely on Multi-AZ to prevent partitions
Stay available on both sides and reconcile conflicts afterward (e.g., last-write-wins or CRDTs)
explain: During a partition you must choose availability or consistency; choosing availability means accepting temporary divergence plus a reconciliation strategy. Blocking writes chooses consistency, single-region routing sacrifices availability during the partition, and Multi-AZ does not span a regional partition.

q: An active/active app runs in two regions but shares one database in region A. Region B users suffer high write latency. Which change addresses the data-gravity problem?
options: Larger instances for the shared database
A CDN in front of the database
Partition data by region with local writes, replicating only what must be global
More read replicas in region B
explain: Writes must travel to where the data lives, so regional partitioning with local writes removes the cross-region write penalty. Larger instances do not shorten distance, CDNs do not cache writes, and read replicas cannot accept writes.

q: A workload runs 100 steady-state VMs 24/7 plus 0-200 extra VMs during business hours. Which purchasing mix minimizes cost without risking capacity?
options: On-demand for everything for maximum flexibility
Three-year reservations for all 300 VMs
Commitments (reserved/savings plans) for the 100-VM baseline; on-demand or spot for the variable burst
Spot instances for the baseline and on-demand for bursts
explain: Commitments discount the predictable baseline while the variable burst stays flexible. All on-demand overpays the baseline, reserving the peak wastes most of the commitment, and spot for the baseline risks interruption of steady-state work.

q: During a blue/green deployment, the new (green) code needs a new non-nullable column, but blue must keep serving during the transition. Which database migration approach is safe?
options: Run the DDL adding the non-nullable column at the moment of cutover
Expand/contract: add the column as nullable first, deploy, backfill, then enforce constraints
Migrate the database after cutting traffic to green
Roll back the database if the deploy fails
explain: Expand/contract keeps both code versions compatible with the schema throughout the transition. Cutover-time DDL breaks blue instantly, post-cutover migration leaves green broken in the meantime, and database rollback is slow and risky compared with forward-compatible migrations.

q: A team canaries releases to 5% of traffic, but engineers watch dashboards manually and sometimes miss regressions for an hour. Which progressive-delivery improvement closes this gap?
options: Automated canary analysis with metric thresholds that halt and roll back on error-budget burn
Increase the canary to 50% so problems are more visible
Replace canary with big-bang deploys for speed
Add more dashboards for engineers to watch
explain: Automated analysis reacts in minutes without human attention. A larger canary increases blast radius, big-bang maximizes risk, and more dashboards do not fix the latency of human observation.

q: Engineers routinely SSH into production servers to hotfix configs, and no two servers match anymore. Which practice eliminates this drift class?
options: A shared wiki documenting each hotfix
Configuration management run more frequently on the same servers
Larger servers to reduce the number of hosts
Immutable infrastructure: bake images, deploy replacements, prohibit SSH changes
explain: Replacing instead of mutating removes drift by construction — there is no path for a snowflake server to form. Documentation does not enforce, config management on mutable hosts still permits out-of-band change, and fewer hosts can still drift.

q: Someone changed a security group in the cloud console, bypassing Terraform. The next apply wants to revert it unexpectedly. What is the durable fix?
options: Delete the Terraform state file and re-import everything
Edit the cloud console to match what Terraform expects
Run drift detection regularly and reconcile from the IaC source of truth
Stop using Terraform for networking
explain: Scheduled drift detection plus reconciliation from the IaC source of truth handles every bypass, not just this one. Deleting state orphans resources, manual console edits repeat the original sin, and abandoning IaC surrenders consistency.

q: A push-based CD pipeline went down during an incident, so urgent cluster changes could not ship. Which model keeps the cluster converging even when CI is unavailable?
options: A bigger, highly available CI cluster
Manual kubectl commands by on-call engineers
GitOps: in-cluster agents pull desired state from git and reconcile continuously
Emailing YAML to the platform team
explain: Pull-based GitOps reconciliation does not depend on CI liveness — the agent keeps converging toward git. A bigger CI cluster retains the same dependency, manual commands lack auditability and repeatability, and email is not a deployment system.

q: A rolling deployment temporarily runs fewer healthy pods than required, causing errors mid-deploy. Which setting preserves capacity during the rollout?
options: Increase the rollout speed to finish faster
Configure surge capacity (e.g., maxSurge) so new pods start before old ones terminate
Use the recreate strategy to simplify the rollout
Deploy during low-traffic hours only
explain: Surge capacity keeps serving capacity at or above desired during the rollout. Faster rollouts shorten but do not remove the dip, the recreate strategy causes a full outage, and timing avoids rather than fixes the capacity hole.

q: A monolith must be replaced without downtime, but a big-bang rewrite has failed twice. Which migration strategy de-risks this?
options: Strangler fig: route traffic to new services incrementally behind the same interface
Freeze all feature work for six months and rewrite
Run two full stacks and switch DNS on launch day
Copy the database nightly to the new system
explain: The strangler pattern validates each slice in production behind a stable interface, so failures are small and reversible. Feature freezes stall the business, DNS cutover is big-bang by another name, and nightly copies migrate data without migrating behavior.

q: A scan finds production database passwords baked into container image layers in the registry. What is the correct remediation pattern?
options: Make the registry private so only the team can pull
Encrypt the image layers at rest
Store the passwords in a .env file in the repo instead
Inject secrets at runtime from a secrets manager; never bake them into images
explain: Runtime injection keeps secrets out of immutable layers entirely. A private registry still exposes secrets to anyone with pull access, encryption at rest does not limit who can decrypt via pull, and a .env file in the repo leaks just as broadly.

q: Each deployment drops in-flight requests when old pods terminate immediately. Which mechanism gives connections time to complete?
options: Send SIGKILL faster to recycle pods
Run more replicas so some survive the rollout
Connection draining with termination grace periods and preStop hooks
Increase pod CPU limits
explain: Draining with a grace period lets in-flight requests finish before the pod dies. Faster SIGKILL worsens the drops, extra replicas still get killed mid-request, and CPU limits are unrelated to termination behavior.

q: A Terraform apply failed halfway: some resources exist, the state file disagrees with reality, and the team is tempted to delete the state file. What is the safe recovery?
options: Delete the state file and start fresh
Hand-edit cloud resources until they look right
Re-run the same apply repeatedly until it passes
Keep versioned, locked state; reconcile with targeted plans and fix forward
explain: Versioned, locked state with deliberate targeted plans recovers safely and auditably. Deleting state orphans real resources, hand-edits deepen divergence, and blind reruns can duplicate partially created resources.

q: The image tested in staging differs from what runs in production because each environment rebuilds from the Dockerfile. Which practice guarantees the tested artifact is the shipped artifact?
options: Rebuild in each environment for freshness
Retag the 'latest' tag at each stage
Build once and promote the same immutable image digest through each environment
Copy Dockerfiles between environment repos
explain: Promoting the identical digest means the tested bytes are the shipped bytes. Per-environment rebuilds introduce variance, the 'latest' tag is mutable and ambiguous, and copying Dockerfiles still rebuilds.

q: After a supply-chain scare, a team wants cryptographic assurance that deployment artifacts were not tampered with between build and deploy. Which control provides it?
options: Record checksums in the team wiki
Transfer artifacts only over the private network
Sign artifacts at build time and verify signatures at deploy/admission time
Use a larger artifact registry
explain: Build-time signing with deploy-time verification gives tamper evidence end-to-end. Wiki checksums are not enforced, a private network does not prove integrity, and registry size is irrelevant to tampering.

q: A new fraud model must be validated against live production traffic without affecting any customer decisions. Which deployment strategy fits?
options: Canary the model to 50% of customers
A/B test with revenue as the metric
Test only on historical data
Shadow deployment: mirror live traffic to the new model and compare outputs offline
explain: Shadowing exposes the model to live data with zero user impact while outputs are compared offline. Canary and A/B both affect real customers, and historical data misses live drift and novel patterns.

q: An app works in dev but crashes in prod; investigation finds different OS library versions. Which practice prevents this class of 'works on my machine' failure?
options: More powerful dev workstations
Identical container images and IaC-defined environments from dev to prod
Test directly in production
Document the library versions in a runbook
explain: Identical images and IaC-defined environments remove environment variance by construction. Bigger workstations do not match prod, testing in prod risks users, and documentation does not enforce anything.

q: Product wants to know whether a new checkout button color increases conversion. Engineering proposes a 1% canary 'to be safe.' Why is an A/B test the better experimental design here?
options: A/B splits users into cohorts to measure the metric; a canary only limits blast radius of a risky release
A canary measures conversion better than an A/B test
1% of traffic is enough to measure conversion changes
Blue/green deployment answers product questions
explain: A/B tests and canaries answer different questions: A/B measures causal effect on a metric across cohorts, while a canary limits the blast radius of a risky release. A 1% canary lacks statistical power for conversion, and blue/green is a deployment technique, not an experiment.

q: An e-commerce company approaches its peak holiday season, when any downtime costs millions per hour. Leadership mandates no production deployments for six weeks except emergency fixes with VP approval. Which release-management practice is this?
options: Feature flags for gradual rollouts
Canary deployments to 5% of traffic
A change freeze (deployment blackout period) with an emergency exception process
Accelerating the CI/CD pipeline for faster recovery
explain: A change freeze trades velocity for stability during critical business periods, with a defined emergency exception path. Feature flags and canary are release techniques, not freezes, and accelerating the pipeline is the opposite of a freeze.

q: A legacy billing system can only change during a Sunday 2-4 AM window and has no automated rollback. Which change practice is appropriate?
options: Deploy whenever; the window is just a suggestion
Skip testing to fit more changes in the window
Make changes directly in production during the window
Use the maintenance window with a tested rollback plan and maintenance-mode communication
explain: Constrained systems need the window plus a rehearsed rollback and clear communication. Ignoring the window risks business impact, skipping testing raises failure odds, and direct production edits lack control and review.

q: A checkout request traverses 12 microservices, and engineers grep 12 separate log stores to reconstruct one failure. Which observability practice fixes this?
options: Increase log verbosity on every service
Store logs only on local disks for speed
Reduce the number of microservices
Propagate a correlation ID in structured logs aggregated centrally
explain: A propagated correlation ID joins the distributed trace into a single query against centralized structured logs. Verbosity without IDs is noise, local disks fragment the trail, and re-architecting service count does not fix observability.

q: p99 latency spikes. The alert fired from metrics, but the team needs the failing service hop and the underlying error. Which pillar combination answers each question?
options: Logs for the alert, metrics for the hop, traces for the error
Metrics detect, distributed traces isolate the slow span, logs provide error detail
Metrics for everything; the other pillars are redundant
Restart the service and skip diagnosis
explain: Each pillar has a role: metrics detect, traces localize the slow span, logs explain the error. The reversed mapping misuses each pillar, metrics alone cannot localize a hop, and restarting destroys evidence.

q: An on-call team receives 400 alerts daily and now ignores pages, missing a real outage. Which alerting change restores signal?
options: Add more alerts so nothing is missed
Deduplicate, tune thresholds, route by severity, and alert on SLO burn instead of raw symptoms
Mute all alerts for a week to recover
Hire more on-call engineers
explain: Fewer, better alerts restore trust in paging: deduplication, tuned thresholds, severity routing, and SLO-based alerts. More alerts worsen fatigue, muting blinds the team, and headcount does not fix noise.

q: A fleet of VMs averages 12% CPU and 20% memory, yet the bill keeps growing. Which cost-optimization action addresses the root cause?
options: Buy reserved instances for the oversized fleet
Rightsize instances based on utilization data
Raise autoscaling minimums for headroom
Move the fleet to spot instances
explain: Rightsizing matches instance size to actual need, removing the waste itself. Reservations merely discount waste, higher minimums add waste, and spot changes pricing rather than sizing.

q: Finance questions a surprise $40k monthly spike, but no one can say which team caused it. Which FinOps practice provides attribution?
options: Delete resources until the bill drops
Ask the cloud vendor for a discount
Enforced tagging, cost allocation, anomaly alerts, and showback reports per team
Reconcile once a year at true-up
explain: Enforced tags with cost allocation attribute every dollar to an owner, anomaly alerts catch spikes early, and showback drives accountability. Blind deletion risks production, discounts do not attribute, and annual true-up is far too late.

q: Backups report 'success' nightly, but the company has never restored one. After a logical corruption, which practice would have proven recoverability beforehand?
options: More frequent backups
Longer retention periods
Scheduled restore drills validating RTO/RPO
Trusting the backup software's green status
explain: Only actual restores prove recoverability against RTO/RPO targets. Frequency and retention do not test integrity, and a green status measures job completion, not restorability.

q: A company must patch 2,000 servers monthly without risking a fleet-wide outage from a bad patch. Which rollout strategy fits?
options: Ring-based rollout: canary group first, then expanding waves in maintenance windows
Patch all servers simultaneously for speed
Never patch; rely on the firewall
Patch manually, one server at a time
explain: Rings contain a bad patch's blast radius to the canary group first. Simultaneous patching maximizes the blast radius, never patching accumulates vulnerability, and manual patching does not scale to 2,000 servers.

q: A deployment made key queries 20% slower, but nobody noticed for three weeks. Which practice catches this at deploy time?
options: Wait for user complaints
Add database indexes after every deploy
Performance baselines with automated regression detection in the pipeline
Buy a larger database
explain: Baselines with automated comparison catch regressions immediately at deploy time. User complaints are a lagging indicator, blind indexing has its own costs, and a larger database masks the regression instead of catching it.

q: During a database failover, the on-call engineer needs exact step-by-step commands, while leadership needs the overall response strategy. Which documents serve each need?
options: A playbook for the engineer, a runbook for leadership
Tribal knowledge for both
A runbook (procedural steps) for the engineer, a playbook (strategy) for leadership
One wiki page titled 'database stuff'
explain: Runbooks are procedural step-by-step guides for operators; playbooks describe strategy and coordination for leadership. The reversed mapping confuses both audiences, tribal knowledge does not scale, and vague wikis fail under pressure.

q: The bill shows $3k/month for unattached volumes, old snapshots, and unused elastic IPs with no owners. Which practice prevents this leak?
options: Increase the budget to cover it
Delete all storage monthly
Ignore it; $3k is immaterial
Lifecycle policies, orphan detection reports, and mandatory owner/cost-center tags
explain: Lifecycle policies expire the unneeded, orphan reports surface it, and owner tags create accountability. Bigger budgets normalize waste, blind deletion risks data loss, and ignoring it lets the leak compound.

q: A team ships daily but reliability is sliding; product keeps pushing features. Which mechanism balances velocity with reliability?
options: A 100% uptime SLA for all services
Freeze all deployments indefinitely
More monitoring dashboards
SLOs with error budgets that gate or slow releases when exhausted
explain: Error budgets make the velocity-reliability tradeoff explicit and enforceable: burn the budget, slow the releases. A 100% SLA is unachievable, freezes kill velocity entirely, and dashboards do not gate anything.

q: Compliance requires 7 years of audit logs, but only the last 30 days are ever queried. Which retention design meets both needs affordably?
options: Keep all 7 years in hot, instantly queryable storage
Tiered retention: hot for recent logs, then warm/cold archive for the remainder
Delete logs after 30 days
Print logs to paper for the archive
explain: Tiering matches storage cost to access pattern: hot for the queried window, cheap archive for compliance. All-hot is wasteful, deletion violates the 7-year requirement, and paper is neither searchable nor practical.

q: An auto-remediation runbook restarted the production database in a loop during a partial outage, worsening it. Which safeguard was missing?
options: More automation to fix things faster
Disabling all automation permanently
Running remediation more frequently
Guardrails: circuit breakers, blast-radius limits, and human approval for destructive actions
explain: Automation needs guardrails — circuit breakers stop loops, blast-radius limits contain damage, and destructive actions need human approval. More or faster automation amplifies the failure, and disabling it entirely loses the benefit.

q: An unreviewed Friday-afternoon firewall change caused a four-hour outage. Which process change reduces this risk while still allowing changes?
options: Freeze all changes permanently
Change control: risk assessment, peer review, scheduled windows, and a rollback plan
Allow changes but skip documentation
Blame the engineer publicly
explain: Lightweight change control — risk assessment, peer review, windows, rollback plan — catches risky changes without stopping work. Freezes stop the business, skipping documentation worsens the next incident, and blame does not prevent recurrence.

q: The disaster-recovery plan exists only as a document nobody has exercised. Which testing progression builds real confidence?
options: Trust the document; testing risks an outage
Unannounced full failover next Friday
Test only the backup jobs
Graduated tests: tabletop walkthrough, then simulated, then full failover
explain: Graduated testing finds gaps safely at each level of realism. Untested documents are hope, unannounced failovers are reckless, and backup jobs alone do not validate end-to-end recovery.

q: A fleet of 500 short-lived spot workers needs basic health telemetry, but installing and updating agents on each is heavy. Which monitoring approach fits?
options: Install full agents on every worker regardless
Agentless collection via cloud APIs and push metrics for the ephemeral fleet; agents where deep OS metrics are needed
No monitoring for spot workers
SNMP polling for everything
explain: Match the method to the lifespan: agentless collection suits ephemeral workers while agents stay where deep OS metrics matter. Forced agents add toil on short-lived hosts, no monitoring blinds operations, and SNMP is legacy-limited.

q: Leadership fears an availability-zone failure, but the team has never experienced one. Which practice builds failure readiness without waiting for a real outage?
options: Wait for a real AZ failure to learn from it
Game days / chaos experiments with hypotheses, blast-radius limits, and rollback plans
Run chaos experiments in production with no limits
Avoid thinking about failures
explain: Controlled game days build muscle memory and validate assumptions safely. Waiting is passive, unlimited chaos in production is reckless, and avoidance guarantees the first failure is a surprise.

q: An attacker steals a user's OAuth access token and replays it from a different device. The token is a standard bearer token. Which mechanism would have made the stolen token useless?
options: Longer bearer tokens
DPoP (proof-of-possession): the token is cryptographically bound to the client's private key
Rotating bearer tokens less frequently
IP allowlisting alone
explain: DPoP sender-constrains tokens: the token only works with proof of the bound private key, so a stolen token cannot be replayed elsewhere. Token length does not bind a token to a device, slower rotation lengthens exposure, and IP allowlists break on mobile and NAT.

q: An API accepts JWTs, but a penetration test shows an attacker can forge valid tokens by changing the algorithm header to 'none'. Which validation practice prevents this?
options: Trust the algorithm header sent by the client
Use longer JWT secrets
Validate the signature with a pinned algorithm and trusted key; verify exp, iss, and aud claims
Encrypt the JWT payload
explain: Pinning the expected algorithm, verifying the signature against a trusted key, and checking claims (expiry, issuer, audience) defeats algorithm-confusion attacks. Trusting the client-sent header is the vulnerability itself, longer secrets do not matter when 'none' skips verification, and encryption provides confidentiality rather than authenticity.

q: CI pulled a malicious public package with the same name as the company's private package. Which control prevents the resolver from choosing the public copy?
options: Rename the private package and hope
Run CI only on the private network
Trust the package manager's defaults
Scoped registries with explicit upstream priority and hash pinning
explain: Scoping plus explicit upstream priority plus hash pinning removes the ambiguity that dependency confusion exploits. Renaming is fragile, network location does not change resolution order, and the defaults are what caused the incident.

q: A critical zero-day affects the customer portal; the vendor patch is two weeks away. Which compensating control reduces exposure immediately?
options: Virtual patching: WAF rules blocking the exploit pattern until the real patch ships
Take the portal offline for two weeks
Wait for the vendor patch
Rewrite the application from scratch
explain: Virtual patching buys time at the edge by blocking the exploit pattern while the application stays up. Taking the portal offline kills the business, waiting leaves full exposure, and a rewrite is infeasible inside the window.

q: A SaaS must provably and instantly delete one tenant's data from shared cloud storage on request. Physical disk destruction is impossible in the cloud. Which technique achieves this?
options: Run DELETE queries and trust them
Crypto-shredding: encrypt each tenant's data with its own key, then destroy the key
Overwrite the underlying disks
Degauss the storage arrays
explain: Destroying the tenant's data-encryption key renders all of its ciphertext unrecoverable instantly — crypto-shredding. DELETE queries leave remnants on shared media, and disk overwrite or degaussing are impossible on cloud storage the provider owns.

q: A NACL allows inbound HTTPS (443) to web servers, but responses never reach clients. Security groups are correctly configured. What is the NACL misconfiguration?
options: The NACL should allow all inbound traffic
Security groups are stateful so NACLs are unnecessary
The web servers need public IPs
NACLs are stateless: outbound rules must allow the ephemeral port range for return traffic
explain: NACLs are stateless, so the return traffic to ephemeral ports needs an explicit outbound allowance — the classic NACL trap. Allow-all defeats the control's purpose, security groups do not fix NACL drops, and public IPs do not address stateless filtering.

q: A payment service times out, the client retries, and the customer is charged twice. The team asks for 'exactly-once' messaging. What is the correct engineering response?
options: Exactly-once is unachievable over unreliable networks; design idempotent operations with idempotency keys
Buy exactly-once messaging from the vendor
Disable retries to prevent duplicates
Make the network perfectly reliable
explain: Exactly-once delivery is unachievable over networks that can fail; idempotency keys make retries safe instead. No vendor sells true exactly-once, disabling retries trades duplicates for failed payments, and perfectly reliable networks do not exist.

q: An attacker with a phished password spams a user with MFA push notifications until the exhausted user taps 'Approve'. Which MFA upgrade defeats this push-bombing attack?
options: Send more push notifications to confirm intent
Fall back to SMS codes
Number matching or phishing-resistant MFA (e.g., FIDO2/WebAuthn)
Lengthen the push approval timeout
explain: Number matching forces the user to confirm the login context shown on screen, and FIDO2/WebAuthn removes the approvable push entirely. More pushes worsen fatigue, SMS codes are phishable and SIM-swappable, and longer timeouts give the attacker more time.

q: Inside a flat VPC, a compromised service spoofs requests to another service that trusts any in-VPC caller. Which control provides strong service-to-service authentication?
options: Security groups restricting ports
Bearer tokens passed in headers
Network segmentation alone
Mutual TLS with workload identities
explain: mTLS authenticates both ends cryptographically with workload identities, defeating spoofing. Security groups filter but do not authenticate, bearer tokens can be stolen and replayed, and segmentation limits scope without proving identity.

q: Encrypting millions of records by calling KMS per record is too slow and costly. Which pattern keeps KMS-managed keys with per-record encryption?
options: One static key hardcoded for all records
Envelope encryption: a unique data key per record, wrapped by a KMS master key
Skip encryption for performance
Encrypt only the database password
explain: Envelope encryption gives per-record data keys at scale while KMS guards only the wrapping keys. A hardcoded static key is a breach waiting to happen, skipping encryption fails compliance, and encrypting the password does not protect the data.

q: An unsigned, vulnerable image was deployed to the production cluster from a public registry. Which control ensures only trusted images can be scheduled?
options: Scan images occasionally
Trust developers to pick good images
Sign images in the build pipeline and enforce signature verification with an admission controller
Use a private registry without signing
explain: Signing plus admission-controller enforcement is preventive: untrusted images cannot be scheduled. Occasional scans are detective and laggy, trust is not a control, and a private registry without signing still accepts bad pushes.

q: When a critical open-source vulnerability is announced, the company takes three days to determine which services are affected. Which artifact shrinks this to minutes?
options: A manual spreadsheet of libraries
A software bill of materials (SBOM) generated per build
Waiting for vendor notifications
Rewriting all dependencies in-house
explain: A per-build SBOM enables instant blast-radius queries across every service. Spreadsheets rot, vendor notifications lag, and rewriting all dependencies is infeasible.

q: Database credentials are hardcoded in application code; rotation requires a redeploy and once broke production. Which pattern makes rotation safe and frequent?
options: Rotate once a year during a maintenance window
Dynamic short-lived credentials issued by a secrets manager at runtime
Share one credential across all apps
Email the new password to the team
explain: Dynamic credentials rotate automatically at runtime with no code changes or redeploys. Annual rotation leaves long exposure windows, sharing maximizes blast radius, and email is not a vault.

q: Five engineers hold standing production admin accounts; one was phished. Which privileged-access model removes the standing target?
options: Just-in-time elevation: request, approve, time-box, and audit — zero standing privilege
Stronger passwords on the admin accounts
More admin accounts for redundancy
Use the break-glass account for daily work
explain: JIT shrinks privilege to approved, time-boxed, audited windows with nothing standing to phish. Stronger passwords do not remove the target, more accounts multiply risk, and break-glass accounts are for emergencies, not daily work.

q: Customer PII sits in the same storage bucket as public marketing assets with identical access policies. Which foundational step drives the right protections?
options: Classify data first, then apply controls (separate storage, encryption, access) per classification
Encrypt everything identically and move on
Make the bucket public for simplicity
Deploy DLP and skip classification
explain: Classification determines proportionate controls — PII gets isolated storage, encryption, and tight access while public assets do not. Uniform encryption ignores access differences, public buckets expose PII, and DLP needs classification to know what is sensitive.

q: A state-level attacker issues a rogue certificate from a compromised CA to intercept the mobile app's API traffic. Which control lets the app reject it?
options: Certificate pinning: the app trusts only specific keys, not any CA-signed certificate
Longer certificate validity periods
Self-signed certificates
Ignoring certificate errors
explain: Pinning constrains trust to known keys, so a rogue CA-signed certificate is rejected. Longer validity lengthens exposure, self-signed certificates break the trust chain, and ignoring errors surrenders entirely.

q: The identity provider is down and no one can authenticate to the cloud console during an outage. Which emergency-access design is appropriate?
options: Break-glass accounts with sealed, monitored credentials used only for emergencies
A shared admin password posted in the team chat
Disabling MFA for all users during outages
No emergency access; wait for the IdP
explain: Break-glass accounts balance availability with accountability: sealed credentials, monitored use, emergencies only. Shared passwords lack attribution, disabling MFA weakens everyone, and no access prolongs the outage.

q: A team writes unit tests after coding and still gets surprised by rejected user stories at sprint review. Which practice moves acceptance criteria to the front of development?
options: ATDD: derive acceptance tests from agreed criteria before development, and develop until they pass
Write more unit tests after coding
Move user acceptance testing earlier but keep it manual at the end
TDD alone, since unit tests cover acceptance
explain: ATDD makes acceptance criteria executable before development starts, so surprises surface when they are cheap. More post-hoc unit tests do not capture acceptance, manual UAT at the end repeats the surprise, and TDD tests design rather than acceptance.

q: A flash sale will drive 10x traffic within 60 seconds. The team must verify the autoscaler reacts in time rather than find the breaking point. Which test type fits?
options: Soak testing: moderate load for 24 hours
Stress testing to the breaking point
Average-load testing at expected traffic
Spike testing: sudden extreme burst to validate rapid scaling response
explain: Spike testing measures response to a sudden burst — exactly the autoscaler question. Soak finds leaks over time, stress finds the breaking point rather than responsiveness, and average load never triggers the burst.

q: A compromised pod inherited its node's IAM role and read every bucket in the account. Which identity design contains this blast radius?
options: IRSA: per-service-account IAM roles so each pod gets only its own least-privilege permissions
Larger nodes with fewer pods each
Network policies alone
One IAM role per cluster for simplicity
explain: IRSA scopes cloud identity to the workload's service account with least privilege. Node sizing does not fix identity, network policies do not authorize cloud APIs, and one role per cluster maximizes blast radius.

q: Fifty developers merge long-lived feature branches monthly; integration week is chaos. Which branching strategy enables continuous delivery here?
options: Stricter GitFlow with more approval gates
Even longer-lived branches to reduce merge frequency
Trunk-based development: short-lived branches, frequent merges, feature flags for incomplete work
No branching; everyone edits main directly without review
explain: Trunk-based development keeps integration continuous through small, frequent merges with flags hiding incomplete work. Stricter GitFlow adds ceremony, longer branches worsen divergence, and unreviewed direct edits risk quality.

q: Where should SAST, SCA, and DAST run in the pipeline for fast feedback without blocking developers unnecessarily?
options: SCA and SAST on pull requests (fast, static); DAST against a deployed staging environment
DAST on every pull request
Annual penetration test only
SAST after production deployment
explain: Static scans (SCA, SAST) are fast enough for pull-request feedback; DAST needs a running application, so it belongs against staging. DAST per-PR is too slow, annual tests miss daily changes, and post-production SAST is too late.

q: Configuration is baked into images per environment, and a production-only bug cannot be reproduced in staging. Which build practice restores parity?
options: Rebuild images per environment for freshness
Bake more config into the image
Debug directly in production
Build one immutable artifact; externalize configuration per environment
explain: One immutable artifact plus externalized configuration means the tested bytes are the shipped bytes in every environment. Per-environment rebuilds diverge, more baked config worsens it, and debugging in production risks users.

q: Two microservices pass their own unit tests, yet break in integration when the provider changes a response field. Which test type catches this at build time?
options: More unit tests on each service
A shared integration environment tested nightly
Bumping the API version number
Consumer-driven contract tests verifying provider responses against consumer expectations
explain: Contract tests verify the provider's responses against consumer expectations in the pipeline, catching interface drift at build time. Unit tests do not cross service boundaries, nightly integration is late feedback, and version bumps do not verify anything.

q: Integration bugs surface only in the shared staging environment, which is always contended and broken. Which environment strategy gives every change an isolated integration test?
options: One bigger shared staging environment
Test in production with feature flags
Ephemeral per-PR environments spun up by the pipeline with seeded data
More documentation of integration points
explain: Per-PR ephemeral environments isolate and parallelize integration testing for every change. A bigger shared environment still contends, production testing risks users, and documentation does not execute.

q: An audit finds the same engineer writes code, approves their own pull request, and approves the production deployment. Which control addresses the segregation failure?
options: Remove all approvals for speed
Separation of duties: production deployment approval by someone other than the author, alongside automated gates
Approve via chat message
More pull-request reviewers on the author's team
explain: Separation of duties requires an independent approver for production deployments, complementing automated quality gates. Removing approvals worsens the risk, chat approvals lack enforcement and audit trails, and more reviewers on the author's own change does not separate deploy authority.

q: A provider renames an API field without warning and breaks three consumers. Which versioning discipline prevents silent breakage?
options: Never change the API again
Change fields silently; consumers should adapt
Put the version only in documentation
Semantic versioning: major bump for breaking changes with a deprecation window
explain: Semantic versioning communicates breaking intent: a major bump plus a deprecation window lets consumers prepare. Freezing the API stalls evolution, silent changes break trust, and docs-only versions are not enforced.

q: A deployment fails but made no database changes. What is the fastest reliable rollback?
options: Always fix forward, never roll back
Manually revert code on the servers
Restore the database from backup
Redeploy the previous immutable artifact
explain: The previous immutable artifact is known-good and redeploys in minutes. Fix-forward gambles on an untested fix, manual reverts are error-prone, and a database restore is unnecessary and slow when the schema never changed.

q: A junior engineer asks for the difference between Terraform and Ansible in their stack. Which distinction is accurate?
options: IaC (Terraform) provisions infrastructure; configuration management (Ansible) configures software on it
They are the same thing with different names
Ansible provisions cloud infrastructure; Terraform configures software
Use only one of them for everything
explain: The standard division: IaC provisions the infrastructure, configuration management configures software atop it — complementary roles. They are not identical, the reversed mapping is wrong, and while one tool can stretch, the concepts remain distinct.

q: An engineer commits a cloud access key to git; it is now in history. Which two-part response is correct?
options: Delete the commit and assume safety
Make the repo private and move on
Ignore it; the key is old
Revoke and rotate the key immediately, plus add pre-commit secret scanning to prevent recurrence
explain: A leaked key must be revoked — git history and clones live forever — and pre-commit scanning prevents recurrence. Deleting the commit does not purge clones, private repos still leak, and age does not equal safety.

q: Builds take 40 minutes, mostly re-downloading dependencies and recompiling unchanged layers. Which optimization attacks the root cause?
options: Cache dependencies and image layers between builds; parallelize independent stages
Bigger runners only
Run fewer tests
Build only nightly
explain: Caching removes the redundant work that dominates build time, and parallelization compresses the rest. Bigger runners speed up waste without removing it, fewer tests cut quality, and nightly builds delay feedback.

q: The suite is 90% end-to-end tests: slow, flaky, and developers avoid running it. Which test distribution fixes the economics?
options: Add more end-to-end tests
Test pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer integration, fewest E2E
Delete all tests and test manually
Only unit tests; delete integration tests
explain: The test pyramid optimizes the speed-confidence tradeoff: cheap fast unit tests at the base, expensive E2E at the tip. More E2E worsens the problem, manual testing does not scale, and unit-only misses integration failures.

q: Jenkins jobs are configured by clicking; no one knows what changed when a build breaks. Which practice makes pipelines auditable and repeatable?
options: Pipeline as code: define pipelines in versioned files in git
Document the clicks in a wiki
A bigger Jenkins server
Shared shell scripts copied between jobs
explain: Pipeline-as-code in git is diffable, reviewable, and repeatable. Wiki documentation rots, bigger servers do not audit, and copied scripts diverge across jobs.

q: After migrating a service to a new IP, some users reach the old server for hours while others see the new one. What best explains this?
options: DNS propagation is instant worldwide
The firewall is blocking the new IP
DNS TTL caching: resolvers honor the old record until its TTL expires
Users need to reboot their routers
explain: DNS TTL governs how long resolvers cache a record — lower it before migrations. Propagation is not instant, a firewall would block uniformly rather than selectively, and reboots do not clear resolver caches.

q: Hosts in a private subnet intermittently fail to establish new outbound connections at peak; existing connections are fine. The NAT gateway shows port allocation errors. What is the cause and fix?
options: DNS failure
Security group blocking
Instance CPU exhaustion
NAT gateway port exhaustion: distribute load across multiple NAT gateways/AZs and tune idle timeouts
explain: Each NAT gateway has finite ports per destination; peak concurrency exhausts them, so new connections fail while existing ones persist. DNS failure would be uniform, security groups do not produce port-allocation errors, and CPU is unrelated to NAT ports.

q: After a VM restore, users get authentication failures with 'ticket expired' errors though passwords are correct. System time is 12 minutes fast. What is the cause?
options: Clock skew: Kerberos tickets are time-sensitive; sync via NTP
Passwords expired during the restore
The firewall blocks authentication
The domain controller needs more CPU
explain: Kerberos tolerates only about 5 minutes of skew, so a 12-minute-fast clock invalidates tickets. Passwords are unaffected by system time, a firewall would block all authentication rather than producing ticket errors, and CPU does not cause time validation failures.

q: 'Top' shows 85% CPU usage, but the breakdown is mostly iowait, and the app's EBS volume shows throttled throughput. What is the actual bottleneck?
options: CPU: add more vCPUs
Memory: add more RAM
Disk I/O: the CPUs are waiting on storage, not computing
Network: increase bandwidth
explain: High iowait means CPUs are idle waiting on disk — the bottleneck is storage throughput, confirmed by the throttled volume. More vCPUs cannot help idle CPUs, RAM does not fix volume throttling, and the network is uninvolved.

q: Under load the app throws connection timeouts, but the database shows low CPU and plenty of capacity. What should be investigated first?
options: Scale the database vertically
Connection pool exhaustion or leaks in the app tier
Add more application servers
Restart the database
explain: A healthy database plus app-side timeouts points at the layer between them: the connection pool — exhaustion or leaked connections. Vertical scaling wastes money on an idle database, more app servers multiply pool pressure, and restarts mask leaks.

q: After disabling legacy TLS ciphers server-side, some clients fail with handshake errors while others connect fine. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server certificate expired
Cipher suite mismatch: affected clients only support the disabled ciphers
DNS is misconfigured
The firewall blocks port 443
explain: Selective failures immediately after a cipher change indicate negotiation mismatch — those clients cannot agree on a cipher. An expired certificate would fail for all clients, and DNS or firewall issues would not correlate with the cipher change.

q: Pods show status OOMKilled with no application errors logged. Memory graphs show a steady climb before each kill. What is happening?
options: CPU throttling is killing the pods
The disk is full
The network policy blocks the pods
The container exceeds its memory limit — likely a memory leak; check OOM events and heap
explain: OOMKilled means the cgroup memory limit was hit, and the steady climb suggests a leak rather than a spike. CPU throttling slows without killing, disk pressure produces evictions with different signals, and network policies do not kill pods.

q: At peak scale, API calls intermittently fail with 429 responses; off-peak everything works. Infrastructure metrics are healthy. What is the cause and fix?
options: API rate limiting/throttling: add exponential backoff with jitter and request a quota increase
Failing instances; replace them
Firewall misconfiguration
DNS caching issues
explain: HTTP 429 is the explicit throttling signal, and healthy infrastructure rules out instance failure. Backoff with jitter smooths retries while a quota increase raises the ceiling. Firewalls and DNS do not return 429s.

q: After deploying a new UI, users still see the old interface until they hard-refresh. What is the root cause and durable fix?
options: The deployment failed; redeploy
Stale CDN/browser cache: version asset filenames and set proper cache invalidation
The CDN is too small
Users' browsers are broken
explain: A hard-refresh fixing it proves the new code deployed but caches serve the old — the fix is cache-busting filenames plus invalidation rules. Redeploying identical assets repeats the problem, CDN size is irrelevant, and blaming users fixes nothing.

q: New instance launches fail in one subnet with no 'capacity' error from the cloud, while other subnets work. What should be checked?
options: Subnet IP exhaustion: check available addresses in the subnet
The AMI is corrupted
The instance type is unavailable
The key pair is invalid
explain: A subnet-scoped failure without capacity errors means no free IP addresses remain in that subnet. AMI, instance-type, and key-pair issues are not subnet-specific.

q: TCP handshakes complete through a firewall, but data transfer stalls and connections hang. Captures show return traffic taking a different path. What is the issue?
options: Insufficient bandwidth
Application bug
Asymmetric routing: the stateful firewall never sees the return path, so it drops the flow
MTU mismatch
explain: Stateful firewalls must see both directions; asymmetric return paths mean the firewall drops packets for flows it never tracked — hence completed handshakes that then stall. Bandwidth would not permit clean handshakes, and MTU issues are size-dependent rather than path-dependent.

q: Targets flap between healthy and unhealthy, but the application responds fine to manual requests. What is the most likely misconfiguration?
options: The instances are too small
More availability zones are needed
The health check itself: wrong path, too-aggressive interval/thresholds, or a slow endpoint
The application has a bug
explain: Manual success combined with check failure means the check is wrong — bad path, aggressive thresholds, or an endpoint too slow for the interval. Instance size does not explain manual success, AZs do not fix checks, and an app bug would fail manual requests too.

q: After five simultaneous changes, the system degrades and no one knows which change caused it. Which troubleshooting discipline applies?
options: Make more changes to compensate
Reboot everything at once
Isolate variables: revert or test recent changes one at a time (divide and conquer)
Guess the most likely cause and move on
explain: Single-variable isolation establishes causality — divide and conquer through the recent changes. More changes compound the unknown, mass reboots destroy evidence, and guessing is not a method.

q: A scheduled job ran at the wrong hour after the team moved it to a region observing daylight saving. Which practice prevents timezone bugs?
options: Schedule in UTC everywhere, with explicit timezone conversion at the edges
Adjust the schedule manually twice a year
Use the server's local time and hope
Disable daylight saving on the servers
explain: UTC is unambiguous everywhere; convert to local time only at display. Manual DST adjustments are error-prone, local time varies by host, and disabling DST on servers does not standardize anything.

q: The app builds fine locally but fails in the pipeline; a transitive dependency released a breaking minor version overnight. Which practice pins the dependency tree?
options: Always use the latest versions
Commit lockfiles and pin versions for reproducible builds
Rebuild until it works
Vendor nothing; trust the registry
explain: Lockfiles freeze the entire resolved dependency tree so builds are reproducible regardless of upstream releases. 'Latest' invites exactly this breakage, rebuilding does not pin anything, and trust is not a control.

q: During an incident, critical logs are missing — the pipeline dropped them under burst load. Which design prevents log loss?
options: Log even more verbosely during incidents
Buffered ingestion with backpressure handling, sampling policies, and independently scaled pipeline capacity
Bigger disks on the log servers
Stop logging to reduce load
explain: Buffers with backpressure absorb bursts, sampling sheds load intelligently, and independent pipeline scaling keeps up. More verbosity worsens drops, disk size does not fix ingestion throughput, and stopping logging blinds the response.
